ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flexible KL-Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: 
Design an adaptive KL regularization term that approximates the marginal KL divergence as a weighted sum of the KL divergences along individual denoising steps of the diffusion process, then optimize the weightings using a small validation set. This approach aims to mitigate the need for full trajectory KL regularization as described in RSO and RAFT, while still leveraging some information about the conditional likelihoods.
CONTROLS:
- Baseline: KL-divergence of entire denoising trajectories
- Ablation: weightings are fixed and not optimized
- Comparison to KL-divergence with direct optimization of marginal likelihoods, if feasible
COST: 6412.3
PREDICTION: This method will improve over the full trajectory KL regularization baseline but underperform direct marginal likelihood optimization if feasible; potential failure is the lack of robustness to non-optimal weightings.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Flexible KL-Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: 
Modify the adaptive KL regularization term from Proposal 1 to incorporate a noise schedule that varies the weighting based on the noise level of the denoising step. This will help tailor the regularization to be more aggressive in areas of the noise space where the pre-trained distribution has less mass and the fine-tuned distribution is more uncertain. This refinement can be implemented using a piecewise noise schedule where different noise levels are optimally weighted separately. Additionally, train the model using a probabilistic distillation method [43] to further align the distributions of individual denoising steps.
CONTROLS:
- Baseline from Proposal 1: KL-divergence of entire denoising trajectories
- Comparison to Proposal 1 without either modification
- Ablation: without probabilistic distillation, to isolate its contribution
COST: 17280
PREDICTION: This modified approach should improve over both baselines, with probabilistic distillation further enhancing the quality of the fine-tuned model; potential failure is insufficient validation for the piecewise noise schedule.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-based Representation Alignment using Gromov-Wasserstein Distance
PROPOSAL: 
Propose a novel representation alignment method for pre-trained diffusion models, focusing on leveraging the hierarchical structure of flow models. This method will use the Gromov-Wasserstein distance to align the distributions of intermediate noisy states between the pre-trained and fine-tuned diffusion processes. This approach can mitigate the need for explicit rewards and directly correct errors in the pre-trained model by aligning their intermediate distributions.
CONTROLS:
- Baseline: standard KL-divergence alignment without using Gromov-Wasserstein distance
- Ablation: without considering the hierarchical structure of flow models
- Comparison to standard probabilistic distillation [43]
COST: 17280
PREDICTION: This method will improve over the baseline and show comparable results to probabilistic distillation; potential failure is the computational cost of computing Gromov-Wasserstein distance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multistep Sampling and KL Regularization using Conditional Importance Sampling
PROPOSAL: 
Propose an efficient strategy for computing an unbiased estimate of the marginal KL-divergence for KL-regularized reward maximization. This will use conditional importance sampling to estimate the marginal likelihoods of the pre-trained and fine-tuned diffusion processes, respectively. This approach will enable an efficient, direct estimation of the marginal KL-divergence without requiring full trajectory KL regularization or approximations.
CONTROLS:
- Baseline: full trajectory KL regularization using KDE
- Comparison to kgf SN and median trick SO (refine urls https://web5.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/user/jinthi/www/06!kgf-slides!jaw.t (Redirected).html , http://students.mimuw.edu.pl/~jstsz/2009.pdf )
- Ablation: without using conditional importance sampling
COST: 34560
PREDICTION: This method will improve over the baseline and show comparable results to more involved approaches; potential failure is the difficulty in choosing an optimal importance sampling proposal distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-tuning of Diffusion Models for Text-to-Image Generation using Reward Shaping
PROPOSAL: 
Apply the techniques from Proposals 1, 2, and 3 to a text-to-image generation task, focusing on fine-tuning the pre-trained Diffusion Model using a reward function that evaluates the similarity between generated images and the target images. This will involve reward shaping to guide the learning process and using the multistep sampling technique from Proposal 3 for efficient KL regularization. Additionally, flow-based representation alignment will be used to align the distributions of intermediate noisy states between the pre-trained and fine-tuned diffusion processes.
CONTROLS:
- Baseline: Diffusion Model fine-tuning without reward shaping and KL regularization
- Comparison to using standard KL-divergence alignment
- Ablation: without flow-based representation alignment
COST: 51840
PREDICTION: This method will show a significant improvement over the baseline and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed techniques in text-to-image generation; potential failure is the difficulty in finding an optimal reward function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trajectory KL Constraint for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment the trajectory KL method with different types of diffusion models (DDPM, DDIM, Improved-DDIM) on three real-world datasets (e.g. CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedrooms) using four evaluation metrics (PSNR, SSIM, Inception Score, FID Score). textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Invertible KL Regularization for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL:  Experiment to develop and evaluate Invertible KL Regularization (IKLR), a novel KL regularization technique which directly computes the marginal KL divergence required for theory. IKLR builds upon recent advances in normalizing flows by parametrizing a specific invertible neural network (NN) that learns a mapping between the pre-trained diffusion model's samples and the fine-tuned model's samples. This invertible NN is trained to minimize the KL divergence, enabling direct marginal KL regularization without relying on trajectory KL relaxations. We expect IKLR to address the efficiency and stability issues of existing approaches.
CONTROLS: We will compare IKLR to the state-of-the-art KL regularization method (trajectory KL) and the baseline of ignoring the KL term. Additionally, we will ablate the invertible NN by removing it, to demonstrate the necessity of its presence.
COST: 8295
PREDICTION: Expected result: IKLR outperforms both the baseline and the trajectory KL method by a considerable margin, and the ablated IKLR shows a noticeable degradation in performance, highlighting the importance of the invertible NN. Potential failure: The development of IKLR might be computationally demanding, and the invertible NN might not always be invertible, potentially leading to optimization issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Flow-based KL Regularization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate whether a flow-based approach can effectively provide a tractable lower bound to the marginal KL regularization. Specifically, we will use a Normalizing Flow (NF) to model the pre-trained diffusion model's distribution directly. Then, when fine-tuning, we will maximize the reward while minimizing the NF-based KL divergence with the pre-trained model's distribution. This approach leverages the strengths of both diffusion and flow-based models.
CONTROLS: We will compare the flow-based KL regularization to IKLR, the trajectory KL method, and the baseline of ignoring the KL term. Additionally, we will also compare the NF-based KL to a vanilla KL between the embedded distributions.
COST: 11692
PREDICTION: Expected result: The flow-based KL regularization shows competitive performance with IKLR and outperforms the baseline and trajectory KL method. Potential failure: The NF might struggle to model the complex distributions of the diffusion models, leading to subpar performance and high variance.

TITLE: Sample-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models via Variational Inference
PROPOSAL: Theoretical result: We propose a novel framework for fine-tuning diffusion models via variational inference. We show that, under mild assumptions, the optimal fine-tuned distribution can be obtained by minimizing the KL divergence between the variational distribution and the reference distribution. This framework leverages the structure of the diffusion model and provides a sample-efficient approach to fine-tuning. The key idea is to use a variational distribution that captures the changes in the reference distribution caused by the reward function.
CONTROLS: None, as this is a theoretical result. We will provide a detailed proof and discuss the implications of this result.
COST: 133.2
PREDICTION: Expected result: The variational inference framework provides a sample-efficient way to fine-tune diffusion models and can be used to derive new algorithms for fine-tuning diffusion models. Potential failure: The assumptions required for this result might not hold in all cases, potentially limiting the applicability of this framework.

TITLE: Invertible KL Regularization for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL:  Experiment to develop and evaluate Invertible KL Regularization (IKLR), a novel KL regularization technique which directly computes the marginal KL divergence required for theory. IKLR builds upon recent advances in normalizing flows by parametrizing a specific invertible neural network (NN) that learns a mapping between the pre-trained diffusion model's samples and the fine-tuned model's samples. This invertible NN is trained to minimize the KL divergence, enabling direct marginal KL regularization without relying on trajectory KL relaxations. We expect IKLR to address the efficiency and stability issues of existing approaches.
CONTROLS: We will compare IKLR to the state-of-the-art KL regularization method (trajectory KL) and the baseline of ignoring the KL term. Additionally, we will ablate the invertible NN by removing it, to demonstrate the necessity of its presence.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Expected result: IKLR outperforms both the baseline and the trajectory KL method by a considerable margin, and the ablated IKLR shows a noticeable degradation in performance, highlighting the importance of the invertible NN. Potential failure: The development of IKLR might be computationally demanding, and the invertible NN might not always be invertible, potentially leading to optimization issues.

TITLE: Improved KL Regularization for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models Using Trajectory Resampling
PROPOSAL: This experiment revisits the KL regularization term in fine-tuning diffusion models by repeatedly sampling the denoising trajectories from the pre-trained model using importance sampling, which yields unbiased estimates of the marginal KL divergence. We will compare this approach with existing relaxations (e.g., trajectory KL constraint) and ablate the importance sampling schedule.
CONTROLS: Our baseline control is the existing approach of using the trajectory KL constraint, and our ablations will include: (1) no importance sampling (trajectory KL constraint only), (2) using a fixed importance sampling schedule, and (3) applying the pseudo-marginal theorem to estimate the KL divergence.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: By using trajectory resampling, we expect to consistently outperform the baseline control on text-to-image generation and document layout generation tasks, with reduced variance and faster convergence. However, for molecule generation, the problem's brittleness may lead to increased variability and potential decreased performance.

PROPOSAL: We propose a new fine-tuning method for diffusion models called Flow GSM (Generative State Manipulation), which leverages the structural properties of flow models and integrates prior knowledge from the pre-trained model using a Gaussianizing layer. This layer can be used to steer the sampling distribution towards the desired outcome by modifying the prior's noise distribution. For example, for text-to-image generation, we can pre-train a model that produces noise with similar statistics to the target image noise and then fine-tune the model with Flow GSM to incorporate the desired image features.

TITLE: Revisiting the Pseudo-Marginal Theorem for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We revise the proposal 1 "Improved KL Regularization for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models Using Trajectory Resampling" by revisiting the pseudo-marginal theorem. Instead of relying on importance sampling to estimate the KL divergence, we will develop a novel algorithm that uses a combination of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and particle filtering to efficiently estimate the marginal KL divergence. This approach should provide a more accurate and reliable estimate of the KL divergence.
CONTROLS: Our baseline control is the original importance sampling approach, and we will also ablate the use of MCMC and particle filtering to understand their contributions.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect that the revised approach will improve the stability and accuracy of fine-tuning diffusion models, particularly in settings where the KL divergence is estimated inaccurately. However, it may come at the cost of increased computational complexity.

TITLE: Reward-Inspired Choice Sampling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel fine-tuning method that uses reward-inspired choice sampling to select high-reward samples from the pre-trained model. The method combines the strengths of rejection sampling and exploratory wrapper methods. By adaptively adjusting the proportion of high-reward samples included in the update, the method actively seeks promising high-quality samples. This should allow targeted improvement in fine-tuned diffusion models, making them better suited for complex downstream applications.
CONTROLS: Our baseline control is the vanilla fine-tuning method, and we will also compare our method to others that use rejection sampling, explore-based and exploitation methods across 3 heterogeneous downstream applications: text-to-image, document layout, and molecule generation.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel fine-tuning method that uses contrastive learning to correct the errors of a pre-trained diffusion model without any explicit reward signals. This should allow for targeted improvement in the fine-tuned model without requiring any additional supervision or reward signals.

TITLE: Informative Prior KL Control for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to fine-tune a pre-trained diffusion model with a KL-regularized objective that uses an informative prior KL control. The prior is the learned pre-trained model's distribution conditioned on the input, rather than the unconditional distribution alone, to better match the trajectory likelihoods used in the regularization. We will test this approach on the Imagenette dataset for text-to-image generation, using the DALL-E model as the pre-trained diffusion model and a specific task-agnostic reward function.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a baseline with unconditional prior KL regularization, and to an ablation with no regularization at all, as well as to the state-of-the-art methods RSO, RAFT, and Reinforce-Rej for autoregressive models.
COST: 534.75185
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to significantly outperform the unconditional prior baseline, achieving better sample quality and stability at fine-tuning, but note that the true test will be whether our KL control outperforms RSO, RAFT, and Reinforce-Rej in adapting to the task, a harder task. If the informative prior KL control improves fine-tuning in this way but fails to match or surpass the state-of-the-art methods for autoregressive models, this could suggest important differences in fine-tuning optimization between diffusion models and autoregressive models.

TITLE: Conditioning Noise on Task-Agnostic Features for Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to fine-tune diffusion models by conditioning the noise on task-agnostic features, such as log-frequency spectrum features, rather than relying solely on the input data. We hypothesize that incorporating global features of the input will improve the diffusion model's adaptation to the task, by capturing the commonalities between samples in different classes. We will evaluate this on document layout generation, using the pre-trained model DDPM and a dataset of document layout images.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a baseline without noise conditioning, and to a baseline that conditions on task-specific features derived from the input data, as well as to ablations that use a reduced set of log-frequency spectrum features.
COST: 1674.76
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvement in fine-tuning performance through conditioning the noise on task-agnostic features, which would help to fill the gap in adaptation to the task even when KL regularization is intractable. However, the true challenge is whether this improvement generalizes to task-specific features, or can be effectively combined with informative prior KL control, which could prove limited when the preconditioning cannot separate well from task-specific patterns: if the results don't translate to difficult tasks like molecule generation, it might indicate overfitting to noise features.

PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to apply Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) to the weight update process of diffusion models during fine-tuning. We will test whether EWC can improve the fine-tuning performance of pre-trained diffusion models, by incorporating it into theweight update process. We will evaluate this on text-to-image generation, using the pre-trained model DALL-E and the Imagenette dataset.

PROPOSAL: We refine the previous proposal by introducing a media subspace transformation for diffusion model refinement that focuses on capturing essential features of the task at hand. Specifically, we propose to utilize a learned transformation matrix that sends samples in the media space to the vicinity of task-agnostic features learned from pre-training. This allows us to refine the model's representations in a way that is both task-agnostic and task-specific. We will evaluate this approach on molecule generation tasks, leveraging the pre-trained model RDMM and a dataset of chemical structures.

TITLE: Optimal Sampling Strategies for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to investigate the impact of different sampling strategies on the fine-tuning performance of diffusion models. Specifically, we will study the effects of sampling with respect to different metrics, such as KL divergence, log likelihood, and rough Helmwic objective das principles, on the adaptation of pre-trained diffusion models to downstream tasks. We will evaluate this on document layout generation, using the pre-trained model DDPM and a dataset of document layout images.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a baseline without any sampling strategy, as well as to ablations with different sampling strategies (e.g., random sampling, importance sampling).
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We predict that optimal sampling strategies will lead to significant improvements in fine-tuning performance, particularly when combined with other techniques such as informative prior KL control and media subspace transformations, potentially allowing for more efficient adaptation to downstream tasks.

TITLE: Elastic Weight Consolidation for Diffusion Model Weight Update
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment to apply Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) to the weight update process of diffusion models during fine-tuning. EWC is a technique designed to preserve the knowledge in the frozen weights of a pre-trained model while adapting to new tasks. We will test whether EWC can improve the fine-tuning performance of pre-trained diffusion models, by incorporating it into theweight update process. We will evaluate this on text-to-image generation, using the pre-trained model DALL-E and the Imagenette dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a baseline without EWC, as well as to an ablation with a fixed learning rate.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We predict that EWC will lead to improved fine-tuning performance, by effectively preserving the knowledge in the pre-trained model's weights and adapting it to the new task, but we also note that the effectiveness of EWC may depend on the specific characteristics of the pre-trained model and the fine-tuning task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continuous Activation Steering through Layer-Specific Normalization
PROPOSAL: We will modify existing activation steering methods to perform the edit in the space of layer-specific activation magnitudes instead of the raw activations. Then we will add a learnable, activation-dependent control parameter that takes into consideration the relative magnitude of the feature direction vector in each layer to facilitate continuous control over the target behavior. We will explore its effectiveness on refusal of harmful requests and emotion control of generated text across various LLM sizes and models.
CONTROLS: We compare our proposed method against existing activation addition and ablation methods, using directional projection as a baseline control without the learnable parameter.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to provide better control and less brittleness, with a slight drop in fluency when the control parameter reaches the full suppression or inversion threshold, as the model starts to engage in inaccurate or unnatural behavior due to the reduced magnitude.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Alternating Between Activation Addition and Ablation for Improved Control
PROPOSAL: We will investigate if alternating between activation addition and ablation (dynamically switching between the two) according to a learned or fixed schedule, in addition to our continuous control parameter, can improve granularity and reduce brittleness in the model's behavior. This technique will allow the model to (temporarily) escape the 'dead zone' around the full suppression or inversion threshold where it may start to produce inaccurate responses. We will explore this strategy in conjunction with the layer-specific normalization method from experiment 1.
CONTROLS: We will compare our alternating method against the single edit approach from experiment 1, and also include a control using only activation addition with a constant coefficient, effective for some cases but more prone to brittleness.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect our alternating approach to significantly reduce brittleness and improve control, allowing the model to mitigate losses in fluency and accuracy when traversing the behavioral landscape. However, it may require careful tuning of the scheduling or transition criteria, and may not be universally applicable.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Alternating Between Activation Addition and Ablation for Improved Control with Diagnostics
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous proposal to include an additional innovation: in the context of attention over input sequences, we seek to dynamically adjust the soft attention weights associated with tokens in the input sequence that are diagnostic indicators of the target behavior (e.g., keywords related to refusal). This attention biasing will effectively guide the model's focus when attempting to steer its behavior, and could provide additional means to exploit orthogonal feature directions or strengthens weak activation cues.
CONTROLS: We retain the same set of controls from our previous version, including comparisons to the single edit approach, constant-coefficient activation addition, and also include a baseline with standard attention mechanisms unaffected by our steering method.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: Our method should show improved effectiveness in the complex and ambiguous real-world settings where suboptimal activation cues are plentiful and driving individual attention weights is cost-effective. However, in simple synthetic settings where all relevant information can be easily integrated, there might be a limited additive effect on model steering due to the extra computational expense and computational difficulty involved.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Debiasing Activation Normalization
PROPOSAL: We investigate whether integrating a bias term into the activation normalization process can help improve the effectiveness and robustness of our steering methods, particularly in situations where the target behavior is liable to be negatively impacted by the model's natural emphasis on the activation magnitude. We will explore the impact of adding position and layer embedding projections as bias terms in the activation normalization layers, and compare our results with the corresponding methods from the two previous experiments.
CONTROLS: We compare our debiased methods to the standard RMS normalization used in the baseline, as well as the layer-specific normalization with and without diagnostics provided by the attention biasing in the second experiment.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating debiasing terms could improve control and safety in cases where target behaviors are delicate or negatively impacted by current normalisation practices. Though, they may incur small explosions in gradients for the related edge cases and components fitting disconnected parts of layers.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a Distillation Objective for Behavior Control
PROPOSAL: We propose learning a novel distillation objective that encourages the model to maintain its original behavior (and subsequently the target behavior we induce) on the internal activations, rather than just the final output. This will allow our steering methods to achieve fine-grained and transferable control across different tasks and scenarios, rather than just one-off fluency-enhancing manipulations. The distillation objective will be comprised of a regularizer term that encourages such behavior preservation.
CONTROLS: We compare our distillation-based approach to the standard fine-tuning objective used in the baseline, as well as our steering methods placed in isolation without the distillation mechanism. The same layer-specific normalization, alternating addition/ablation with diagnostics, and debiased activation normalization tools will be integrated in order to compare at different levels and approaches of indiction and support against threats.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect that our distillation objective should lead to improved, more adaptive behavior control, but could potentially lead to unstable training dynamics or competing objectives with other task-specific or high-impact regularizers.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED: Debiasing Activation Normalization
PROPOSAL: We extend the idea of incorporating bias terms into activation normalization by learning a conditional neural bias term that is predictive of each activation's contribution to the behavior of interest. We hypothesize that such a bias term can boost the steerability of our methods, allowing us to control the model's behavior more effectively in complex scenarios.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised debiased method to the standard RMS normalization used in the baseline, as well as the layer-specific normalization and the alternating addition/ablation with diagnostics from the first two experiments, which will help evaluate the effectiveness of our conditional bias term and learn if bias capture with constant-training parameters implies relevant iterative derivative information.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Our learning-based debiasing approach should allow us to better control the model's behavior, especially when multiple factors complicate the scenario, without impacting other tasks - and negative prompts should see notable alignment towards rejection with fewer or no alerts of danger compared to unaligned steer-based encouragement instructions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments on Early Stopping to Mitigate Overfitting
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of early stopping mechanisms during training to mitigate overfitting, particularly in scenarios where the model's behavior is sensitive to fine-grained adjustments. We will implement and compare different early stopping criteria, such as monitoring changes in fluency, task performance, or specific behavior metrics. We also consider the use of ensembles to combine multiple early stopping criteria for improved performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: We will compare our early stopping method against the standard training procedure used in the baseline, as well as some of our steering methods from previous experiments to see if early stopping can improve the behavior control and safety in scenarios involving steering for performance preservation. Baseline reserves resource use dynamically.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect that implementing early stopping will help to prevent overfitting of our steering methods in challenging scenarios and improve their practicality, however careful tuning of the stopping criteria might be required, and some performance might be sacrificed especially if improperly adapted on present usage.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Behaviorally Agnostic Local Perturbation Analysis
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel analysis technique, locally perturbing the activations near the feature directions corresponding to the target behavior, and analyzing the resulting behavior changes. This will allow us to gain deeper insights into how our steering methods affect the model's behavior, both globally (in terms of the mean behavior) and locally (in terms of the behavior near specific feature directions). We will develop a statistical framework to quantify the effects of such perturbations and identify any potential vulnerabilities or bottlenecks in our steering methods.
CONTROLS: We will analyze the behavior changes caused by local perturbations around the target behavior in both our steering methods and the baseline model. We will also compare our locally perturbation-based analysis to other analysis techniques, such as gradient-based analysis or input-based analysis, to identify its strengths and limitations.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Our perturbation analysis should provide valuable insights into the behavior control mechanisms and the potential interactions between them. Additionally, we may identify new vulnerabilities or areas of improvement in our steering methods, allowing us to refine and generalize them more effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Activation Steering Performance on Refusal of Harmful Requests
PROPOSAL: We experimentally evaluate the performance of activation addition and directional ablation on a set of benchmarks evaluating the refusal of harmful requests (jailbreaking) in language models. The experiments compare these two popular primitives with a simple baseline that applies no steering. We evaluate the performance using the accuracy of refusal, the fluency of generated responses, and the coherence of text output.

However, both methods will struggle to balance refusal and fluency, leading to potential trade-offs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Activation Steering Performance on Refusal of Harmful Requests
PROPOSAL: We experimentally evaluate the performance of activation addition and directional ablation on a set of benchmarks evaluating the refusal of harmful requests (jailbreaking) in language models. The experiments compare these two popular primitives with a simple baseline that applies no steering. We evaluate the performance using the accuracy of refusal, the fluency of generated responses, and the coherence of text output.
CONTROLS: Baselines: no steering, addition with optimal coefficients, ablation with pre-normalized activations.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect activation addition to significantly improve refusal accuracy and fluency, while ablation will remove the feature entirely, leaving some room for refusal but decreasing fluency. However, both methods will struggle to balance refusal and fluency, leading to potential trade-offs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: We theoretically and experimentally investigate how RMS normalization affects the behavior of activation addition and directional ablation. Specifically, we will derive a framework that characterizes how each primitive behaves in the presence of RMS normalization and analyze its implications for controlling model behavior. We will also experimentally validate this framework using the same benchmarks as proposal 1 and evaluate the performance of these primitives after applying RMS normalization.
CONTROLS: Ablations: removing RMS normalization, evaluating addition and ablation under pre-normalization, simulating variation of activation norms within real layers.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Our results are expected to reveal how RMS normalization interacts with activation steering, potentially clarifying the role of this normalization in model behavior control and identifying areas where new research is needed to overcome its limitations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating the Effect of RMS Normalization on Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: To better understand the interaction between RMS normalization and activation steering, we revise proposal 2 to focus on analyzing the normalization effect in the contrastive examples used to estimate feature directions. Specifically, we will investigate the impact of normalization on the ability to distinguish desired and undesired behaviors, which is crucial for the accurate estimation of feature directions. We will also explore using different normalization techniques or strategies to improve the robustness of our steering methods.
CONTROLS: Evaluating the effectiveness of various normalization techniques (e.g., layer-specific normalizations, batch normalization) and contrastive learning methods on our benchmarks.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: Our results should provide insights into the impact of RMS normalization on the estimation of feature directions and shed light on potential strategies to improve the robustness of contrastive learning. This can positively impact activation steering performance, enabling more accurate control over model behavior.

Specifically, we will use a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to learn a steering primitive that can generate a wide range of control signals, from simple to complex, and evaluate the performance of this primitive on benchmarks for refusal of harmful requests and emotion control of generated text. We will compare the performance of our new primitive to existing steering primitives and baselines.

TITLE: Bootstrap Federated Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Models
PROPOSAL: This proposal involves the development of a novel federated multi-task learning approach that utilizes a self-training paradigm to enable heterogeneous models to collaboratively learn a shared representation space. Specifically, each user's model will generate pseudo-labels on a synthetic dataset created based on its task-specific local data, and then all the users' models will be trained together on the distilled knowledge transferred from the synthetic datasets to the shared representation space.
CONTROLS: Federated local fine-tuning of pre-trained models, and federated distillation of knowledge among users with homogeneous architectures
COST: 11692
PREDICTION: The bootstrapped representation would be more robust and adaptable to a diverse set of tasks and model architectures, but heterogeneous models with different capacities may not synergize effectively and model characteristics might be hindered by vast task divergence.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Federated Multi-Task Learning Baseline with Decoupled Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We will replicate and extend the knowledge-distillation-based method by Xu et al. (2020) to the multi-task federated learning setting. We replace the global model with a server, which maintains the entire task space and correspondingly separates the knowledge distillation process for each task. Each user sends their local model outputs on their task-specific dataset to the server, which aggregates the information. The server trains a pseudo global model representing the shared knowledge among all users by knowledge distillation, with a communication protocol that limits the exchange of raw local model outputs. Then, the server computes outputs on unlabeled public data from previous baselines used as an intermediate step, which minds the privacy.
CONTROLS: We will use the baseline Federated Multi-Task Learning (FMTRL) algorithm, which assumes model congruity, and compare our results against it. We also provide a comprehensive ablation study to investigate the contribution of our decoupled knowledge distillation approach.
COST: 333.8623
PREDICTION: Our method achieves significantly better performance compared to FMTRL, especially when users have diverse tasks and architectures. However, the method may suffer from knowledge drift when users having different fine-tuned foundation models upload their current uploaded weights as pseudo-labels to the server, so there might be a performance degradation due to this issue.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Model Heterogeneity with Heterogeneous Multi-Layer Perceptron (HMLP)
PROPOSAL: To better understand the challenges posed by model heterogeneity in federated multi-task learning, we extend the well-known Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) model and propose the Heterogeneous Multi-Layer Perceptron (HMLP) model, which allows each user to choose a different number of hidden layers and units within those layers.
CONTROLS: We will investigate the impact of HMLP on the performance of existing federated multi-task methods, particularly for tasks with varying complexities. We will compare our results with a baseline MLP using the two models to adapt to the same task and with other HMLPs for use with a range of complex tasks.
COST: 670
PREDICTION: The HMLP significantly improves the robustness of federated multi-task learning methods in the presence of model heterogeneity. However, scaling HMLP to a large number of users and a diverse range of tasks may require more computational resources, leading to potential communication bottlenecks.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED Gramian-Based Contrastive Learning for Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We apply the Gramian-based contrastive loss to the multi-task federated setting, allowing for simultaneous alignment of representations across multiple models. To address the computational complexity and potential numerical instability of the original Gramian-based contrastive loss, we propose an efficient analytic approximation using the Taylor series expansion. This approximation maintains the theoretical validity of the original loss while significantly reducing the computational cost. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying hyperparameters, such as the number of gradient descent iterations and the learning rate, on the convergence of the Gramian-based contrastive loss.
CONTROLS: The original Gramian-based contrastive loss with varying hyperparameters and an ablation study to investigate the benefits of the proposed approximation.
COST: 670
PREDICTION: Our approach yields competitive or better performance than the original Gramian-based contrastive loss on various federated learning benchmarks, while achieving a substantial reduction in computation time and memory requirements. However, it might still be prone to instability in cases where the number of models or the size of the datasets is extremely large.

PREDICTION: Our framework improves the classification accuracy of federated multi-task learning methods and offers insights into the relationships between tasks, which could be useful for designing more effective task assignments. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Federated Multi-Task Learning Baseline with Decoupled Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We will replicate and extend the knowledge-distillation-based method by Xu et al. (2020) to the multi-task federated learning setting. We replace the global model with a server, which maintains the entire task space and correspondingly separates the knowledge distillation process for each task. Each user sends their local model outputs on their task-specific dataset to the server, which aggregates the information. The server trains a pseudo global model representing the shared knowledge among all users by knowledge distillation, with a communication protocol that limits the exchange of raw local model outputs. Then, the server computes outputs on unlabeled public data from previous baselines used as an intermediate step, which minds the privacy.
CONTROLS: We will use the baseline Federated Multi-Task Learning (FMTRL) algorithm, which assumes model congruity, and compare our results against it. We also provide a comprehensive ablation study to investigate the contribution of our decoupled knowledge distillation approach.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our method achieves significantly better performance compared to FMTRL, especially when users have diverse tasks and architectures. However, the method may suffer from knowledge drift when users having different fine-tuned foundation models upload their current uploaded weights as pseudo-labels to the server, so there might be a performance degradation due to this issue.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: To better understand the challenges posed by model heterogeneity in federated multi-task learning, we extend the well-known Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) model and propose the Heterogeneous Multi-Layer Perceptron (HMLP) model, which allows each user to choose a different number of hidden layers and units within those layers.
CONTROLS: We will investigate the impact of HMLP on the performance of existing federated multi-task methods, particularly for tasks with varying complexities. We will compare our results with a baseline MLP using the two models to adapt to the same task and with other HMLPs for use with a range of complex tasks.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: The HMLP significantly improves the robustness of federated multi-task learning methods in the presence of model heterogeneity. However, scaling HMLP to a large number of users and a diverse range of tasks may require more computational resources, leading to potential communication bottlenecks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting Federated Multi-Task Learning with Adversarial Alignment
PROPOSAL: We design a new loss function that combines InfoNCE with an adversarial component. The adversarial component perturbs the representations of each model, forcing the InfoNCE loss to align these perturbed representations across models. We apply this loss on a shared dataset sampled from the users' local datasets. The intuition behind this approach is that the adversarial perturbations will encourage the models to learn task-agnostic, shared representations that are more robust to input variations.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the baseline federated multi-task learning methods assuming model congruity, as well as to methods that use Gramian-based contrastive loss but lack theoretical justification.
COST: 10500
PREDICTION: Our approach should be able to capture the dependencies among representations across multiple models and improve knowledge transfer, but it may require careful tuning of the adversarial component to prevent overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Projection-based Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method that uses a projection-based approach to align representations across multiple models. Specifically, each model projects its representations onto a shared latent space using a learned transformation matrix. We enforce a structure on the transformation matrices across models using a graph regularization term that encourages proximity among representations. Through this approach, we can effectively capture the dependencies among representations and learn task-agnostic information.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the baseline federated multi-task learning methods assuming model congruity, as well as to existing methods that rely on pairwise alignment (e.g. InfoNCE) or heuristic contrastive regularization.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform existing approaches in aligning representations across multiple models and achieve better knowledge transfer, but it may require careful initialization of the transformation matrices and learning rates to prevent overfitting.

TITLE: Augmenting Federated Multi-Task Learning with Adversarial Alignment
PROPOSAL: We design a new loss function that combines InfoNCE with an adversarial component. The adversarial component perturbs the representations of each model, forcing the InfoNCE loss to align these perturbed representations across models. We apply this loss on a shared dataset sampled from the users' local datasets. The intuition behind this approach is that the adversarial perturbations will encourage the models to learn task-agnostic, shared representations that are more robust to input variations.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the baseline federated multi-task learning methods assuming model congruity, as well as to methods that use Gramian-based contrastive loss but lack theoretical justification.
COST: 31500
PREDICTION: Our approach should be able to capture the dependencies among representations across multiple models and improve knowledge transfer, but it may require careful tuning of the adversarial component to prevent overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Projection-based Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method that uses a projection-based approach to align representations across multiple models. Specifically, each model projects its representations onto a shared latent space using a learned transformation matrix. We enforce a structure on the transformation matrices across models using a graph regularization term that encourages proximity among representations. Through this approach, we can effectively capture the dependencies among representations and learn task-agnostic information.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the baseline federated multi-task learning methods assuming model congruity, as well as to existing methods that rely on pairwise alignment (e.g. InfoNCE) or heuristic contrastive regularization.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform existing approaches in aligning representations across multiple models and achieve better knowledge transfer, but it may require careful initialization of the transformation matrices and learning rates to prevent overfitting.

TITLE: Federated Multi-Task Learning with Heterogeneous Models and Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the Federated Self-Supervised Learning (FSSL) algorithm, a federated meta-learning framework that adaptively selects the most informative representation for knowledge sharing. In FSSL, each user trains a meta-model that predicts the optimal local representations for their task given the global shared representations. The meta-model is then fine-tuned to minimize the difference between the optimal local representations and the actual local representations.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline method where the server chooses the global shared representations without user interaction, and an ablation study without the meta-learning component.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: FSSL significantly outperforms the baseline in terms of tasks' average accuracy on private data, but may fail to adapt when task distribution is highly skewed.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Representation Alignment through Federated Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Develop a Federated Knowledge Distillation (FKD) algorithm, where each user distills knowledge from the shared representations and transfers it to their local task-specific predictors through a teacher-student setup. The students (local models) learn to mimic the shared representations, which helps to align the local features with the global shared features.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline method without FKD, where each user transfers knowledge independently without alignment, and an ablation study without the knowledge distillation component.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: FKD improves the task-agnostic knowledge transfer and leads to higher average accuracy across users, but may face scalability issues with large numbers of users and tasks.

PROPOSAL: Develop a Federated Contrastive Learning (FCL) algorithm, which aims to align representations across all users in a multi-task setting. FCL extends the popular InfoNCE loss to a multi-task scenario, where the loss function encourages the shared representations to be consistent across all tasks and users, while pushing representation from different tasks and users apart.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline method where each user applies InfoNCE loss independently for each task, and an ablation study without the multi-task contrastive loss.

PREDICTION: FCL improves the alignment and generalizability of representation across tasks and users, but may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters to balance the trade-off between alignment and divergence.

TITLE: Evaluating Asymmetric Loss Functions for Robust Label Correction
PROPOSAL: We compare the effectiveness of several asymmetric loss functions that are designed to handle instance-dependent label noise, including the warped cross-entropy loss (WCE), the label smoothing loss (LSL), and the adaptive label correction loss (ALCL). We also investigate the impact of combining these loss functions with a standard cross-entropy loss in a hybrid framework. For experiments, we will use the CIFAR-10-C dataset, which introduces instance-dependent label noise, and employ the accuracy and mean squared error (MSE) metrics to evaluate the models' performance. PREDICTION: We expect the asymmetric loss functions to outperform the standard cross-entropy loss in models trained on the noisy data. However, we also anticipate potential degradations in performance on clean test data due to the risk of correct labels being corrupted, and the nasty possibility that there is a steadily decreasing effective number of clean samples &/or FS and offenders dominating >25%, incorporate error trajectories without unreliable stimuli.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Model-Based Label Correction Strategies
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of model-based uncertainty estimation techniques, we propose two strategies that leverage the predictive uncertainty of a clean model to identify and correct noisy labels. The first strategy, called Label Corrector (LC), adjusts the predictive distribution of the clean model to better match the observed label distribution in the noisy dataset. The second strategy, called Label Advisor (LA), uses the model's predicted uncertainty to adaptively select labels that are deemed most reliable. We evaluate these strategies on the CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C datasets and compare their performance to the state-of-the-art label correction methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed strategies against the standard label correction baselines (e.g., co-teaching,VoteNet) and explore the impact of using different levels of uncertainty quantification (e.g., confidence, entropy) on the performance of the strategies.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the model-based label correction strategies will demonstrate improved performance on noisy datasets, while also providing deeper insights into the relationship between model uncertainty and label noise. However, we also expect that the strategies may face challenges in selecting the most reliable labels, particularly in scenarios with severe label noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Learning with Model-Based Label Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: We propose a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages model-based label uncertainty to detect and adapt to noisy labels. The framework combines a teacher model trained on clean data with a student model that learns from noisy data with the help of label uncertainty estimates. We use the predictions from the teacher model to generate a set of candidate labels for each instance, and we then use the label uncertainty estimates to select the most confident labels for the student model to learn from. We evaluate this framework on the CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and Corrupted CIFAR-10 datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against the standard semi-supervised learning baselines (e.g., Mean Teacher, VAT), as well as the model-based label correction strategies proposed in this study.
COST: 1728
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our framework will demonstrate significant improvements over standard semi-supervised learning methods on noisy datasets, and we expect that the model-based label uncertainty estimates will provide a robust and adaptable way to handle noisy labels. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in selecting the optimal set of candidate labels and balancing the confidence of the teacher and student models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Graph-Based Label Correction Techniques
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph-based approach to label correction, where we represent each instance as a node in a graph, and connect nodes with edges based on their similarity in features and predictions. We then use a graph convolutional network (GCN) to propagate label corrections from confident instances to uncertain instances based on their graph connectivity. We evaluate this approach on the CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art label correction methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against the standard graph-based classification baselines (e.g., Graph Convolutional Network), as well as the model-based label correction strategies proposed in this study.
COST: 1261.44
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our graph-based approach will provide a more robust and explainable way to correct labels, by leveraging the structure of the instance similarity graph. However, we also expect that the computational cost of the GCN may be high, and that the method may face challenges in handling datasets with complex instance relationships.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Model-Based Label Correction Strategies
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous proposal to incorporate an attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most reliable labels when correcting noisy labels. We also investigate the impact of using a two-stage training procedure, where the model is first trained on a subset of clean labels, and then fine-tuned on the entire dataset with the attention mechanism activated. Additionally, we explore the effect of using different types of attention mechanisms (e.g., self-attention, attention with external knowledge) on the performance of the model-based label correction strategies.
CONTROLS: We keep the same controls as before, and add an ablation study to investigate the impact of each component on the performance of the attention-based model-based label correction strategies.
COST: 1431
PREDICTION: We expect the attention mechanism to further improve the performance of the model-based label correction strategies, by selectively focusing on the most reliable labels. However, we also anticipate potential challenges in tuning the hyperparameters of the attention mechanism, and inscaling up the two-stage training procedure to larger datasets.

TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Label Correction
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training framework that learns to correct noisy labels by adversarially attacking the model's predictions and forcing it to learn more robust features. We use a generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate adversarial examples that target the model's predictions, and then use the gradients of the loss function to update the model's weights and correct the noisy labels. We evaluate this framework on the CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art label correction methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against the standard adversarial training baselines (e.g., PGD, FGSM), as well as the model-based label correction strategies proposed in this study.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the adversarial training framework will provide a robust and effective way to correct noisy labels, by forcing the model to learn more robust features. However, we also expect that the GAN-based framework may be challenging to train and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

TITLE: Evaluating Local vs. Global Label Correction for Noisy Datasets
PROPOSAL: Design and conduct an experiment to compare two different label correction methods: a local approach that manipulates only the most confidence-affected noisy points, and a global approach that adjusts the label distribution for the entire noisy dataset. To do this, we'll select different noisy versions of popular benchmark datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, SVHN), generate noisy labels using class-conditional or instance-dependent noise models, and then apply both local and global correction methods. Local correction methods (e.g. Noise2Self, BADN) will utilize the confidence estimates of different models to isolate the corruption of individual predictions. Global correction methods will then leverage these corrected labels to reweight the classification loss according to the estimated probabilities of correct labels.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed correction methods to those that reweight samples based on their likelihood of being clean.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Local correction methods should provide more robust models for more types of noisy label distributions, but at the cost of increased computational complexity. However, their effectiveness may vary greatly depending on the distribution of the noise and other properties of the data, limiting their generalizability across different label noise scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the effects of different label noise types on deep neural network generalization
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 20% symmetric noise, 10% noisy labels in minority classes, and 20% random flip noises to understand the effect of different noise types on the generalization performance of deep neural networks. We train a baseline ResNet-18 model and four variants with different noise mitigation methods, such as label smoothing, mean teacher, peer-review, and noise-robust loss function. We use the standard classification accuracy and top-5 accuracy as evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: We compare our methods with a simple noise-tolerant baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without any additional regularization or mitigation techniques. We also ablate each method by training the model without the respective mitigation technique.
COST: 76.135
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the model trained without any noise mitigation techniques suffers from poor performance, particularly in the presence of instance-dependent noise. The peer-review method should show robustness against symmetric noise but struggle with minority class noise. The noise-robust loss function should provide a good trade-off between noise robustness and clean data performance. Note that our experiments might struggle with the random flip noise, due to its similarity to rotational and flip augmentations, and as such may only offer a minor distinction between classes.

TITLE: Exploring the effects of different label noise types on deep neural network generalization
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal by incorporating instance-dependent noise correction techniques into the baseline model. We train a baseline ResNet-18 model with a simple reweighting method that adjusts the loss function to downweight the instances with suspected noisy labels. We use the standard classification accuracy and top-5 accuracy as evaluation metrics, and compare the performance with the baseline model trained without instance-dependent noise correction.
CONTROLS: We compare the instance-dependent noise correction technique with the simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without any additional regularization or mitigation techniques. We also ablate the reweighting method by training the model without downweighting the suspected noisy instances.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: We expect the baseline model with instance-dependent noise correction to show improved performance on clean data, particularly in scenarios with high levels of instance-dependent noise. However, this may come at the cost of reduced performance on noisy data, and the method may still struggle with symmetric noise and random flip noise due to its simplicity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the efficacy of active learning on noisy labels
PROPOSAL: We design an active learning experiment where we iteratively select a subset of instances with high uncertainty or mismatch between the teacher and student models. We train a new neural network with the selected instances and update our model by combining the old and new model predictions. We use the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 20% symmetric noise and compare the performance of our active learning method with a random sampling baseline and a variant that uses a more complex uncertainty estimation model.
CONTROLS: We compare our active learning method with a simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without using active learning. We also ablate the active learning method by selecting instances using a random sampling strategy.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: We expect the active learning method to show improved performance by selectively focusing on the most informative instances with high uncertainty or mismatch. However, the method may suffer from overfitting to the initial set of selected instances, and its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the uncertainty estimation model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the trade-offs between label correction and sample selection
PROPOSAL: We compare and contrast different label correction methods (peer-review, instance-dependent reweighting) with sample selection methods (active learning, retraining) on the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. We analyze the trade-offs between label correction and sample selection in terms of clean data performance, noisy data performance, and the amount of data required for each method.
CONTROLS: We compare our methods with a simple baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without using any label correction or sample selection techniques. We also ablate the label correction and sample selection methods to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect to observe different trade-offs between label correction and sample selection methods, with some methods showing strong performance on clean data but poor performance on noisy data, while others show robust performance on noisy data but poor performance on clean data. The results will provide insights into the design of more effective noise-robust training methods that balance different trade-offs.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Investigating the trade-offs between label correction and sample selection
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal by incorporating a theoretical analysis of the trade-offs between label correction and sample selection. We derive analytical bounds on the generalization error of label correction and sample selection methods, and use these bounds to understand the trade-offs in terms of clean data performance and noisy data performance. We compare these analytical bounds with experimental results on the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare our analytical bounds with the experimental results from the previous proposal, and also ablate the label correction and sample selection methods to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect the analytical bounds to provide a useful perspective on the trade-offs between label correction and sample selection methods, and to help identify potential design strategies for more effective noise-robust training methods. However, the results may also highlight limitations of the analytical bounds, such as neglecting noise-dependent complexities of the neural network, and in some cases the approximations used may lead to over-optimistic estimates of performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a multiswarm evolutionary algorithm for learning from noisy labels
PROPOSAL: We propose a multiswarm evolutionary algorithm to learn from noisy labels, where each swarm is responsible for learning a distinct labeling hypothesis. We use a novel fitness function that combines the performance on both clean and noisy data, and use a competition mechanism between swarms to adapt to the noisy data distribution. We test our multiswarm evolutionary algorithm on the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our multiswarm evolutionary algorithm with a simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without using any label correction or sample selection techniques. We also ablate the multiswarm architecture to understand the individual contributions of each component.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: We expect the multiswarm evolutionary algorithm to show strong performance on both clean and noisy data, particularly in scenarios with high levels of instance-dependent noise. However, the algorithm may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and its computational cost may increase rapidly with the number of swarms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the robustness of learning from noisy labels in high-dimensional feature spaces
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of learning from noisy labels in high-dimensional feature spaces, where the data distribution is highly complex and the noise is more challenging to handle. We use a combination of dimensionality reduction techniques and robust optimization methods to learn from noisy labels on high-dimensional datasets such as ImageNet. We compare the performance of our methods with state-of-the-art methods, and analyze the trade-offs between robustness, accuracy, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We compare our methods with a simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without using any label correction or sample selection techniques. We also ablate the dimensionality reduction techniques and robust optimization methods to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: We expect the high-dimensional feature space to introduce additional challenges to learning from noisy labels, such as increased susceptibility to noise and difficulty in handling high-dimensional distributions. However, the results may also highlight opportunities for advancing robust learning methods that can effectively handle complex high-dimensional data distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a unified theory of learning from noisy labels: a single-probability framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a unified theory of learning from noisy labels by developing a single-probability framework that captures both instance-dependent and instance-independent noise. We derive a unifying expression for the expected risk of a learner with noisy labels, and provide a range of applications for this expression in studies of robust optimization, active learning, and sophisticated sample selection methods. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the performance of various methods for learning from noisy labels, and highlight connections between different optimization problems and the framework presented here.
CONTROLS: N/A
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: We expect the unifying framework to provide a fundamental understanding of the importance of noise in the data, enabling the development of practical algorithms that are universally applicable to different domains and noise patterns. The results will have significant implications for a wide range of disciplines, from deep learning to statistical decision theory, and will provide a funnel for the study of diverse questions involving learning from noisy data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the effects of different label noise types on deep neural network generalization
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 20% symmetric noise, 10% noisy labels in minority classes, and 20% random flip noises to understand the effect of different noise types on the generalization performance of deep neural networks. We train a baseline ResNet-18 model and four variants with different noise mitigation methods, such as label smoothing, mean teacher, peer-review, and noise-robust loss function. We use the standard classification accuracy and top-5 accuracy as evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: We compare our methods with a simple noise-tolerant baseline that trains the model with the noisy labels without any additional regularization or mitigation techniques. We also ablate each method by training the model without the respective mitigation technique.
COST: 230
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the model trained without any noise mitigation techniques suffers from poor performance, particularly in the presence of instance-dependent noise. The peer-review method should show robustness against symmetric noise but struggle with minority class noise. The noise-robust loss function should provide a good trade-off between noise robustness and clean data performance. Note that our experiments might struggle with the random flip noise, due to its similarity to rotational and flip augmentations, and as such may only offer a minor distinction between classes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the robustness of peer-review based label correction methods
PROPOSAL: We extend the previous experiment to investigate the robustness of the peer-review based label correction method. We train a deep neural network to mimic the prediction and uncertainty of a pre-trained teacher model on the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with 20% symmetric noise. We compare the robustness of the peer-review method with two variants: one with instance-specific weights for the teacher predictions and one with a robustness-enhanced loss function. We use the same evaluation metrics as before and add the robustness of the corrected labels as an additional metric.
CONTROLS: We compare our methods with the previous ablated baseline that trains the model without the peer-review mitigation technique, and we ablate the instance-specific weights and the robustness-enhanced loss function. We also compare with a simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the corrected labels without using the peer-review method.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: We expect the peer-review method to show improved robustness against symmetric noise and minority class noise, while struggling with random flip noise due to its similarity to rotational and flip augmentations. The variant with instance-specific weights should show better performance in minority class noise scenarios, while the robustness-enhanced loss function should provide a good trade-off between robustness and clean data performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Improving the robustness of peer-review based label correction methods through uncertainty estimation
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous proposal by adding an uncertainty estimation module to the peer-review method. We use ensembles of neural networks and dropout-based uncertainty estimation to generate uncertainty scores for the predictions on the noisy CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. We then adjust the weights of the teacher predictions based on these uncertainty scores. We compare the robustness of the revised peer-review method with the original peer-review method and the previous ablated baseline. We use the same evaluation metrics as before and add the robustness of the corrected labels as an additional metric.
CONTROLS: We keep the same ablations as before and compare with a simple retraining baseline that trains the model with the corrected labels without using the peer-review method. We also compare with a variant of the revised peer-review method that uses a more complex uncertainty estimation model.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: We expect the revised peer-review method to show improved robustness against symmetric noise and minority class noise, particularly when uncertainty estimation is used to adjust the weights of the teacher predictions. However, this may come at the cost of reduced performance on clean data, and the method may still struggle with random flip noise due to its similarity to rotational and flip augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Deep Label Correction with Noisy Labels
PROPOSAL: Train a baseline deep neural network on the CIFAR-10 dataset with introducing synthetic label noise (e.g., using the Pairwise Confidential Labeling framework), then evaluate its performance in comparison to a previously published label correction method, such as Co-teaching (Hendrycks & Liberia, 2018). The model will be trained with a supervised loss and without any label correction.
CONTROLS: Baseline model without label correction, and Co-teaching (Hendrycks & Liberia, 2018) as reference; ablation study to evaluate the impact of varying the noise levels and types on the robustness of the model.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: The baseline model will exhibit poor robustness to noisy labels, while Co-teaching will improve the robustness but might still struggle with more complex, instance-dependent noise; this will motivate the need for additional exploration of label correction techniques.

Note: Co-teaching (Hendrycks & Liberia, 2018) is a widely recognized label correction method that uses two models to identify and remove noisy labels together. The baseline model and comparison to Co-teaching will help assess the current state-of-the-art in label correction methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning for Noisy Label Correction with Uncertainty Sampling
PROPOSAL: Train a deep neural network on a subset of the Clothing1M dataset with synthetic label noise, then implement active learning with uncertainty sampling (Lewis et al., 1994) to select a subset of noisy samples to correct. Use the model's uncertainty estimates (e.g., predicted probabilities) to identify samples that require correction. Next, fine-tune the model using the corrected subset to assess improvement in robustness and performance on clean test data.
CONTROLS: Baseline model trained on the full noisy dataset without active learning; ablation study to evaluate the impact of varying the number of selected samples on the model's robustness; comparison to passive filtering techniques (e.g., Model-based Label Correction (Masumura et al., 2019)).
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: Active learning with uncertainty sampling will improve the robustness of the model by focusing correction efforts on the most uncertain samples, but the approach might struggle with instance-dependent noise and memory constraints for large datasets.

Note: Active learning (Lewis et al., 1994) is a paradigm that selects a subset of the most informative samples to label and incorporate into training to improve model performance, reducing the overall labeling effort requirements. This proposal will test active learning for noisy label correction to explore its potential benefits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Iterative Semisupervised Learning for Instance-Dependent Noise Reduction
PROPOSAL: Train a deep neural network on a subset of the Clothing1M dataset with instance-dependent label noise, then iterate between three stages: (a) training a classifier to obtain pseudo-labels for unlabelled samples, (b) training a denoiser to predict the true labels of noisy samples, and (c) retraining the classifier on the corrected dataset. Assess improvement in robustness and performance on clean test data.
CONTROLS: Baseline model trained on the full noisy dataset without iterative semisupervised learning; ablation study to evaluate the impact of varying the number of iterations on the model's robustness; comparison to noise-robust training objectives (e.g., Mean Absolute Error (MAE)).
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: This iterative approach will help reduce instance-dependent noise by denoising noisy samples and refining the classifier's pseudolabels for unlabeled samples, but it may require significant iterations to converge and achieve optimal results.

Note: This approach combines elements of semi-supervised learning and active learning, exploring using the classifier's output to correct noisy samples. The selected iterative semisupervised learning framework will be tested to assess its capacity to alleviate instance-dependent noise.
