PROPOSAL: Introduce a Bayesian neural network reward model (BNN-RM) as a probabilistic extension of discriminative models. Train a neural network with a probabilistic output that represents the response's quality as a Gaussian distribution, capturing both the mean performance (a calibrated score) and uncertainty (as variance). The BNN-RM is optimized using Bayesian learning and a specific objective that encourages calibrated scores and controlled variance. Compare BNN-RM against state-of-the-art discriminative models (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) and assess its performance in selecting high-quality responses, expressed through the AUC-PR metric on datasets for chatbot response quality evaluation and LLM reward modeling for RLHF alignment.
CONTROLS: Compare against Skywork-Reward and InternLM2-Reward in a controlled Best-of-N setup with variable N to demonstrate adaptability. Evaluate the impact of adding quality labels with 30%, 50%, and 70% coverage on the BNN-RM's performance to quantify its amortization of high-quality supervision.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: BNN-RM outperforms discriminative models in selecting high-quality responses, especially when quality labels are partially available. BNN-RM will provide interpretable and calibrated scores with an approximation of response uncertainty, a key advantage over traditional discriminative models. Its performance may be best in best-of-n scenarios for low-N values.

TITLE: Characterizing Ground Truth Preferences for Efficient Reward Model Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate various annotated datasets with known ground truth preference structures, such as preference pairs, global prefs, and attitude scales, to understand their impact on training and evaluation of discriminative and generative reward models. We will use datasets like Importance-MarkingData, Bentham-Rewards, and SK-WT to analyze responsiveness, calibration, and robustness of reward models under different preference representations.

PREDICTION: Reward models trained on datasets with richer preference information will achieve better calibration and robustness, especially when handling uncertainty, but models may struggle to generalize across different preference structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Probabilistic Reward Models with Hierarchical Attitude Cues
PROPOSAL: Design a probabilistic reward model that integrates hierarchical attitude cues (HACs) learned from preference hierarchies to estimate absolute quality scores and capture the uncertainty in human preference judgments. We propose a novel probabilistic neural network incorporating the hierarchical cues in a Bayesian framework, enabling predictions of probabilistic quality scores.
CONTROLS: Compare our proposed model with existing discriminative and generative reward models, including the emphasis on quantile-based models like quantile-REL and bayesian variants such as Bayesian-LightSystem on a set of HAC-based synthetic and real-world preference datasets including human-generated-shift, benchmark-perception-CTL, and CEW Matrix Dyn preference pairs.
COST: 550 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model will outperform existing ranking-based reward models in capturing absolute response quality with calibrated uncertainty estimates, but may struggle with computational efficiency in large-scale settings due to its probabilistic nature.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: RAGNorm: Normalizing External and Internal Utilization Signals
PROPOSAL: We propose RAGNorm, a novel method for quantifying an LLM's utilization of external context and internal knowledge during generation. RAGNorm operates by introducing two normalization terms to the output embedding of each token in the LLM's output sequence: a normalization term for external context utilization (NCUE) and a normalization term for internal knowledge utilization (NCKI). These normalization terms are computed as the coefficient of variation of the cosine similarity between the token embedding and a query-wise aggregate of the retrieved document embeddings, and the coefficient of variation of the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the token embedding and the aggregate hidden state representations, respectively. Then, the internal and external context utilization signals are computed as the squared magnitude of the normalized token embedding. Finally, we use these signals to detect hallucinations by thresholding their ratio.
CONTROLS: We compare RAGNorm with ReDeEP, the previous state-of-the-art method, on the following benchmarks: RAG-Duo, BoolQ, NewsSum, and DROP, and evaluate its performance using the [F1-score, Accuracy, and Precision] metrics.
COST: 300000
PREDICTION: We expect RAGNorm to outperform ReDeEP on most of the evaluation metrics due to its independence from model-specific hyperparameters and data-driven normalization terms, whereas ReDeEP relies heavily on hand-tuned heuristics. However, RAGNorm may struggle when the quality of the retrieved documents is poor or the query is too broad, potentially leading to inaccurate or noisy normalization terms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-based Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph-based approach, coined GraphHD, to detect hallucinations in RAG systems. The approach represents the input query, the retrieved documents, and the generated response as a graph, where vertices correspond to tokens and edges represent attention weights between tokens. By leveraging the structural properties of this graph, GraphHD computes features such as the strength of the weak consensus between the query and the documents, the centrality of the response tokens, and the density of attention weights. These features are then used to train a few-shot learning classifier, which detects hallucinations based on the presence of 'anomalous' tokens that are strongly connected to the query but have weak connections to the context. We validate GraphHD on the same benchmarks used to evaluate RAGNorm (RAG-Duo, BoolQ, NewsSum, and DROP) and compare its performance against ReDeEP and RAGNorm.
CONTROLS: We conduct a comprehensive ablation study on GraphHD by varying the graph construction heuristics, vertex and edge representations, and the classifier architectures.
COST: 450000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that GraphHD will demonstrate competitive performance with RAGNorm and outperform ReDeEP, particularly on the NewsSum and DROP benchmarks, due to its ability to capture complex relationships between the query and the context. However, the success of GraphHD might heavily depend on the quality of the graph construction heuristics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data-driven Contextual Attention for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to contextualize attention weights for hallucination detection by learning a task-specific attention model. The approach relies on a simple, task-agnostic neural network architecture that predicts attention weights conditioned on a token's position, the corresponding retrieved document's representation, and the query's representation. We formulate this as a multi-task learning problem, where we jointly train on the hallucination detection task and a downstream task that requires accurate context utilization (e.g., extractive summarization). By leveraging the learned attention weights and a confusion matrix-based metric, we define a 'Contextual Attention Score' to reflect external context utilization. We evaluate our approach on the same benchmarks as RAGNorm and GraphHD, including real-world news summarization and question answering datasets.
CONTROLS: We perform extensive hyperparameter tuning, validation, and ablation studies to evaluate the impact of different architectures, fusion strategies, and downstream tasks on the Corteste performance.
COST: 495000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that Corteste will outperform GraphHD and RAGNorm by better capturing specific context-dependent attention patterns, particularly on datasets with highly ambiguous queries (NewsSum, RAG-Duo). However, Corteste might require additional computational resources due to the increased complexity of the multi-task learning formulation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spurious Correlation-free Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretically-founded approach to mitigating spurious correlations between internal knowledge, external context, and hallucination signals. By leveraging the properties of neural networks as kernel embeddings, we develop a method to split the input features into two disjoint sets: features contributing to the task-specific decision and features contributing to spurious correlations. We then apply correction coefficients to the task-relevant features to obtain a corrected signal, which serves as the input for the hallucination detection framework. This correction step reduces the impact of spurious correlations and improves the robustness of the hallucination detection model.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the spurious correlation-free method to GraphHD and Corteste+ on various hallucination-prone datasets (e.g., RAG-Duo, NewsSum), testing its ability to retain its effectiveness in the presence of correlations and robustness to noise.
COST: 1080000
PREDICTION: We expect the spurious correlation-free method to provide state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance, significantly reducing the over-reliance on spurious correlations and positional biases. However, its high computation cost may hinder its practical applicability in low-resource settings.

CONTROLS: We compare the performance of RAGNorm with external knowledge graph prior to the standalone RAGNorm on datasets such as SQu

PROPOSAL: We revise Corteste to incorporate a novel dual-resolution attention mechanism (DRAM), allowing for simultaneous exploration of both local context and long-range dependencies. DRAM consists of a high-resolution attention module for explicit contextualization and a low-resolution attention module for implicit contextualization. This dual-resolution mechanism enhances the contextual understanding, enables effective attention-weighted feature aggregation, and improves overall hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: We compare Corteste with DRAM to GraphHD and revised RAGNorm on diverse datasets.

PREDICTION: We expect Corteste with DRAM to demonstrate state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance, leveraging the advantages of dual-resolution attention to capture rich contextual information and reduce hallucination.

TITLE: Active Learning for Weakly-Supervised Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose an active learning approach, coined 'Hall-AL', for weakly-supervised hallucination detection. Hall-AL selects the most informative examples from the unlabeled pool based on a novel hallucination-score maximization criterion. Starting from an initial hallucination model, Hall-AL iteratively collects imported data and leverages this data to train the model through a novel meta-update mechanism and an attention-based hallucination signal, thus converting the weakly-supervised hallucination detection problem into a more tractable one. We assess the effectiveness of Hall-AL on real-world datasets with limited annotated labels.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the Hall-AL approach in combination with the deepest hallucination detection models and compare its performance with strong baselines.

STP integrates contextualized intensities from transformer-based embeddings to confer strong entity understanding, promotes explicit example analysis, and thereby further enhances overall hallucination detection performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Criterion-Based External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: We propose a new method to quantify external context utilization by using a distance-based criterion that measures the similarity between the generated response and the retrieved context. Specifically, we calculate the Minimum Skipgram Word Embedding Distance (MSWED) between the response tokens and the context tokens, which captures their semantic similarity. We also calculate the document-level MSWED to quantify the overall similarity between the response and the retrieved document. We then use these distances as features to train a learner that predicts the quality of the response based on its relation to the context, in a way that is independent from specific attention heads or transformer layers.
CONTROLS: We will use ReDeEP as a baseline and compare our MSWED-based approach to it on several real-world datasets for hallucination detection in RAG.
COST: 333.8623
PREDICTION: We expect our MSWED-based approach to outperform ReDeEP on most datasets, as it is less sensitive to the specific selection of attention heads and transformer layers. However, it may struggle with datasets where the context and response are highly semantic similar, as the MSWED distance might not capture the underlying relationship correctly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Internal Knowledge Signal via Textual Entailment
PROPOSAL: We propose to quantify internal knowledge utilization by using a Textual Entailment (TE) framework. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained TE model to generate a set of entailed statements for each word in the response, which captures the word's relationships with the model's internal knowledge. We then calculate a TE score for each word, which reflects the degree to which the word is supported by the internal knowledge. By aggregating these scores, we can obtain a measure of the total internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: We will use the ReDeEP approach without the Jensen-Shannon divergence component as a baseline, which relies solely on attention head selection. We will also evaluate the TE-based approach on a range of real-world datasets for hallucination detection in RAG.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect the TE-based approach to capture a wide range of internal knowledge utilization patterns, but it may be susceptible to overfitting on certain datasets where the internal knowledge is very extensive.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Robustifying Multitask Learning for Context-Neutral and Context-Aware Response Generation
PROPOSAL: We revise the Multitask Learning (MTL) approach by adding a robustness component to make it less susceptible to overfitting and sensitive to the specific selection of attention heads and transformer layers. Specifically, we will use a ensemble-based approach to combine the outputs of multiple weak models, each trained on a different subset of the training data, and apply regularization techniques to prevent overfitting. This will allow the MTL approach to rely less on local optima and more on the generalization capabilities of the models.
CONTROLS: We will use the previously proposed ReDeEP approach without the Jensen-Shannon divergence component as a baseline, and the other two approaches (Criterion-Based External Context Utilization and Internal Knowledge Signal via Textual Entailment) with modified architectures to compete directly with the MTL approach.
COST: 936
PREDICTION: We expect the revised MTL approach to exhibit improved robustness and generalization performance across a wide range of datasets, but it may still be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised contrastive learning approach to detect hallucinations in RAG systems. Specifically, we will use the generated responses and the retrieved context to create positive and negative pairs, and use a contrastive loss function to learn a hallucination detector that captures the differences between the responses and the context. We will use a pre-trained language model as a feature extractor and add a contrastive learning head to it.
CONTROLS: We will use the previously proposed approaches (Criterion-Based External Context Utilization, Internal Knowledge Signal via Textual Entailment, and Robustifying Multitask Learning for Context-Neutral and Context-Aware Response Generation) as baselines, and evaluate the self-supervised contrastive learning approach on several real-world datasets for hallucination detection in RAG.
COST: 1064.94129
PREDICTION: We expect the self-supervised contrastive learning approach to perform well on datasets with diverse context and response pairs, but it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not generalise well to new domains or datasets with different characteristics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unbiased Retrieval-Augmentation Evaluation Metric (UREM)
PROPOSAL:  Develop a new, unbiased metric to evaluate RAG systems based on their use of external context. UREM works by analyzing the similarity between the generated text and the context, while discounting similarity due to internal knowledge. This is done by comparing the contextualized embeddings of context tokens and generated tokens, separately contextualized using contextualizers that operate on external context and internal knowledge respectively. By taking their difference, UREM measures how much of the generated text is actually informed by external context.
CONTROLS: Comparison to traditional metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, demonstration on standard benchmarks for RAG such as reanking and COAR localized conversational datasets.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: UREM should effectively measure the use of external context in RAG systems, yielding lower scores for models that heavily rely on internal knowledge. This could help identify which re-ranking strategies encourage external context utilization. 

However, there might be challenges in implementing this metric effectively due to variations in contextualizer performance and contextualization differences between tasks.

TITLE: Knowledge-Gradient Attention Analysis
PROPOSAL:  Implement a black-box attention analysis technique that evaluates how individual attention weights contribute to the overall reliance of the model on external vs internal knowledge. By computing the gradients of output w.r.t the attention weights, we can expect a more global understanding of the knowledge utilization in the model. We analyze these gradients to determine the impact of focusing on external knowledge on the output and compare it to that of internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Contrast attention weights of RAG models to those of non-RAG models under identical tasks. Investigate how human feedback on incorrect information is reflected in similar gradients.

PREDICTION: This attention analysis should complement UREM and other existing methods to completely diagnose the utilization of external context and internal knowledge in RAG, although the gradients can sometimes be noisy, and need careful interpretation. 

However, accurate gradient-based analysis could also provide a lower-bounded estimate of the complexity and interpretability of LLMs.

TITLE: External Context Aware Suppression Loss for Hallucination Reduction
PROPOSAL: Introduce a suppression loss term in the training objective that is specifically geared towards discouraging outputs that are based heavily on internal knowledge, by considering how such outputs align with the retrieved context. In the loss function, the model will be encouraged to penalize high internal reliance scores, as measured by any light-weight proxy metric of internal knowledge utilization. This loss is only applied to the parameters of the decoder and the attention module, to avoid affecting retrieval and encoding.
CONTROLS: Baseline with respect to a RAG model trained with standard objectives (cross-entropy loss), comparing performance on generalization benchmarks to standard models trained for in-context seen hallucinations.
COST: 18720
PREDICTION: The proposed loss function will make a significant contribution to reducing hallucinations by forcing models to prefer utilizing contextual information over personal knowledge and potentially enhance generalization as well.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Evaluating Attention Head Sufficiency for Unsupervised External Context Utilization Estimation
PROPOSAL: We train a meta-model to predict the importance of attention heads in RAG systems using a mask-and-predict framework. Specifically, we mask the attention weights of each head in a transformer layer and predict the original attention weights, then use this supervision signal to train a meta-model that assigns a sufficiency score to each attention head based on its contribution to the overall attention distribution. We evaluate the meta-model on multiple tasks and datasets, and show that the sufficiency scores correlate with the amount of information used from the external context. We propose to use this meta-model as an unsupervised proxy for external context utilization, by setting a threshold on the sufficiency score to determine when a generator is "over-relying" on its internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison with ReDeEP and the follow-up work combining it with semantic entropy probes.
COST: 333.8623
PREDICTION: our unsupervised proxy should show significant correlation with external context utilization, but may struggle to capture more nuanced aspects of utilization; interesting variations may emerge in news summarization vs. data-to-text generation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigating Density Ratio Estimation for Balanced Evaluation of Internal and External Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: We explore using density ratio estimation to balance the evaluation of internal and external knowledge utilization. Specifically, we use the ratio of the probability density of generated responses in the absence of external context to the probability density of generated responses with access to external context to estimate the relative utilization of internal knowledge. We propose to use this density ratio as a control variate to reduce the impact of the imbalance in the evaluation of internal and external knowledge utilization, and apply a regularized maximum likelihood estimation to ensure the stability and robustness of the density ratio estimation. We investigate the performance of the proposed method on multiple datasets and tasks.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with the metastudy from ReDeEP and its variants
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our approach should improve the balance and robustness of the evaluation metrics, allowing for more accurate detection of hallucinations driven by over-reliance on internal knowledge; however, it may require substantial tuning to adapt to diverse datasets and tasks.

PREDICTION: Our adaptive weighting scheme should improve the accuracy and robustness of the density ratio estimation, but may require careful tuning to adapt to diverse tasks and datasets; additionally, the meta-learning framework may require a significant amount of computational resources to adapt to new tasks.

TITLE:  Evaluating Attention Head Sufficiency for Unsupervised External Context Utilization Estimation
PROPOSAL: We train a meta-model to predict the importance of attention heads in RAG systems using a mask-and-predict framework. Specifically, we mask the attention weights of each head in a transformer layer and predict the original attention weights, then use this supervision signal to train a meta-model that assigns a sufficiency score to each attention head based on its contribution to the overall attention distribution. We evaluate the meta-model on multiple tasks and datasets, and show that the sufficiency scores correlate with the amount of information used from the external context. We propose to use this meta-model as an unsupervised proxy for external context utilization, by setting a threshold on the sufficiency score to determine when a generator is "over-relying" on its internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison with ReDeEP and the follow-up work combining it with semantic entropy probes.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: our unsupervised proxy should show significant correlation with external context utilization, but may struggle to capture more nuanced aspects of utilization; interesting variations may emerge in news summarization vs. data-to-text generation.

TITLE:  Investigating Density Ratio Estimation for Balanced Evaluation of Internal and External Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: We explore using density ratio estimation to balance the evaluation of internal and external knowledge utilization. Specifically, we use the ratio of the probability density of generated responses in the absence of external context to the probability density of generated responses with access to external context to estimate the relative utilization of internal knowledge. We propose to use this density ratio as a control variate to reduce the impact of the imbalance in the evaluation of internal and external knowledge utilization, and apply a regularized maximum likelihood estimation to ensure the stability and robustness of the density ratio estimation. We investigate the performance of the proposed method on multiple datasets and tasks.
CONTROLS: Comparative analysis with the metastudy from ReDeEP and its variants
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our approach should improve the balance and robustness of the evaluation metrics, allowing for more accurate detection of hallucinations driven by over-reliance on internal knowledge; however, it may require substantial tuning to adapt to diverse datasets and tasks.

TITLE:  Revising Investigating Density Ratio Estimation for Balanced Evaluation of Internal and External Knowledge Utilization

This adaptive weighting scheme allows the model to weigh the importance of internal knowledge utilization more heavily when the retriever fails to provide sufficient information. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Adapting BERT-Style Masking for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the effectiveness of adaptive masking strategies for pretraining multivariate time-series encoders. Inspired by the sliding window masking used in BERT, we propose to use these masks to selectively remove temporal or channel dependencies in the input sequence, requiring the encoder to focus on other dependencies. For example, we could use masks that span different time intervals or channels to adaptively weigh the importance of different temporal or channel relationships. We will evaluate these adaptive masking strategies on various real-world multivariate time-series datasets, including temperature, electricity, and traffic databases, and compare their performance to traditional masking and channel-independent encoders as baselines.
CONTROLS: Baselines include traditional masking technique used in BERT, channel-independent encoders, and a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder. Control for different masking strategies is implemented by repurposing pre-existing parameters in the encoder.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in forecasting accuracy over traditional masking and channel-independent encoders, but unsure about the relative performance of adaptive masking strategies. The approach may fail to generalize across different datasets and masking strategies.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Variational Decoder for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a variational decoder to improve the predictive distribution of multivariate time-series forecasting models. Specifically, we propose to use a variational autoencoder (VAE) as the decoder, allowing it to learn a probabilistic representation of future values that can capture both temporal and channel dependencies. The VAE will be trained jointly with a pre-trained channel-dependent encoder using a reconstruction objective, and the latent space will be used to generate predictions. We will evaluate this variational decoder on real-world datasets in various domains, including weather, electricity, and traffic.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a simple linear projection decoder, a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder, and a VAE-based encoder trained separately.
COST: 1350
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in forecasting accuracy and evaluation metrics such as NMAE and CRPS, particularly in capturing complex temporal dynamics. However, the model may suffer from high computational costs and difficulties in disentangling channel dependencies.

TITLE: Hierarchical Channel-Attention Module for Channel-Dependent Encoders
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical channel-attention (HCA) module to improve the ability of channel-dependent encoders to capture cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series data. The HCA module will consist of multiple layers, each of which aggregates information from different channels using adaptive attention mechanisms. This hierarchical structure will allow the encoder to selectively focus on relevant channels for each time step and temporal frequency, leading to better forecasting performance. We will experiment with various architectures of the HCA module and evaluate its effectiveness on real-world datasets from various domains.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder without the HCA module, a channel-independent encoder, and an ablation study for different HCA module architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Channel-Dependent Encoder with Reduced Computational Cost
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture, dubbed "Shift-Attention", which leverages the strengths of both attention and channel-wise convolutional components to efficiently capture cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series data. This architecture splits the input channels into smaller groups, applies learned channel-wise convolutional filters to each group, and then aggregates the convolutional outputs using a lightweight attention mechanism. By grouping channels and applying channel-wise convolution, we reduce the number of unnecessary computations compared to traditional channel-dependent encoders.
CONTROLS: This experiment compares the performance of Shift-Attention with the original Transformer architecture and a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder, addressing the findings in our prior work. Baselines include a simple baseline with only channel-independent encoders and an ablation study using a channel-independent encoder with reduced transformer layers.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: By using Shift-Attention, we expect to outperform channel-independent encoders, especially in cases where the channels exhibit significant cross-channel dependencies. However, it might struggle to learn such dependencies in scenarios where channels have distinct patterns, potentially leading to suboptimal performance on challenging benchmarks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feynman Neural Networks for Efficient and Accurate Time-Series Decoding
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of simple linear projections in decoding, we introduce Feynman Neural Networks (FNNs). Inspired by the Feynman principle in physics, FNNs iteratively add simpler models, each of which refines the previous one, to learn increasingly complex output sequences from the encoded representations. This iterative process effectively captures the temporal dynamics of time-series data and mitigates the limitations of the vanilla linear decoder. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FNNs scale efficiently for long-range forecasting tasks by utilizing a caching mechanism, pre-computing values and transferring them across iterations.
CONTROLS: Compared to its nearest neighbors, i.e., linear projections with iterative refinement on top, our FNNs model will be validated on real-world benchmarks, such as the M3 dataset and the M4 forecasting competition, and analyzed with respect to both forecasting precision and scalability.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: FNNs are expected to yield noticeable improvements in forecasting accuracy compared to linear projections, notably in applications with complex temporal patterns and large forecasting horizons. However, the effectiveness of FNNs may degrade significantly when dealing with the M4 competition's notably challenging time-series.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multistage Training for Improved Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: To bridge the gap between pretraining-finetuning pipelines and the model's architectural design, we propose a Multistage Training (MST) framework. MST involves three stages: (1) Channel-Specific Learning, where each channel is first trained independently to capture its unique properties; (2) Cross-Channel Reconstruction, where channels that exhibit significant dependencies are paired for reconstruction and learning; and (3) Model Consolidation, where all learned representations are combined for overall forecasting tasks. This iterative approach aligns the training objective with the model's architecture and enables more effective learning of temporal dynamics.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of MST with the original pretraining-finetuning pipeline, ablation studies using separate two-stage pipelines for encoders and decoders, and a baseline with fixed encoders during the final forecast generation stage.

TITLE: Score-Based Generative Modeling for Time-Series Decoding
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel approach to time-series decoding by leveraging score-based generative modeling. Instead of directly predicting the output sequence, we learn to model the likelihood of the sequence given the encoded representation. This approach enables the model to capture complex temporal patterns and relationships by exploiting the properties of likelihood functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on various time-series decoding tasks and datasets.
CONTROLS: Compared to the original Feynman Neural Networks, we will evaluate the performance of the score-based generative modeling approach on a range of real-world datasets and compare it to established decoding methods, such as linear projections and sequential neural networks.

PREDICTION: The score-based generative modeling approach is expected to outperform existing decoding methods, particularly in tasks with complex temporal dynamics and relationships. However, it may face challenges in maintaining computational efficiency due to the need to compute and optimize likelihood functions, potentially impacting real-time applications.

TITLE: Channel-Dependent Encoder with Reduced Computational Cost
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture, dubbed "Shift-Attention", which leverages the strengths of both attention and channel-wise convolutional components to efficiently capture cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series data. This architecture splits the input channels into smaller groups, applies learned channel-wise convolutional filters to each group, and then aggregates the convolutional outputs using a lightweight attention mechanism. By grouping channels and applying channel-wise convolution, we reduce the number of unnecessary computations compared to traditional channel-dependent encoders.
CONTROLS: This experiment compares the performance of Shift-Attention with the original Transformer architecture and a state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder, addressing the findings in our prior work. Baselines include a simple baseline with only channel-independent encoders and an ablation study using a channel-independent encoder with reduced transformer layers.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: By using Shift-Attention, we expect to outperform channel-independent encoders, especially in cases where the channels exhibit significant cross-channel dependencies. However, it might struggle to learn such dependencies in scenarios where channels have distinct patterns, potentially leading to suboptimal performance on challenging benchmarks.

TITLE: Feynman Neural Networks for Efficient and Accurate Time-Series Decoding
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of simple linear projections in decoding, we introduce Feynman Neural Networks (FNNs). Inspired by the Feynman principle in physics, FNNs iteratively add simpler models, each of which refines the previous one, to learn increasingly complex output sequences from the encoded representations. This iterative process effectively captures the temporal dynamics of time-series data and mitigates the limitations of the vanilla linear decoder. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FNNs scale efficiently for long-range forecasting tasks by utilizing a caching mechanism, pre-computing values and transferring them across iterations.
CONTROLS: Compared to its nearest neighbors, i.e., linear projections with iterative refinement on top, our FNNs model will be validated on real-world benchmarks, such as the M3 dataset and the M4 forecasting competition, and analyzed with respect to both forecasting precision and scalability.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: FNNs are expected to yield noticeable improvements in forecasting accuracy compared to linear projections, notably in applications with complex temporal patterns and large forecasting horizons. However, the effectiveness of FNNs may degrade significantly when dealing with the M4 competition's notably challenging time-series.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Autoregressive Transformers for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare an autoregressive Transformer with a standard multi-horizon multi-step (MHMS) encoder-decoder architecture on weather forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting datasets (e.g., M4 dataset, International Energy Agency's Electricity Forecasting dataset). Use a autoregressive head to predict future values from previous encoded representations. Evaluate on metrics like Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), and Symbol-based Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (sMAPE). Baselines include MHMS, MHMS with attention, and a gradient-boosted regressor. Compute predictions every 10 steps as the model predicts at most 50 steps using a forecasting horizon of H=50.
CONTROLS: MHMS with attention, MHMS, gradient-boosted regressor
COST: 432.13
PREDICTION: The autoregressive Transformer is expected to improve forecasting accuracy over MHMS due to its use of a temporal dependence ordering strategy and learnable context embedding. However, the performance gap may narrow as the horizon increases due to MHMS's ability to model longer-range behaviors. However, the gradient-boosted regressor baseline could potentially outperform the MHMS or autoregressive Transformer architectures due to its unequalled interpretability and ability to directly handle noisy features present in real-world electricity consumption datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Autoregressive Transformers for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare an autoregressive Transformer with a standard multi-horizon multi-step (MHMS) encoder-decoder architecture on weather forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting datasets (e.g., M4 dataset, International Energy Agency's Electricity Forecasting dataset). Use a autoregressive head to predict future values from previous encoded representations. Evaluate on metrics like Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), and Symbol-based Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (sMAPE). Baselines include MHMS, MHMS with attention, and a gradient-boosted regressor. Compute predictions every 10 steps as the model predicts at most 50 steps using a forecasting horizon of H=50.
CONTROLS: MHMS with attention, MHMS, gradient-boosted regressor
COST: 1300
PREDICTION: The autoregressive Transformer is expected to improve forecasting accuracy over MHMS due to its use of a temporal dependence ordering strategy and learnable context embedding. However, the performance gap may narrow as the horizon increases due to MHMS's ability to model longer-range behaviors. However, the gradient-boosted regressor baseline could potentially outperform the MHMS or autoregressive Transformer architectures due to its unequalled interpretability and ability to directly handle noisy features present in real-world electricity consumption datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Masking Patterns for Effective Pretraining of Time-Series Encoders
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate various masking patterns for pretraining time-series encoders on time-series data (e.g., Weather.css and M4 datasets) with different numbers of sequential time-steps and involvement of cross-channel dependencies. These masking patterns would be a combination of sequential masking, random masking, or other complex masking strategies (e.g., inverse masking, external masking, long-range periodic masking). The key is to determine which masking strategy results in better pretraining of time-series encoders by assessing the adaptation performance on the following tasks: electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting.
CONTROLS: Compare with current masking strategy used in BERT, evaluate the need for cross-validation using different masking strategies to understand if these pretraining strategies is over represented.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Certain masking patterns will be superior in pretraining time-series encoders, outperforming the baseline masking strategy used in BERT, and offering improved generalization on specific forecasting tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Two-Stage Training for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive, two-stage training pipeline that adjusts its learning focus throughout training: an initial self-supervised stage where the model predicts masked time-steps in the sequences and a subsequent supervised stage where the model is trained on ground-truth target values. Design an adaptive strategy to switch between the stages, evaluating its benefits for time-series forecasting on six different tasks: weather forecasting (e.g., NWP dataset), traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, electricity transformer temperature forecasting, and compare the model performance with existing state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS:  Evaluate using ablation study where the two-stage training is removed and fixed-stage training where the model is trained using just one or the other stage without ever switching between the stages; examine how these strategies affect time-series forecasting performance.
COST: 6700
PREDICTION: The adaptive two-stage training pipeline achieves better performance or at least competitive performance against state-of-the-art models on most time-series forecasting tasks and eventuates a faster convergence when compared to single-stage training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Simple Linear Projections for Time-Series Forecasting Decoding
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of simple linear projections with attention-based decoders on various time-series forecasting benchmarks (e.g., Weather.css dataset, M4 dataset) to assess their limitations. Specifically, design a framework that simultaneously evaluates both decoding architectures on 5 different tasks (weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting, and electricity transformer temperature forecasting) using a single unified experiment setup.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing state-of-the-art models, ETS (Exponential Smoothing) and Naive, as essential baselines.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Linear projections may achieve competitive results in simpler forecasting tasks but struggle with more complex tasks such as those involving non-linear relationships and seasonal changes in the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Masking Patterns for Effective Pretraining of Time-Series Encoders
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate various masking patterns for pretraining time-series encoders on time-series data (e.g., Weather.css and M4 datasets) with different numbers of sequential time-steps and involvement of cross-channel dependencies. These masking patterns would be a combination of sequential masking, random masking, or other complex masking strategies (e.g., inverse masking, external masking, long-range periodic masking). The key is to determine which masking strategy results in better pretraining of time-series encoders by assessing the adaptation performance on the following tasks: electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting.
CONTROLS: Compare with current masking strategy used in BERT, evaluate the need for cross-validation using different masking strategies to understand if these pretraining strategies is over represented.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Certain masking patterns will be superior in pretraining time-series encoders, outperforming the baseline masking strategy used in BERT, and offering improved generalization on specific forecasting tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Two-Stage Training for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive, two-stage training pipeline that adjusts its learning focus throughout training: an initial self-supervised stage where the model predicts masked time-steps in the sequences and a subsequent supervised stage where the model is trained on ground-truth target values. Design an adaptive strategy to switch between the stages, evaluating its benefits for time-series forecasting on six different tasks: weather forecasting (e.g., NWP dataset), traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, electricity transformer temperature forecasting, and compare the model performance with existing state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS:  Evaluate using ablation study where the two-stage training is removed and fixed-stage training where the model is trained using just one or the other stage without ever switching between the stages; examine how these strategies affect time-series forecasting performance.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: The adaptive two-stage training pipeline achieves better performance or at least competitive performance against state-of-the-art models on most time-series forecasting tasks and eventuates a faster convergence when compared to single-stage training.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive Two-Stage Training for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: REVISED - Introduce an attention-based adaptive two-stage training pipeline that adjusts its learning focus throughout training, selectively focusing on specific time-steps and channels based on their importance for improving time-series forecasting performance. In the self-supervised stage, the model predicts masked time-steps, whereas in the subsequent supervised stage, it is trained using a weighted objective function that prioritizes correctly predicted channels and time-steps. Design a strategy to dynamically adjust this weighting and assess its benefits for time-series forecasting on the previously mentioned six tasks: weather forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, electricity transformer temperature forecasting, and compare the model performance with existing state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS: Evaluate with ablation study where the two-stage training is removed, which models the standard one-stage training case, and where the adaptive-attention mechanism is replaced with a static mechanism, representing previous approaches for time-series forecasting models.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: The adaptive two-stage training pipeline achieves better performance or at least competitive performance against state-of-the-art models on most time-series forecasting tasks and speeds up the convergence when compared to single-stage training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Value of Pretraining in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the theoretical benefits and the resulting practical performance when incorporating pretraining objectives for multivariate time-series forecasting, utilizing established datasets like the M4 dataset and Weather.css dataset. Specifically, compare the model performance when pretraining objectives are used (comparing different masking strategies) and when no pretraining is utilized, which can highlight instances like weather forecasting scenarios with long range dependencies.
CONTROLS: Compare baseline results of pretrainer-free model and evaluate coefficients used to investigate generalising pretraining to unseen real-world scenarios.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Incorporating pretraining will consistently show improved performance in time-series forecasting tasks on a controlled dataset.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Channel-Dependent Encoders with Hierarchical Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: REVISED - Design and evaluate a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture with hierarchical attention that selectively focuses on relevant channels and time-steps for improving time-series forecasting performance. In this architecture, each time-step and channel are associated with a hierarchical set of masks that enable the model to model larger temporal dependencies across multiple channels and handle long-range temporal correlations and important informative features. Then, test this model on the baseline time-series forecasting tasks (weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting, and electricity transformer temperature forecasting) as well as on the adapted additional task.
CONTROLS: Experimentally compare against existing models, compare initial static settings, assess am provide expected gains due to incorporation of error analysis models
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: Considering the hierarchical masking and selective focus mechanism, the novel encoder architecture will improve forecasting accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art models by leveraging information from relevant time-steps and channels across multiple scales, while offering a good generalization to unseen time-series data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Linear Channel Interaction Exploitation via Two-Stream Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose using two-stream Transformers architecture to effectively exploit cross-channel dependencies in multivariate time-series forecasting. The first stream encodes the input variables independently using a standard Transformer encoder, while the second stream captures channel interactions by jointly encoding multiple input variables using attention and cross-attention mechanisms. The two streams are then fused to produce the final encoded representation.
CONTROLS: Standard Transformer with channel-independent encoding, Two-stream Transformer without channel interaction stream
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in forecasting accuracy over the channel-independent Transformer baseline, with a notable advantage in datasets with strong cross-variable interactions (e.g., traffic flow and solar power generation forecasting). We anticipate a 2-5% reduction in forecasting error in these datasets, but may struggle with datasets having weak channel interactions (e.g., weather forecasting).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Channel-Aware Residual Learning for Improved Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the high computational cost associated with channel-dependent encoders, we introduce a channel-aware residual learning (CAREL) module. CAREL adds a lightweight residual connection between the channel-dependent encoder and the channel-independent encoder, enabling the model to leverage the strengths of both architectures. The residual connection is learned across channels, allowing the model to adaptively adjust its representation based on the presence of strong channel interactions.
CONTROLS: Two-stream Transformer without channel interaction stream, Standard Transformer with channel-independent encoding
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect CAREL to significantly improve the forecasting accuracy of channel-independent encoders, reducing the performance gap with channel-dependent encoders by 15-25%. In turn, we anticipate CAREL to perform competitively with channel-dependent encoders in datasets with strong cross-variable interactions. However, in datasets with weak channel interactions, CAREL might not fully leverage channel-dependent information, leading to a smaller improvement over the standard Transformer baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Decoding for Temporal Dynamics: An Information-Theoretic Approach
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel decoding method to better capture complex temporal structures in time-series forecasting. Our approach is based on information theory, which motivates the use of a differential entropy regularization term to guide the decoding process. This term encourages the model to preserve as much information as possible in the encoded representation, leading to more accurate and loyal predictions. Our method can be applied to any encoder architecture, including the ones proposed in 1 and 2.
CONTROLS: Linear projection decoding, learned linear projection decoding
COST: 829.5
PREDICTION: We expect our information-theoretic approach to significantly outperform linear projection decoding, which may struggle with complex temporal patterns (e.g., weather forecasting and solar power generation forecasting). In turn, we anticipate that our method will yield results comparable to simple linear projection decoding in datasets with relatively simple temporal structures (e.g., traffic flow forecasting).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Aligning Training Objective with Model Architecture via Masked XLNet for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the effectiveness of masked prediction tasks in self-supervised learning, we introduce masked XLNet, a training objective tailored to multivariate time-series forecasting tasks. We modify the original XLNet training procedure by masking both individual tokens and whole sequences of tokens, forcing the encoder to learn a more robust representation of temporal dynamics and cross-channel dependencies. Our method can be used as a pretraining step for any encoder architecture, or as a finetuning objective for the decoders proposed in 3.
CONTROLS: Masking-and-reconstruction task, BERT pretraining for time-series forecasting
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect masked XLNet to outperform the masking-and-reconstruction task and BERT pretraining objectives, achieving better generalization capabilities in multivariate time-series forecasting. In particular, we anticipate a 5-10% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with strong temporal and channel dependencies (e.g., weather and traffic flow forecasting). However, we might struggle to fully adapt masked XLNet to strongly domain-specific tasks, such as solar power generation forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization of Encoder-Decoder Dynamics for Improved Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel regularization technique for the encoder-decoder dynamics in multivariate time-series forecasting models. Our method involves injecting noise into the encoder's output and forcing the decoder to learn to recover the original input. This regularizer encourages the encoder-decoder pair to develop more robust and informative interactions, improving the overall forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Standard training with no regularization, dropout regularization on encoder output
COST: 1261.44
PREDICTION: We expect our regularization technique to lead to a 4-9% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with complex temporal structures (e.g., weather forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting). However, we might struggle to achieve consistent gains in datasets with strong cross-channel dependencies (e.g., solar power generation and traffic flow forecasting), where the proposed CAREL adaptation might be more effective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robustness Against Covariate Shifts in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training scheme to improve the robustness of multivariate time-series forecasting models against covariate shifts, which occur when the input distribution changes over time. Our approach involves training a discriminator to distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, and using this discriminator to guide the training of the forecasting model.
CONTROLS: Standard training, adversarial training without discriminator guidance
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect our adversarial training scheme to lead to a 6-12% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with significant covariate shifts (e.g., solar power generation forecasting). However, we might see minimal gains in datasets with limited covariate shifts (e.g., traffic flow forecasting), where the proposed channel-aware decoders might focus more on temporal patterns.

In particular, we anticipate a 5-10% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with strong temporal and channel dependencies (e.g., weather and traffic flow forecasting). However, we might struggle to fully adapt masked XLNet to strongly domain-specific tasks, such as solar power generation forecasting.

PROPOSAL: To further improve the alignment between the training objective and the model architecture, we modify masked XLNet to include a channel-specific attention mechanism. This mechanism enables the model to focus on the most relevant channels when reconstructing masked tokens, reflecting the channel-dependent nature of the forecasting task. This adaptation can be integrated with the other proposals (1, 2, and 3).
CONTROLS: Masked XLNet without channel-specific attention, original masked XLNet

PREDICTION: We expect this extension of masked XLNet to further improve forecasting accuracy by 3-7% in datasets with strong cross-channel dependencies (e.g., solar power generation and traffic flow forecasting). ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Channel-Aware Residual Learning for Improved Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We modify the CAREL module by replacing the lightweight residual connection with a heavier, learnable mixture of experts. Each expert is responsible for a subset of the input channels, enabling the model to selectively focus on the most relevant channels for the forecasting task. This adaptation can lead to improved capture of channel dependencies and temporal dynamics.
CONTROLS: Original CAREL module, CAREL with mixture of experts without channel awareness
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: We expect this adaptation to improve CAREL's performance by 8-15% in datasets with strong cross-channel dependencies (e.g., solar power generation and traffic flow forecasting). However, we anticipate potential increased risk of overfitting in datasets with complex temporal structures (e.g., weather forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization of Encoder-Decoder Dynamics for Improved Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel regularization technique for the encoder-decoder dynamics in multivariate time-series forecasting models. Our method involves injecting noise into the encoder's output and forcing the decoder to learn to recover the original input. This regularizer encourages the encoder-decoder pair to develop more robust and informative interactions, improving the overall forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Standard training with no regularization, dropout regularization on encoder output

PREDICTION: We expect our regularization technique to lead to a 4-9% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with complex temporal structures (e.g., weather forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting). TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robustness Against Covariate Shifts in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training scheme to improve the robustness of multivariate time-series forecasting models against covariate shifts, which occur when the input distribution changes over time. Our approach involves training a discriminator to distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, and using this discriminator to guide the training of the forecasting model.
CONTROLS: Standard training, adversarial training without discriminator guidance

PREDICTION: We expect our adversarial training scheme to lead to a 6-12% improvement in forecasting accuracy in datasets with significant covariate shifts (e.g., solar power generation forecasting). PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical attention mechanism to efficiently handle high-dimensional channel data in multivariate time-series forecasting. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Information Landscapes for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Design a new neural network module called "Aufklärer" that estimates the novel information introduced by each individual view for an instance. Aufklärer will be trained as a separate discriminator, using a learned representation of the original and transformed views as input. The estimated new information will be combined with the contrastive loss, to dynamically weight the contribution of each view. Perform an ablation study on datasets such as CIFAR-10 and STL-10 to compare the performance of SimCLR with and without Aufklärer.

COST: 1600
PREDICTION: By dynamically weighting the views, Aufklärer should adaptively expand the representational capacity of the model, improving performance and robustness on real-world data sets, while it is possible that uneven weighting might cannibalize quality of the expanding views submitted.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-theoretic Decomposition of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Theoretically decompose the contrastive learning objective into its information-theoretic components, analyzing the mutual information between the original and transformed views, as well as the misleading information introduced by the noise contrast function. Derive a bound on the performance of the contrastive model in terms of these information-theoretic quantities. Experimentally validate this analysis on linear and non-linear neural networks using the fixed-point method and validate that the theoretical bound matches the observed performance.
CONTROLS: Baselines: SimCLR, MoCo and their variants for comparison.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This decomposition should provide deep insights into the underlying information dynamics governing contrastive learning, identifying key factors such as the quality and diversity of views and witness its expression via empirical learning traces that depart significantly from random initializations.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of View Entropy on Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the mutual information gain between views of an instance in various contrastive learning models (e.g. SimCLR, MoCo) with different augmentation pipelines, using a quantitative measure of view entropy. We will train models on ImageNet-64x64 (a smaller version of the full ImageNet dataset) with different groups of augmentations and calculate the mutual information between views using a neural estimator. This will provide insight into how the diversity and complexity of augmentations impact the information gained through contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: Trained models will be tested on the same task with a static augmentation pipeline and a different random seed for augmentation.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that more complex augmentation pipelines lead to higher mutual information gain between views, demonstrating that adaptively increasing the diversity of views can be beneficial for contrastive learning, but may also lead to overfitting and the inability to properly transfer learned representations to new tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Selection for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to adaptively select views for an instance during training based on their relative entropy, aiming to dynamically regulate the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity. Specifically, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that tracks the mutual information gain between views and selects the most informative views for each instance. We will experiment with this method on a range of real-world datasets (e.g. CIFAR-10, STL-10, ImageNet) to demonstrate its effectiveness in contrastive learning tasks.
CONTROLS: Non-adaptive views will be selected based on a fixed random order, and standard contrastive learning objectives will be used for comparison.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Our adaptive method is expected to improve the performance of contrastive learning models by more effectively balancing the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity, especially in cases where the augmentation pipeline provides diverse but potentially misleading information. However, the overhead from training and incorporating the RL agent may lead to increased training time and computational resources.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of View Entropy on Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the mutual information gain between views of an instance in various contrastive learning models (e.g. SimCLR, MoCo) with different augmentation pipelines, using a quantitative measure of view entropy. We will train models on ImageNet-64x64 (a smaller version of the full ImageNet dataset) with different groups of augmentations and calculate the mutual information between views using a neural estimator. This will provide insight into how the diversity and complexity of augmentations impact the information gained through contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: Trained models will be tested on the same task with a static augmentation pipeline and a different random seed for augmentation.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that more complex augmentation pipelines lead to higher mutual information gain between views, demonstrating that adaptively increasing the diversity of views can be beneficial for contrastive learning, but may also lead to overfitting and the inability to properly transfer learned representations to new tasks.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Develop a method to adaptively select views for an instance during training based on their relative entropy, aiming to dynamically regulate the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity. We will experiment with this method on a range of real-world datasets (e.g. CIFAR-10, STL-10, ImageNet) to demonstrate its effectiveness in contrastive learning tasks.
CONTROLS: Non-adaptive views will be selected based on a fixed random order, and standard contrastive learning objectives will be used for comparison.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: Our adaptive method is expected to improve the performance of contrastive learning models by more effectively balancing the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity, especially in cases where the augmentation pipeline provides diverse but potentially misleading information. However, the overhead from training and incorporating the RL agent may lead to increased training time and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Divisive Normalization in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of unsupervised divisive normalization (UDN) on the representational capacity and semantic consistency of self-supervised contrastive models. Specifically, we will implement a UDN layer that dynamically renormalizes the feature embeddings to encourage representational diversity while preserving semantic coherence. We will experiment with SimCLR-v2 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k with various UDN settings and compare to the original SimCLR-v2 model.
CONTROLS: Standard SimCLR-v2 model, UDN with fixed renormalization factor, no UDN
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The UDN layer will lead to improved representational diversity and better generalization capabilities, but might introduce instability issues for certain renormalization factors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation by Predictive Information
PROPOSAL: Design an adaptive augmentation approach that selects augmentations based on the predictive information shared between different views of an instance. We will implement a meta-learning module that learns to predict the mutual information between a given view and its augmented counterpart, and use this information to guide the selection of augmentations. We will experiment with this approach on SimCLR-v2 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k and compare to the original SimCLR-v2 model and UDN (proposal 1).
CONTROLS: Standard SimCLR-v2 model, UDN (proposal 1), fixed augmentation pipeline
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: The adaptive augmentation approach will lead to improved representational capacity and semantic coherence, but might require careful hyperparameter tuning to avoid over-adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Invariance Metric for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a dynamic invariance metric to evaluate the representational diversity and semantic coherence of contrastive learning models. This metric will be based on the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the distributions of feature embeddings for different views of the same instance and different instances. We will experiment with this metric on SimCLR-v2 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k and analyze its correlation with model performance.
CONTROLS: Standard SimCLR-v2 model, UDN (proposal 1), Adaptive Augmentation (proposal 2)
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The dynamic invariance metric will provide valuable insights into the trade-off between representational diversity and semantic coherence in contrastive learning models, but might require careful implementation to avoid numerical instability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  Dynamic Invariance Metric for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: REVISED: The dynamic invariance metric will be extended to account for instance-specific uncertainty in the feature embeddings, using a Bayesian approach to propagate uncertainty in the Jensen-Shannon divergence calculation. This will enable a more nuanced evaluation of representational diversity and semantic coherence, particularly in settings where the data distribution is uncertain or noisy.
CONTROLS: Standard SimCLR-v2 model, UDN (proposal 1), Adaptive Augmentation (proposal 2)
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The revised dynamic invariance metric will provide a more accurate and robust evaluation of contrastive learning models, but might require significant computational resources to estimate instance-specific uncertainty in high-dimensional feature spaces.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bounding the Information Gain in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will derive information-theoretic bounds on the mutual information between views in contrastive learning, aiming to quantify the diversity of views in terms of how much new information each view contributes. Specifically, we will analyze the growth rate of mutual information between views as the number of augmentations increases, and relate this to the structure of the data graph. This will provide a principled framework for evaluating the effectiveness of different augmentation strategies and for understanding the scaling properties of contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bounds to those obtained via a random augmentation strategy, as well as to the empirical mutual information measured from training data.
COST: 16,200
PREDICTION: We expect to derive sharp bounds that demonstrate a significant gap between the information gain of static augmentations and more dynamic or adaptive strategies. However, we anticipate challenges in deriving useful bounds for extreme augmentation scenarios (e.g., extremely high or extremely low numbers of augmentations), where the empirical mutual information may diverge from our analytical predictions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation Strategies for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a meta-learning approach that enables the model to adaptively select augmentations for each instance, based on the uncertainty of the model's representations. Specifically, we will train a meta-model that predicts the required magnitude and type of augmentation given a batch of data points. This meta-model will be conditional on the model's representations, allowing it to scale with the data size and adapt to changing characteristics of the data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive approach to existing static augmentation strategies (e.g., SimCLR, MoCo), as well as to a random augmentation strategy. We will also investigate ablations to understand the importance of different meta-learning components, such as the uncertainty measure and the augmentation selector.
COST: 46,656
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in representation quality and learning speed when using adaptive augmentations, particularly in regimes where the data is highly non-stationary or has varying distributions. However, we may face challenges in stabilizing the training process, especially when using complex uncertainty measures or augmentations with high variability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Contrastive Learning on Small-Batch Settings
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the performance of contrastive learning methods in small-batch settings, where traditional batch methods are often NP-hard to optimize. Specifically, we will develop a new theoretical framework for analyzing the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity in these settings, and evaluate our findings on a range of real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our methods to existing state-of-the-art methods for small-batch training, such as GBP and SNR, and evaluate their performance on various metrics including accuracy, robustness, and efficiency.
COST: 80,000
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant improvements in performance and efficiency when using our new theoretical framework, particularly in regimes where the batch size is very small. However, we may face challenges in proving convergence and robustness guarantees for these methods.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED - Adaptive Augmentation Strategies for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will refine our previous approach to adaptive augmentation strategies by making it more efficient and scalable. Specifically, we will develop a new meta-learning framework that uses a neural network to predict the required magnitude and type of augmentation for each instance, and incorporate techniques such as Importance Weighting and Exponential Moving Averages to stabilize the training process.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach to the original adaptive augmentation strategy and existing static augmentation methods, such as SimCLR and MoCo. We will also investigate the effect of different meta-learning components and techniques on the performance of our approach.
COST: 93,600
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in representation quality and learning speed when using our revised adaptive augmentation strategy, particularly in regimes where the data is highly non-stationary or has varying distributions. However, we may still face challenges in stabilizing the training process for very large or complex datasets.

TITLE: Towards Sample-Efficient Contrastive Learning: Analyzing the Role of Views
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the effects of view quality and diversity on the performance of contrastive learning methods. Specifically, we will analyze the relationship between the quality of views (e.g. high-quality vs. low-quality) and the diversity of views (e.g. diverse vs. non-diverse) on the performance of contrastive learning methods.
CONTROLS: We will experiment with different view quality and diversity settings and evaluate the performance of contrastive learning methods under these settings. We will also compare our findings to prior work on view quality and diversity.
COST: 320,000
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key challenges and limitations of existing view quality and diversity metrics, and develop new insights into the design of contrastive learning methods that can effectively utilize suboptimal views.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED - Evaluating Contrastive Learning on Small-Batch Settings
PROPOSAL: We will extend our previous analysis to explicitly consider the relationship between small-batch scalability and the temporal dynamics of contrastive learning. Specifically, we will investigate the effects of limited iteration budget, neighborhood sampling, and early stopping on the optimization landscape of contrastive learning methods, and analyze the resulting implications for small-batch training.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach to existing state-of-the-art methods for small-batch training, such as GBP and SNR, and evaluate their performance on various metrics including accuracy, robustness, and efficiency.
COST: 110,000
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant improvements in scalability and robustness when considering the temporal dynamics of contrastive learning, particularly in regimes where the batch size is very small. However, we may face challenges in deriving generalizations that hold across different methods and settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Enhanced Contrastive Learning via Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a novel knowledge distillation framework for contrastive learning, which aims to leverage the strengths of a pre-trained teacher model to improve the performance of a student model. Specifically, we will design a contrastive distillation loss function that encourages the student model to mimic the behaviour of the teacher model on a set of augmented views, while minimizing the expected loss on a set of hard negative samples.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to existing knowledge distillation methods and contrastive learning methods, and evaluate the performance of our approach on a range of real-world benchmarks.
COST: 400,000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in representation quality and learning speed when using our knowledge distillation framework, particularly in regimes where the teacher model is well-versed in the underlying task.

PROPOSAL: We will derive information-theoretic bounds on the mutual information between views in contrastive learning, aiming to quantify the diversity of views in terms of how much new information each view contributes. Specifically, we will analyze the growth rate of mutual information between views as the number of augmentations increases, and relate this to the structure of the data graph. This will provide a principled framework for evaluating the effectiveness of different augmentation strategies and for understanding the scaling properties of contrastive learning.

However, we anticipate challenges in deriving useful bounds for extreme augmentation scenarios (e.g., extremely high or extremely low numbers of augmentations), where the empirical mutual information may diverge from our analytical predictions.

This meta-model will be conditional on the model's representations, allowing it to scale with the data size and adapt to changing characteristics of the data.
