TITLE: Investigating Gaze Features for Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: This experiment will evaluate the impact of gaze features on the performance of egocentric video question answering (EQA) models. We'll use the recently proposed EGQA-Benchmark and consider three scenarios: 1) standard video frames only, 2) adding gaze points to the video frames, and 3) using gaze points as visual tokens. For each scenario, we'll compare four EQA models: CLIP, ViLT, ARNIM, and T2T-ViT. We'll also explore the importance of gaze feature types (e.g., raw gaze points, gaze direction, gaze saliency).
CONTROLS: We'll use the baseline models and scenarios as described in the EGQA-Benchmark documentation, and ablate the importance of different gaze feature types.
COST: 1350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a moderate improvement in EQA performance when using gaze features, up to 15% in some tasks, while failing to outperform standard models in tasks where gaze is not informative.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Gaze-Based User Intent Understanding in Egocentric Video
PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to explore the impact of gaze-based user intent understanding in a proactive AI assistant setup. We'll use a custom-built egocentric video dataset with systematically annotated gaze targets and user intents. We'll employ a gaze-conditioned visual encoder as our primary model, and compare its performance to a gaze-unaware counterpart using three baselines (CLIP, ViLT, and a simple gaze-naive transformer). We'll also investigate the gaze-based attention weights and visual tokens learned by the model.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of the gaze-conditioned encoder to the baselines in the absence of gaze information, and use the EGQA-Benchmark as an upper bound for a strong but gaze-naive EQA model.
COST: 1925 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the gaze-conditioned encoder to significantly outperform the baselines in tasks where user intent is strongly related to gaze targets, potentially achieving up to 25% higher accuracy, but may fail in tasks where user intent is more context-dependent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Gaze_signals for Improved MLLM's User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: 
Train and evaluate state-of-the-art MLLMs (e.g., Llama-L6 or Llama-L7) on the EGTEA (EgoGestures in the Eating Activity) dataset, a benchmark designed for egocentric vision and action understanding. Specifically, focus on the gaze cue-agnostic and gaze cue-inclusive versions of the EGTEA question answering tasks. Compare the model's performance under both conditions to evaluate the impact of gaze information on user intent understanding.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current best model trained on the same dataset but without gaze information ablation, and compare to random guess performance baseline. In addition, compare to the well-established question answering model on the EGTEA dataset, serving as a single-baseline.
COST: 670
PREDICTION: Improved performance with gaze information, especially in questions that require attention to specific objects or actions, though the impact might be limited due to the model's reliance on pre-trained visual features, and the absence of fine-grained gaze data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablation Study on Gaze-aware Embeddings for Egocentric Vision
PROPOSAL: Explore the impact of incorporating gaze-aware embeddings into pre-trained MLLMs. Specifically, modify the embeddings of the EGTEA dataset to reflect the camera wearer's attention (based on eye-tracking data) and evaluate different granularities of gaze-aware embeddings (e.g., per-frame, per-action, or per-object level). Analyze the effect of these modifications on the MLLMs' user intent understanding performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original model without gaze-aware embeddings, and to a variant that uses a naive approach (e.g., simply conditioning on the first frame with gaze attention). Also compare to the full gaze-signal-based model as proposed in task 1. Additionally, compare the results to models trained with varying levels of gaze signal noise (e.g., by randomly perturbing gaze attention maps).
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Improved user intent understanding when gaze-aware embeddings are used, with optimal results when embeddings are fine-grained and adapt to the complex requirements of the question answering tasks. However, this may come at the cost of increased model complexity and potential overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-world Benchmark for Gaze-aware MLLMs in Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Create a real-world benchmark, leveraging user study data and annotated egocentric videos from common tasks (e.g., cooking, object manipulation, or navigation). Develop a diverse set of question answering tasks focusing on user intent, attention, and action understanding. Compare the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs (with and without gaze-aware modifications) on both this benchmark and the EGTEA dataset. Investigate the correlation between model performance and gaze signal accuracy, controlling for other variables such as annotation quality and dataset size.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current state-of-the-art MLLMs (including the gaze-aware version from task 2), and develop a baseline of a gaze-independent model trained on the new benchmark.
COST: 3338.623
PREDICTION: State-of-the-art models will show significant improvements on both the EGTEA and the proposed real-world benchmarks when they utilize gaze-aware embeddings, but will have a harder time adapting to the nuances of the real-world benchmark and might struggle to generalize robustly across varying gaze signal accuracies.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Gaze-aware MLLMs across Different Egocentric Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether gaze-aware embeddings can be transferred across different egocentric tasks (e.g., from cooking to object manipulation), maintaining or even improving performance despite the domain shift. Train gaze-aware MLLMs on one task and then fine-tune them on a new, unseen task. Evaluate the transfer performance and compare to a model that is re-trained from scratch. This will shed light on whether gaze-aware embeddings capture general, task-agnostic representations of user intent and attention.
CONTROLS: Compare the fine-tuned model to a re-trained model without gaze-aware embeddings (on the new task), and to a model that is re-trained on a related but different task (serving as a related task baseline).
COST: 2163.69
PREDICTION: Gaze-aware embeddings will show robust transfer performance across related egocentric tasks, leveraging the shared structure of attention and user intentions. However, they might struggle to adapt to highly dissimilar tasks (e.g., vastly different action spaces or modalities), where the gaze-aware model may over-emphasize irrelevant features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Can We Predict Eye-tracking Error Tolerance of Gaze-aware MLLMs?
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a method to assess the robustness of gaze-aware MLLMs to eye-tracking signal degradation or errors. Investigate how the accuracy of eye-tracking data affects the overall performance of the gaze-aware models. Introduce a small perturbation in the eye-tracking data during training and measure the model's ability to generalize to different noise levels. This study will help quantify the gain in performance through the use of expensive and hard-to-find high-accuracy eye-tracking data.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline model that has not seen any noise in the data, and to a model trained with perfect eye-tracking data.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Gaze-aware MLLMs will show significant degradation in performance with the introduction of increasing levels of noise in eye-tracking data, including marginal to moderate accuracy drops when only introducing small amounts of noise (even as low as ± 5%), where smallest noise threshold may vary as much as 3 times between different bottom-k frozen k-component Llama variants)

Specifically, focus on the gaze cue-agnostic and gaze cue-inclusive versions of the EGTEA question answering tasks. Compare the model's performance under both conditions to evaluate the impact of gaze information on user intent understanding.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current best model trained on the same dataset but without gaze information ablation, and compare to random guess performance baseline. In addition, compare to the well-established question answering model on the EGTEA dataset, serving as a single-baseline.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Improved performance with gaze information, especially in questions that require attention to specific objects or actions, though the impact might be limited due to the model's reliance on pre-trained visual features, and the absence of fine-grained gaze data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablation Study on Gaze-aware Embeddings for Egocentric Vision
PROPOSAL: Explore the impact of incorporating gaze-aware embeddings into pre-trained MLLMs. Specifically, modify the embeddings of the EGTEA dataset to reflect the camera wearer's attention (based on eye-tracking data) and evaluate different granularities of gaze-aware embeddings (e.g., per-frame, per-action, or per-object level). Analyze the effect of these modifications on the MLLMs' user intent understanding performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original model without gaze-aware embeddings, and to a variant that uses a naive approach (e.g., simply conditioning on the first frame with gaze attention). Also compare to the full gaze-signal-based model as proposed in task 1. Additionally, compare the results to models trained with varying levels of gaze signal noise (e.g., by randomly perturbing gaze attention maps).
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: Improved user intent understanding when gaze-aware embeddings are used, with optimal results when embeddings are fine-grained and adapt to the complex requirements of the question answering tasks. However, this may come at the cost of increased model complexity and potential overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-world Benchmark for Gaze-aware MLLMs in Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Create a real-world benchmark, leveraging user study data and annotated egocentric videos from common tasks (e.g., cooking, object manipulation, or navigation). Develop a diverse set of question answering tasks focusing on user intent, attention, and action understanding. Compare the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs (with and without gaze-aware modifications) on both this benchmark and the EGTEA dataset. Investigate the correlation between model performance and gaze signal accuracy, controlling for other variables such as annotation quality and dataset size.
CONTROLS: Compare to the current state-of-the-art MLLMs (including the gaze-aware version from task 2), and develop a baseline of a gaze-independent model trained on the new benchmark.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: State-of-the-art models will show significant improvements on both the EGTEA and the proposed real-world benchmarks when they utilize gaze-aware embeddings, but will have a harder time adapting to the nuances of the real-world benchmark and might struggle to generalize robustly across varying gaze signal accuracies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Gaze-aware MLLMs across Different Egocentric Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether gaze-aware embeddings can be transferred across different egocentric tasks (e.g., from cooking to object manipulation), maintaining or even improving performance despite the domain shift. Train gaze-aware MLLMs on one task and then fine-tune them on a new, unseen task. Evaluate the transfer performance and compare to a model that is re-trained from scratch. This will shed light on whether gaze-aware embeddings capture general, task-agnostic representations of user intent and attention.
CONTROLS: Compare the fine-tuned model to a re-trained model without gaze-aware embeddings (on the new task), and to a model that is re-trained on a related but different task (serving as a related task baseline).
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: Gaze-aware embeddings will show robust transfer performance across related egocentric tasks, leveraging the shared structure of attention and user intentions. However, they might struggle to adapt to highly dissimilar tasks (e.g., vastly different action spaces or modalities), where the gaze-aware model may over-emphasize irrelevant features.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Gaze_signals for Improved MLLM's User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: 
Modify task 1 to focus on the insightful subset of EGTEA questions that exclusively require the understanding of the user's focus and intention from the isolated egocentric video frames, thereby allowing the model to effectively leverage the power of gaze signals for a user-centric AI experience. Include evaluations using the triplet-based metric (R@1, R@5) which maintains the ranked relevance between the prompt's context, user's gaze, and the predicted answer.
CONTROLS: Keep the same set of controls as in task 1, with the addition of the novel triplet-based metric evaluation.
COST: unchanged at 2000
PREDICTION: The performance improvement due to the utilization of egocentric gaze signals will be to be more pronounced on the improved task definition, with notable gains in recall at high ranks (R@1, R@5), showing how gaze information is integral to user-centric answering tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Can We Predict Eye-tracking Error Tolerance of Gaze-aware MLLMs?
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a method to assess the robustness of gaze-aware MLLMs to eye-tracking signal degradation or errors. Investigate how the accuracy of eye-tracking data affects the overall performance of the gaze-aware models. Introduce a small perturbation in the eye-tracking data during training and measure the model's ability to generalize to different noise levels. This study will help quantify the gain in performance through the use of expensive and hard-to-find high-accuracy eye-tracking data.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline model that has not seen any noise in the data, and to a model trained with perfect eye-tracking data.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Gaze-aware MLLMs will show significant degradation in performance with the introduction of increasing levels of noise in eye-tracking data, including marginal to moderate accuracy drops when only introducing small amounts of noise (even as low as ± 5%), where smallest noise threshold may vary as much as 3 times between different bottom-k frozen k-component Llama variants)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Novel Dataset: Ground Truth Egocentric Gaze Data for MLLM Training and Evaluation
PROPOSAL: 
Create and release a novel, large-scale dataset focused on capturing high-quality, accurate ground truth egocentric gaze data for use in MLLM training and evaluation. Include 10 hours of manually annotated video recordings featuring everyday tasks, demonstrating a wide range of gaze patterns and user interactions. This dataset will provide the research community with a much-needed resource for studying gaze-aware MLLMs and comparisons of different methods for inferring user intent from eye-tracking data.
CONTROLS: Make this dataset available to the public and compare MLLMs trained with this novel dataset to models trained on existing datasets.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The novel dataset will become a game-changer in the field, having a significant impact on the performance of gaze-aware MLLMs with notable improvements seen across models when training on this high-quality ground truth data, outperforming baseline performance up to 30%.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze-driven Hierarchical Modeling for Egocentric Vision and Action Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel gaze-driven hierarchical modeling approach that combines scene parsing, object detection, and action recognition modules, with gaze information being used to guide the hierarchical structure and decision-making. This will allow for more accurate understanding of user intent and action, particularly in scenarios where context and attention are critical. Evaluate the effectiveness of this model on the EGTEA and the novel dataset from task 6.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard, non-hierarchical model trained on the same data, and to a model with a fixed hierarchical structure trained without gaze information.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: The gaze-driven hierarchical model will outperform both the standard model and the hierarchical model without gaze information on the EGTEA and the novel dataset, showing improved accuracy in action recognition and scene parsing up to 12% for EGTEA.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Egocentric Gaze-aware Multi-task Learning for Unified Vision-language Understanding
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously trains gaze-aware MLLMs to perform multiple tasks relevant to egocentric vision and language understanding, such as question answering, object detection, and action recognition. This framework will leverage gaze information to improve task performance and enable more comprehensive understanding of user intent. Evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on the EGTEA and the novel dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare to a single-task learning model trained on the same data, and to a multi-task learning model without gaze information.
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: The proposed egocentric gaze-aware multi-task learning framework will outperform both the single-task learning model and the multi-task learning model without gaze information on the EGTEA and the novel dataset, demonstrating improved performance across multiple tasks, with up to 20% accuracy gains on object detection and scene parsing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assembling the Components: An Integrated Gaze-aware Egocentric AI Assistant
PROPOSAL: Design and develop an end-to-end gaze-aware egocentric AI assistant that integrates the previously proposed techniques, including gaze-aware embeddings, hierarchical modeling, and multi-task learning. The goal is to create a proactive AI assistant that can understand user intent, provide personalized recommendations, and facilitate seamless interaction. Evaluate the performance of the integrated model on the EGTEA and the novel dataset, and conduct user studies to assess the practical impact of the proposed AI assistant.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standalone models and frameworks proposed in previous tasks.
COST: 38000
PREDICTION: The integrated gaze-aware egocentric AI assistant will outperform the standalone models and frameworks, demonstrating significant gains in user intent understanding, personalized recommendation, and overall user experience. However, it may require careful optimization and tuning to achieve optimal performance, and its practical deployment may be limited by the availability of high-quality gaze data and suitable computing resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Impact of Gaze Signal Quality on MLLM Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the accuracy of target gaze data affects the performance of MLLMs with gaze attention. We'll train the MLLM on high-quality gaze data (e.g., 5Hz) and use it to evaluate on tasks with different levels of noise or occlusion in the gaze signal (e.g., 1Hz, 2Hz, with/without occlusion). This will be done on a fixed egocentric video dataset (e.g., Epic-Kitchens) and a custom real-world eye-tracking dataset collected with different gaze tracking systems.
CONTROLS: Two baselines: 1) MLLM with gaze attention but without gaze data, and 2) MLLM without gaze attention but trained on high-quality gaze data (to test if gaze data helps even without attention).
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: The performance of the MLLM will degrade as the quality of the gaze signal decreases, with the drop in performance most significant when gaze data is paired with gaze attention. If the gaze signal is highly inaccurate, the model may underperform or refuse to learn.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Egocentric Gaze-Aware MLLM Architectures with Self-Attention
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate MLLM architectures that incorporate self-attention mechanisms specifically designed to leverage egocentric gaze information. We'll compare the performance of different gaze-aware MLLM variants (e.g., gaze GUIDED self-attention, gaze-weighted cross-modal self-attention) against a standard MLLM and the variant with gaze attention (Proposal 1). The architectures will be trained on EPIC-Kitchens and evaluated on a range of egocentric video question answering tasks that involve user attention (e.g., "What are you looking at?").
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline architectures 1) standard MLLM, 2) gaze-attended MLLM (Proposal 1), and 3) gaze-paired MLLM without self-attention.
COST: 8295
PREDICTION: The gaze-aware MLLM with the right architectural design (e.g., gaze GUIDED self-attention) should better align the model's focus with the user's gaze and lead to improved performance on tasks involving user attention and focus. However, the optimization challenge might be significant if the gaze signal is highly variable, and the model may fail to converge to a well-performing solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Gaze Signals for Proactive Personal AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: We will use the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark EGTEA+ and its subset, the Restaurants dataset, with real-world gaze data provided by a state-of-the-art eye-tracking technique (Rosenthaler et al., 2006). We'll treat gaze as a multi-dimensional feature vector, and store this vector in addition to the RGB frames in our visual tokens. As a control, we will also train and evaluate on the same dataset but with gaze information present only during testing.
CONTROLS: (1) Using pre-trained Visual BERT as the standard baseline for egocentric video QA, with gaze absent from training data (for examining the baseline's ability to interpret gaze), (2) Multi-task training using both the RGB frames and gaze features (to investigate improved model performance).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a statistically significant improvement when using gaze features, especially in cases of multi-task training, though long-term user intentions might prove challenging for the model to fully grasp due to memory capacity and diffused focus. We also expect the control baseline to reveal limited capacity of the state-of-the-art model for interpreting gaze features even when they are available.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Eye-Tracking Gaze Signal Accuracy on Egocentric MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will analyze how different gaze signal accuracy levels affect the performance of our egocentric MLLM. For this purpose, we will synthetically corrupt the eye-tracking gaze data by introducing a noise variable that controls the gaze signal's reliability. Our baseline experiment 1 will use perfect gaze signals, and in follow-up experiments, we will incrementally increase the noise level. We will then compare the performance of the model across different noise levels and analyze the impact of noisy gaze signals on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Experiment 1 (perfect gaze): same as our first experiment (using EGTEA+ Restaurants), (2) Baseline upper-bound control using the real gaze data (to assess the maximum potential performance), and (3) Ablation experiment using a model with no gaze features.
COST: 8295
PREDICTION: We anticipate that introducing noise into the gaze signal will cause the performance to degrade, with the model being highly sensitive to gaze signal quality, especially for certain types of questions that heavily rely on precise gaze information, which may hinder long-term tracking and interpretation of user intentions.

TITLE: Multi-Modal Fusion for Egocentric User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will explore multi-modal fusion techniques to incorporate both visual (RGB frames and gaze features) and contextual information (e.g., spoken dialogue or text input) into our egocentric MLLMs, to improve their ability to infer user intentions from egocentric video. To this end, we will implement and evaluate various fusion architectures, including attention-based and transformer-based approaches, on the EGTEA+ Restaurants dataset with real-world gaze data.
CONTROLS: (1) RGB-only baseline model, (2) Fusion of RGB frames and gaze features (Experiment 1), (3) Fusion of RGB frames, gaze features, and contextual information.

PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant gain in performance when incorporating contextual information alongside visual and gaze signals, particularly for tasks involving longer-term user intentions or scene understanding, and that choosing the right fusion architecture and models will be crucial for leveraging multiple streams of information effectively.

TITLE: Investigating the Generalizability of Egocentric MLLMs with Gaze to Unseen Environments
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our egocentric MLLMs with gaze in unseen environments, i.e., testing scenarios involving tasks and settings not seen before during training. To this end, we will create synthetic testing environments that vary in complexity (restaurant vs. kitchen vs. living room) and task type (preparing food vs. playing a game), and examine how well our models can adapt to these new scenarios while maintaining their gaze-based performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline model, (2) Our earlier best-performing model from Investigation 1, (3) Model without gaze.
COST: 9360
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the egocentric MLLMs with gaze will perform significantly better than the baseline in unseen environments, as their design allows them to incorporate gaze-based contextual information effectively, thus improving adaptability and generalization abilities. However, the performance may degrade as the environment becomes increasingly dissimilar from the training data or as the tasks become more abstract or abstracted away from direct gaze relevance.

PROPOSAL: We will develop and test a new framework that fuses information from multiple modalities, including gaze-tracking, egocentric video, and user-provided text input, for optimized personalized recommendations. We propose a hierarchical fusion of the diverse modalities to ensure effective and higher-quality recommendations. For this purpose, we will first apply multi-modal fusion techniques to effectively integrate the information from the distinct modalities and then apply dimensionality reduction and attention mechanisms to focus on the features that convey the critical information.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline (Visual-Aid Gaze with no egocentric information), (2) Baseline (Egocentric with no gaze information), (3) Proposed Framework (Visual-Aid + Egocentric), and (4) Interactive Personalized Recommendation System using human weighing visual-aid prediction against egocentric personal interests and user input.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: By leveraging the strengths of different types of modalities and addressing the limitations of traditional methods, we anticipate that the proposed unified framework will provide matched, highly-personalized trajectories for both diverse modalities.

TITLE: Investigating the Application of Egocentric MLLMs with Gaze in Human-AI Collaboration Systems
PROPOSAL: We will explore the practical applications of our egocentric MLLMs with gaze in human-AI collaboration systems, such as virtual assistants, gaming platforms, and other settings where users interact with AI systems in a proactive and goal-oriented manner. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Gaze Signals for Proactive Personal AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: We will use the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark EGTEA+ and its subset, the Restaurants dataset, with real-world gaze data provided by a state-of-the-art eye-tracking technique (Rosenthaler et al., 2006). We'll treat gaze as a multi-dimensional feature vector, and store this vector in addition to the RGB frames in our visual tokens. As a control, we will also train and evaluate on the same dataset but with gaze information present only during testing.
CONTROLS: (1) Using pre-trained Visual BERT as the standard baseline for egocentric video QA, with gaze absent from training data (for examining the baseline's ability to interpret gaze), (2) Multi-task training using both the RGB frames and gaze features (to investigate improved model performance).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a statistically significant improvement when using gaze features, especially in cases of multi-task training, though long-term user intentions might prove challenging for the model to fully grasp due to memory capacity and diffused focus. We also expect the control baseline to reveal limited capacity of the state-of-the-art model for interpreting gaze features even when they are available.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Eye-Tracking Gaze Signal Accuracy on Egocentric MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will analyze how different gaze signal accuracy levels affect the performance of our egocentric MLLM. For this purpose, we will synthetically corrupt the eye-tracking gaze data by introducing a noise variable that controls the gaze signal's reliability. Our baseline experiment 1 will use perfect gaze signals, and in follow-up experiments, we will incrementally increase the noise level. We will then compare the performance of the model across different noise levels and analyze the impact of noisy gaze signals on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Experiment 1 (perfect gaze): same as our first experiment (using EGTEA+ Restaurants), (2) Baseline upper-bound control using the real gaze data (to assess the maximum potential performance), and (3) Ablation experiment using a model with no gaze features.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that introducing noise into the gaze signal will cause the performance to degrade, with the model being highly sensitive to gaze signal quality, especially for certain types of questions that heavily rely on precise gaze information, which may hinder long-term tracking and interpretation of user intentions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Fusion for Egocentric User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will explore multi-modal fusion techniques to incorporate both visual (RGB frames and gaze features) and contextual information (e.g., spoken dialogue or text input) into our egocentric MLLMs, to improve their ability to infer user intentions from egocentric video. To this end, we will implement and evaluate various fusion architectures, including attention-based and transformer-based approaches, on the EGTEA+ Restaurants dataset with real-world gaze data.
CONTROLS: (1) RGB-only baseline model, (2) Fusion of RGB frames and gaze features (Experiment 1), (3) Fusion of RGB frames, gaze features, and contextual information.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant gain in performance when incorporating contextual information alongside visual and gaze signals, particularly for tasks involving longer-term user intentions or scene understanding, and that choosing the right fusion architecture and models will be crucial for leveraging multiple streams of information effectively.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised: Using Hierarchical Video-Mask Representation for Egocentric Visual Understanding with Gaze
PROPOSAL: We will propose a hierarchical video-mask representation method to incorporate gaze information into our egocentric MLLMs, allowing the model to learn to focus on the relevant spatial locations within the video frames. To this end, we will design a novel visual representation of video frames as masked regions based on the gaze location, and process these masked regions in a hierarchical manner to leverage information at different scales. Our goal is to improve the model's ability to selectively focus on gaze-relevant regions and learn more robust and accurate video representations.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline model using RGB frames only, (2) Model without gaze, using only the RGB frames as input.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: This hierarchical approach to integrating gaze information is expected to significantly enhance the model's capacity for egocentric visual understanding, by guiding the model to focus on gaze-relevant regions within the video frames and facilitating the learning of more robust visual representations. However, fine-tuning the hyperparameters of the hierarchical network may be required to achieve the best performance, depending on the trade-off between richer video representations and gaze information incorporation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Investigating Egocentric Gaze Signals for Proactive Personal AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: We will extend our earlier experiment by incorporating user-defined action-based questions in the EGTEA+ Restaurants dataset. These action-based questions are tailored toward evaluating the model's action understanding capabilities when gaze information is provided. To further augment this study, we will introduce an additional control experiment by using the gaze information only during training, but discarding it during evaluation.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline without gaze during training and evaluation (our initial experiment), (2) Baseline with gaze during training but discarded during evaluation, and (3) Our original experiment with gaze provided during both training and evaluation.
COST: 35000
PREDICTION: By expanding the types of questions and evaluation settings, we anticipate observing even more robust performance benefits when employing egocentric gaze signals, as the model becomes more attuned to user intentions and gaze-relevant information, thus outperforming the baseline condition significantly across various understanding and action-related tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Generalizability of Egocentric MLLMs with Gaze to Unseen Environments
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our egocentric MLLMs with gaze in unseen environments, i.e., testing scenarios involving tasks and settings not seen before during training. To this end, we will create synthetic testing environments that vary in complexity (restaurant vs. kitchen vs. living room) and task type (preparing food vs. playing a game), and examine how well our models can adapt to these new scenarios while maintaining their gaze-based performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline model, (2) Our earlier best-performing model from Investigation 1, (3) Model without gaze.
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the egocentric MLLMs with gaze will perform significantly better than the baseline in unseen environments, as their design allows them to incorporate gaze-based contextual information effectively, thus improving adaptability and generalization abilities. However, the performance may degrade as the environment becomes increasingly dissimilar from the training data or as the tasks become more abstract or abstracted away from direct gaze relevance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Evaluating the Impact of Eye-Tracking Gaze Signal Accuracy on Egocentric MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will extend our earlier investigation by incorporating multiple gaze measurement modalities (e.g., pupil centers, gaze points, head pose, timestamped events) in addition to the noise variable, to explore how various gaze signal characteristics influence model performance. Our updated implementation includes incorporating different levels of noise (e.g., signal-to-noise ratio) into the eye-tracking gaze data and selecting multiple features that describe each gaze signal component, as well as methods to visualize the classification biases as well as correlations between the different gaze features and human action perceptions.
CONTROLS: (1) Our earlier Experiment 1 with single noise level, (2) A new set of visualizations to observe how different gaze features affect model performance.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: By considering different modalities of gaze information, we anticipate increased robustness of our model to various gaze signal characteristics, which will result in more reliable performance under a broader range of real-world conditions. Moreover, identifying the types of gaze features relevant for each goal (e.g., food preparation currently sees robustness most impacted on by pupil-centered gaze accuracy) could help us narrow down the critical components of the model for egocentric MLLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Examining Gradient Conflicts in Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate gradient conflicts between text and vision modalities in a modality-shared AR UMM on real-world datasets (e.g., COCO Captions, VQA v2), using a simple control condition where the UMM is trained to predict the next token in each modality separately.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: modality-separated training; Baseline 2: modality-shared training without gradient norm clipping; Ablation 1: equalize the weight of text and vision loss terms.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect gradient conflicts to degrade performance and increase instability, particularly in text-to-image generation tasks, and that ablation 1 can mitigate these conflicts, improving training efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Depth-Dependent Gradient Conflicts in Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Layer-wise analyze the gradient conflicts between text and vision modalities using a subset of the transformer layers in a modality-shared AR UMM, focusing on real-world datasets and using a control condition similar to Experiment 1 (Examining Gradient Conflicts in Modality-Shared AR UMMs).
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: non-modality shared transformer layer analysis; Ablation 1: prohibit weight updates to selected layers; Ablation 2: variance-aware gradient clipping.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that inter-modal conflicts will be more pronounced in intermediate layers where representations become increasingly abstract and semantic, and that ablating or clipping gradients can help reduce these conflicts and improve performance, particularly in text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Modality-Specific Statistics in Discretized Sequences
PROPOSAL: Investigate the statistical properties of discretized image-token and natural language sequences within a modality-shared AR UMM, using both real-world datasets and synthetic data for controlled analysis, and compare these statistics to understand the root cause of inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard discretization; Ablation 1: sentence-level averaging; Ablation 2: sequence-wise uniform quantization; Baseline 2: comparison to natural language statistics.
COST: 8295
PREDICTION: We expect that the statistical differences between image-token and natural language sequences can explain a significant portion of the inter-modal conflicts, and that specific quantization strategies can mitigate these differences and improve performance in modality-shared AR UMMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transformer-Based Adaptive Quantization for Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of adaptive quantization strategies guided by a transformer-based model that predicts the optimal quantization parameters for each input sequence in a modality-shared AR UMM, using real-world datasets and comparing to standard discretization.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard discretization; Baseline 2: simple adaptive quantization; Ablation 1: replace transformer with non-learned quantization; Ablation 2: decouple quantization from input sequence.
COST: 10649.4129
PREDICTION: We anticipate that adaptive quantization can adapt to the input sequence and modalities, reducing inter-modal conflicts and improving performance in modality-shared AR UMMs, especially with a well-designed transformer-based predictor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reduced-Complexity Modality-Shared AR UMMs using Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Explore reducing the complexity of modality-shared AR UMMs with a combination of knowledge distillation and quantization techniques, where the complex original model serves as the teacher to guide a smaller student model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard modality-shared AR UMM; Baseline 2: simple knowledge distillation; Baseline 3: student model with uniform quantization; Ablation 1: compare knowledge distillation with different trigger techniques; Ablation 2: add quantization to the teacher model.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed reduced-complexity modality-shared AR UMM will maintain most of the benefits of modality sharing while achieving faster inference speed, reduced energy consumption, and improved generalizability for applications such as text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of adaptive quantization strategies guided by a transformer-based model that predicts the optimal quantization parameters for each input sequence in a modality-shared AR UMM, using real-world datasets and comparing to standard discretization.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard discretization; Baseline 2: simple adaptive quantization; Ablation 1: replace transformer with non-learned quantization; Ablation 2: decouple quantization from input sequence.
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that adaptive quantization can adapt to the input sequence and modalities, reducing inter-modal conflicts and improving performance in modality-shared AR UMMs, especially with a well-designed transformer-based predictor.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining Transformer-Based Adaptive Quantization for Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Since adaptive quantization relies on additional transformer-based model, refine this model to be more computationally efficient and layers-aggregated, while preserving its predictability of optimal quantization parameters. In addition, explore two types of knowledge distillation techniques, one with teacher-student architecture and the other with soft target generation, for enabling efficient knowledge transfer to the adaptive quantization model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: original adaptive quantization; Baseline 2: knowledge distillation with teacher-student architecture; Baseline 3: knowledge distillation with soft target generation; Ablation 1: remove distillation; Ablation 2: compare teacher-student architecture with soft target generation.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: We expect that the refined adaptive quantization model with knowledge distillation will achieve a better trade-off between efficiency and performance, reducing the burden of additional model training and achieving improved modality-sharing benefits in modality-shared AR UMMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reduced-Complexity Modality-Shared AR UMMs using Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Explore reducing the complexity of modality-shared AR UMMs with a combination of knowledge distillation and quantization techniques, where the complex original model serves as the teacher to guide a smaller student model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard modality-shared AR UMM; Baseline 2: simple knowledge distillation; Baseline 3: student model with uniform quantization; Ablation 1: compare knowledge distillation with different trigger techniques; Ablation 2: add quantization to the teacher model.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed reduced-complexity modality-shared AR UMM will maintain most of the benefits of modality sharing while achieving faster inference speed, reduced energy consumption, and improved generalizability for applications such as text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking State-of-the-Art Modality-Shared AR UMMs for Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of the reduced-complexity modality-shared AR UMM and other state-of-the-art modality-shared AR UMMs on real-world benchmarks such as COCO Captions, VQA v2, and text-to-image generation tasks, providing a comprehensive evaluation of modality-shared AR UMMs for practical use cases.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard modality-shared AR UMM; Baseline 2: simplified modality-shared AR UMM; Ablation 1: compare results on various downstream tasks and datasets; Ablation 2: analyze the generalizability and scales of different state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 55000
PREDICTION: We expect that the reduced-complexity modality-shared AR UMM and other state-of-the-art modality-shared AR UMMs will show significant improvements over previous methods on various real-world benchmarks and datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of modality-sharing for real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Training and Evaluation Strategies for Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate and optimize the training and evaluation strategies for modality-shared AR UMMs, including gradient accumulation, learning rate scheduling, and evaluation metrics, to better capture the strengths and weaknesses of these models.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard training and evaluation protocol; Ablation 1: evaluate different gradient accumulation strategies; Ablation 2: compare various learning rate scheduling techniques; Ablation 3: analyze the impact of different evaluation metrics.
COST: 63000
PREDICTION: We expect that refined training and evaluation strategies will improve the performance and robustness of modality-shared AR UMMs, allowing for better generalization and applicability to real-world tasks such as text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Modality-Split and Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Propose a unified framework that can seamlessly switch between modality-split and modality-shared architectures for AR UMMs, depending on the specific task requirements and modalities involved, and evaluate its performance on various real-world benchmarks and tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard modality-split and modality-shared AR UMMs; Ablation 1: compare performance on different tasks and modalities; Ablation 2: evaluate the impact of framework configuration on model performance.
COST: 78000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the unified framework will provide a more flexible and adaptive approach to modality management in AR UMMs, allowing for improved performance on a wide range of tasks and applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Split and Modality-Shared AR UMMs with a Plug-and-Play Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a plug-and-play framework that allows researchers and practitioners to easily design, modify, and compare various modality-split and modality-shared AR UMMs architectures, facilitating the development of new models and applications in the field.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard modality-split and modality-shared AR UMMs; Evaluation Metrics 1: performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1 score, BLEU score); Evaluation Metrics 2: efficiency metrics (e.g., inference speed, model size).
COST: 98000
PREDICTION: We expect that the proposed plug-and-play framework will significantly accelerate the development of new modality-split and modality-shared AR UMMs and facilitate the creation of new applications, contributing to the advancement of the field.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: PrIncipled Modality Confict Analysis for AutoRegressive UMMs
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the gradient conflicts between text and vision modalities in an AR UMM. Specifically, we will analyze the KL-divergence between their token distributions at each layer, using metrics such as pairwise KL-divergence (pKL) and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JS). The metrics are calculated at each layer to identify which layers exhibit more modality conflicts.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that has separate transformers for text and vision, to understand the impact of modality sharing on conflicts.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see greater modality conflicts in intermediate layers, where the language model develops semantic representations separate from visual tokens. The performance might degrade if our model is overfitting to specific benchmarks, like text-to-image generation.

The goal of this experiment is to establish a foundation for understanding where modality conflicts arise in modality-shared AR UMMs, by assessing how they manifest across different layers and tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Inter-Modal Gradient Flow for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the flow of gradients between text and vision modalities within an AR UMM by analyzing the Eykholt et al. alignment metrics, Infomax ratio and Information Theory's Conditional Mutual Information. These metrics measure how much the gradients of one modality are aligned or misaligned with those of the other, capturing the interplay of the two modalities during optimization.
CONTROLS: Control for information flow by ensuring the separate transformers for text and vision also benefit from the Eykholt metrics analysis, in order to understand information flow in these respective baselines as well.
COST: 1050 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the Eykholt metrics to highlight areas within the network where there is a significant discrepancy between the two modalities, which may correlate with modality conflicts in previous experiments, demonstrating the first connection between gradient flow and modality conflict analysis.

This proposal enhances the previous one by focusing on analyzing inter-modal gradient flow, which can provide a more direct understanding of the performance degradations seen in shared transformer models.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Specific Analysis of Modal Disentanglement
PROPOSAL: Use the modality-specific Contrastive Multi-view Coding (CMC) loss on AR-UMMs to evaluate the layer-wise representations that contribute most to modality conflicts, and disentangle representations in distinct layers. By analyzing which layers are responsible for the observed modality conflicts, we can further pinpoint where and why UMMS struggle when operating across different modalities.
CONTROLS: To isolate the impact of disentanglement, compare with an AR-UMM without the modality-specific CMC loss, to see the variations in modality conflict over layers independently of the additional regularizer.
COST: 1260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect disentangled representations to reveal higher layer-wise connections in modality conflicts by reducing shared representations' generation-power; that could help guide our UMM designs in better selecting pertinent layers to deal with these problems, as well as adjusting the side representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving AR UMMs with Modality-Aware Adaptive Routing
PROPOSAL: Design a novel adaptive routing scheme that conditions the flow of information between the text and vision modalities of the AR UMM based on their expected amount of mutual information. By dynamically adjusting the routing weights to maximize the relevant mutual information during training, we aim to reduce the negative impact of modality conflicts and promote more efficient interactions between the language and vision components.
CONTROLS: Compare against AR UMMs with fixed routing weights, as well as baselines with no routing or hand-coded routing.
COST: 1560 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our adaptive routing approach to yield improved performance across benchmark tasks by striking a better balance between modality conflicts and beneficial mutual information exchange, thus reaching previously observed, yet through other means, optimal sync ratios.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Query-Based Adaptive Training (VQBAT) for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a visual query-based adaptive training (VQBAT) approach that dynamically adjusts the training objectives and priorities for an AR UMM based on the type of task (e.g., visual question answering vs. text-to-image synthesis) and the difficulty level of the task instance. By leveraging a visuospatial attention mechanism to compute the query-based relevance scores, VQBAT enables adaptive modulation of the model's sensitivity to different aspects of the task.
CONTROLS: Evaluate VQBAT against conventional training procedures and existing adaptive training methods for AR UMMs, controlling for the level of task specificity.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that VQBAT will demonstrate improved task-averaged performance and faster adaptation to new tasks due to its ability to selectively focus on task-relevant aspects of the data and modulate the model's adaptability in response to varying task complexities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Modality Interplay through Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Apply meta-learning to AR UMMs to learn an initialization that benefits from modality interaction by making them more compatible. Train a series of AR UMMs on the same task but with different levels of modality conflict, then select the weights that best generalized across conflicts. By enabling the model to learn over a diverse range of conflicts, we can identify an initialization that generalizes well to modality-rich scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines of randomly initialized AR UMMs and meta-learning over fixed weights, to understand the additive benefit of modality-aware initialization.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect meta-learning to reveal valuable insights into model initialization by highlighting its capacity to leverage modality interplay under challenging conflict scenarios and pushing upstream sim-to-real compatibility.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reconciling Text and Image Modalities through Dual-Path Cross-Modal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel dual-path cross-modal transformer architecture in the AR UMM, where the separate paths maintain the original modal identities by using side information like labels and non-overlapping token spaces to facilitate robust and shared representation learning. By training with the dual-path framework, we aim to modulate the protagonists of both paths, module by module.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our method against a baseline model trained without these dual paths, and compare performance with existing cross-modal transformers.
COST: 2700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the dual-path approach will successfully split and distinguish related and irrelevant information between the two paths, leading to enhanced cross-modal understanding and improved generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Validation of Cross-Modal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Test the robustness of our proposed cross-modal transformers under real-world conditions by training on text-to-image datasets and evaluating their performance on diverse visual question answering and image editing tasks drawn from the real-world datasets. We will verify the cross-modal learning mechanisms' impact in production-ready models.
CONTROLS: Compare against AR UMMs not using dual-path cross-modal transformers, and evaluate their performance in terms of user satisfaction ratings and data augmentation effectiveness, quantifiable in inferior error rates in domain adaptation.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our novel approach to perform well across a range of diverse tasks, showing performance superior to cross-modal models not leveraging the multi-access route to text and image data.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Cross-Modal Learning with Guarantees
PROPOSAL: Establish a theoretical framework for analyzing the effects of modality conflicts in AR UMMs using tools from information theory. Specifically, prove a relation between the coherence and expected error of a UMM trained with a specific learning objective, and leverage the Mutual Information (MI) and conditional MI to quantify these effects and interpret results in terms of relative influence due to noise and entropy introduced by modality conflicts. This framework offers interpretable and provable guarantees on cross-modal interactions in AR UMMs.
CONTROLS: Experimental results will be used to demonstrate the feasibility of applying this framework to align the principles established by our results.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed theoretical framework to provide crucial insights into the fundamental limitations of cross-modal interaction in AR UMMs and meaningful correlations with the models we have previously developed, particularly with regards to the mitigating of noise and disparities.

TITLE: Layer-wise Modality Conflict Analysis for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interplay between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared autoregressive (AR) transformer by computing the divergence between gradients at each layer, using the optimal transport (OT) distance as a principled measure of modality conflict. We will analyze the OT-dissimilarity of gradients between text and vision embeddings across layers of a pre-trained AR UMM, on diverse visual-question-answering tasks. 
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) a simple text-language model, (ii) a standard vision-language model without autoregressive transformer, and (iii) a random initialization of the transformer. 
COST: 670
PREDICTION: We expect to find that modality conflicts primarily arise in intermediate layers, where the network representations are increasingly abstract and semantic. UMMs performance may fail when the modality conflicts grow, hindering network convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-wise Modality Conflict Analysis for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interplay between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared autoregressive (AR) transformer by computing the divergence between gradients at each layer, using the optimal transport (OT) distance as a principled measure of modality conflict. We will analyze the OT-dissimilarity of gradients between text and vision embeddings across layers of a pre-trained AR UMM, on diverse visual-question-answering tasks. 
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) a simple text-language model, (ii) a standard vision-language model without autoregressive transformer, and (iii) a random initialization of the transformer. 
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that modality conflicts primarily arise in intermediate layers, where the network representations are increasingly abstract and semantic. UMMs performance may fail when the modality conflicts grow, hindering network convergence.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-aware Gradient Normalization for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a modality-aware gradient normalization scheme to reduce inter-modal conflicts in modality-shared AR UMMs, leveraging insights from the modality conflict analysis (proposal 1) to normalize gradients with an adaptive scalar for each modality. We will experiment with projecting gradients onto a modality-specific manifold using the Fisher information matrix and examine its impact on both text and vision generation in a multi-task training setup.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) training without gradient normalization, (ii) using a fixed scalar normalization, and (iii) employing an existing normalization technique like spectral normalization. 
COST: 1064.94129
PREDICTION: We expect to see improvements in both text and vision generation by reducing gradient conflicts, with stable training and convergence, especially in scenarios where modality conflicts are pronounced, such as high-entropy text and abstract visual representations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Depth-aware Modality Routing for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a depth-aware routing mechanism to selectively route text and vision inputs through the autoregressive transformer, conditioned on the layer depth and modality-specific task requirements, allowing for more efficient modality-specific optimization. This approach will explore the relationship between representation abstraction, modality conflict, and depth in AR UMMs. Implementation details include a learnable per-layer modality flag and a probabilistic routing scheme.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) using a simple modality-aware attention mechanism, (ii) routing both modalities through all layers uniformly, and (iii) skipping modality-normalization at certain layers. 
COST: 1332
PREDICTION: We expect to see performance improvements in visual-question-answering and text-to-image synthesis tasks as modality-specific routing adapts to task requirements and reduces modality conflicts, especially when dealing with high-level tasks involving abstraction and reasoning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-conditioned Self-Attention for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel modality-conditioned self-attention mechanism to better handle inter-modal conflicts by conditioning on modality-specific information, facilitating information exchange and alignment across modalities. This mechanism will allow for modality-aware integration of self-attention and its application in both text and vision representations.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) standard self-attention mechanism, (ii) using modality-aware attention mechanisms without conditioning on modalities, and (iii) a modality-specific multi-head attention setup. 
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: We anticipate improvements in both modality-specific and joint-task performances, as modality-conditioned self-attention effectively integrates and optimizes the representations of text and vision within the AR UMM, reducing the negative impacts of inter-modal conflicts and enhancing the modeling capacity of the network.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revised Depth-wise Modality Conflict Analysis for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Refine the original layer-wise modality conflict analysis (proposal 1) by incorporating the insights from depth-aware modality routing (proposal 3) and modality-conditioned self-attention (proposal 4), examining how different route and attention mechanisms influence modality conflict and optimize AR UMM performance in various depth layers. 
CONTROLS: Compare with revised baselines: (i) revised single-task AR UMM, (ii) incorporating depth-aware routing with basic modality-aware mechanisms, and (iii) using the existing depth-wise analysis with self-attention. 
COST: 864.65
PREDICTION: By integrating multiple modality-aware mechanisms, we anticipate that the revised depth-wise analysis will uncover nuanced depth-wise dependencies and uncover ways to reduce modality conflicts, improving AR UMM performance and optimizing for better multi-task efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: AR-Uncur: An AutoRegressive Uncurriculum Learning Framework for Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce an AR-Uncur curriculum learning framework to progressively expose AR UMMs to increasingly complex and diverse text and image samples, regulated by the depth-aware routing mechanism and modality-specific normalization, allowing the model to adapt to varying modality complexities and optimize representation generalizability.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) random curriculum learning, (ii) standard multi-task learning without uncurriculum adaptation, and (iii) using curriculum learning without modality-aware routing. 
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: By guiding the learning process via structured difficulty adaptation, AR-Uncur is expected to significantly improve model robustness, better handle modality complexities, and facilitate knowledge generalization across different tasks, resulting in enhanced joint-task performance for AR UMMs.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: M-Adapter: A Modality-Adaptive Transformer for AutoRegressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a modality-adaptive M-Adapter transformer that utilizes a neural arch with dynamically switchable modules between text and vision modalities, ensuring modality-specific parameterizations and tailor-made depth routing for advanced representations within AR UMMs. Our M-Adapter will stabilize inter-modal conflicts and foster better expressive capacity across modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare with baselines: (i) naively stacked transformers (standard), (ii) using a fixed-depth alternate architecture, and (iii) employing an expert GN adapter without post-decoding training. 
COST: 1835
PREDICTION: We expect the M-Adapter to showcase notable gains in modality-specific and joint performance, enabling flexible and effective full-capability optimization in auto-regressive unified transformers, exhibiting state-of-the-art performance on key vision-text tasks.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-based Decomposition of Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers
PROPOSAL: Analyze the gradient descent process of a modality-shared autoregressive vision-language transformer on two real-world benchmarks (e.g., Flickr8k-Captions, Notre Dame Visual Question Answering). Decompose the conflict between vision and language gradients into its constituent parts using tensors or spectral analysis. Compute the layer-wise contribution of inter-modal conflicts to the overall gradient dissimilarity.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to a vanilla transformer with no modality-sharing, as well as a baseline UMM with explicit image and text encoders (e.g., MUNIT or MRT).
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: The decomposition will reveal a significant contribution of inter-modal conflicts in intermediate layers of the network. The results for the vanilla transformer will show a stark difference from the modality-shared architecture, while the baseline UMM will confirm the superiority of a single, shared transformer in some regimes, but at the cost of explicit modality separation and locally optimal solutions. We expect the method to underperform in tasks or environments where modality conflicts are unusually pronounced (e.g., human faces or complex images with novel, unseen object classes).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Rank Gradient Projections: A Debugging Tool for Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for projecting the inter-modal conflicts along the depth of a modality-shared transformer onto lower-dimensional subspaces using low-rank singular value decomposition. This will allow for a layer-wise assessment of the gradient dissimilarity between vision and language. Use this approach on a common dataset for text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption) and image editing (e.g., Editing50).
CONTROLS: Compare the low-rank projections to the standard tensor decomposition from proposal 1, and analyze the effect of different rank choices on the interpretation and visualization of inter-modal conflicts.
COST: 36991.861
PREDICTION: The low-rank gradient projections will reveal cluster-like patterns in the gradient dissimilarity matrices corresponding to different layers, and these patterns will show a clear relationship with the texture and composition statistics inherent in different types of visual data. We predict this method will be useful in mitigating conflicts for earlier layers with simpler representations but may struggle with late-stage abstract representations due to over-compression and mismatch between texture and object features.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Aware Auxiliary Masks for Reduced Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate incorporating task-aware auxiliary masks to modulate the propagation of vision and language gradients within the transformer architecture. This would involve computing a mask at each layer based on the input type (vision or language) and task requirements. Use this approach on image editing (e.g., Editing50), visual question answering (e.g., VQA2.0), and text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption) datasets.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different mask designs and thresholds on conflict reduction and task performance relative to a vanilla transformer and a baseline UMM with task-specific branches.
COST:  30000
PREDICTION: The task-aware auxiliary masks will lead to consistent improvements in task performance and reduced gradient dissimilarity between vision and language for some tasks, particularly those with well-defined, linguistic representations (e.g., Editing50), but may need adjustments to meet specific requirements and sometimes even introduce conflicts for abstract tasks like VQA due to the strongly entangled matrix-like texture of scene graphs, violating our wish for transparency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modality Regularizers for Gradient Alignment in Unified Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Design and implement a set of regularizers to align the gradients of vision and language during training and address inter-modal conflicts by imposing constraints between modalities. Evaluate this approach on diverse datasets for text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption), visual reasoning (e.g., VQA2.0), and image editing (e.g., Editing50).
CONTROLS: Compare the regularizer-based approach to the baseline UMM and the transformer architecture without regularization, using metrics that assess alignment and task performance.
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: The gradient alignment regularizers will show a moderate improvement in task performance and a reduction in inter-modal conflicts, especially for language-driven tasks. However, this method may lead to under-specialization of modalities, degrading the performance when a specific modality significantly dominates the other (e.g., learning topography in one task poorly affects the map projections of the other).

TITLE: Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation for Reduced Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers
PROPOSAL: Use cross-modal knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from task-specialized models or modal encoders to a modality-shared transformer, thereby reducing inter-modal conflicts. Specifically, train a modality-shared transformer on a distilled version of the task data, which is obtained by distilling knowledge from a task-specialized model. Evaluate this approach on various vision-language tasks, including text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption), visual question answering (e.g., VQA2.0), and image editing (e.g., Editing50).
CONTROLS: Compare the cross-modal knowledge distillation approach to a transformer without distillation, as well as a baseline UMM with explicit image and text encoders, using metrics that assess task performance and modality conflict reduction.

PREDICTION: The cross-modal knowledge distillation approach will lead to a reduction in inter-modal conflicts and improved task performance, as it transfers knowledge from task-specialized models to reduce the need for explicit modality encoders. However, this method may require careful choice of knowledge distillation temperatures and ratios, as large or small temperature values might prevent optimal retention or diffusion of modality information between task regions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-based Decomposition of Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers
PROPOSAL: Analyze the gradient descent process of a modality-shared autoregressive vision-language transformer on two real-world benchmarks (e.g., Flickr8k-Captions, Notre Dame Visual Question Answering). Decompose the conflict between vision and language gradients into its constituent parts using tensors or spectral analysis. Compute the layer-wise contribution of inter-modal conflicts to the overall gradient dissimilarity.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to a vanilla transformer with no modality-sharing, as well as a baseline UMM with explicit image and text encoders (e.g., MUNIT or MRT).
COST: 72000
PREDICTION: The decomposition will reveal a significant contribution of inter-modal conflicts in intermediate layers of the network. The results for the vanilla transformer will show a stark difference from the modality-shared architecture, while the baseline UMM will confirm the superiority of a single, shared transformer in some regimes, but at the cost of explicit modality separation and locally optimal solutions. We expect the method to underperform in tasks or environments where modality conflicts are unusually pronounced (e.g., human faces or complex images with novel, unseen object classes).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-Rank Gradient Projections: A Debugging Tool for Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for projecting the inter-modal conflicts along the depth of a modality-shared transformer onto lower-dimensional subspaces using low-rank singular value decomposition. This will allow for a layer-wise assessment of the gradient dissimilarity between vision and language. Use this approach on a common dataset for text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption) and image editing (e.g., Editing50).
CONTROLS: Compare the low-rank projections to the standard tensor decomposition from proposal 1, and analyze the effect of different rank choices on the interpretation and visualization of inter-modal conflicts.
COST: 110000
PREDICTION: The low-rank gradient projections will reveal cluster-like patterns in the gradient dissimilarity matrices corresponding to different layers, and these patterns will show a clear relationship with the texture and composition statistics inherent in different types of visual data. We predict this method will be useful in mitigating conflicts for earlier layers with simpler representations but may struggle with late-stage abstract representations due to over-compression and mismatch between texture and object features.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED - Automated Analysis and Mitigation of Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers
PROPOSAL: 1. Gradient-based Decomposition of Inter-Modal Conflicts in Vision-Language Transformers (as initially proposed) 
           2. Extend low-rank gradient projections to include automated methods for mitigating inter-modal conflicts by adaptively refactoring the transformer weights to reduce gradient dissimilarity. Test this approach on datasets for text-to-image generation (e.g., COCO-Caption), visual question answering (e.g., VQA2.0), and image editing (e.g., Editing50).
CONTROLS: Compare the refactored models to: baseline models that did not undergo adaptation; models with fixed, pre-defined knowledge specialization for different tasks or modalities (e.g., fork-based or expertise-based UMM); and models with otherwise complex structures like MUNIT or deep network fusion on NN-SFashion.
COST: 162000
PREDICTION: The adaptive mitigation method will yield significant performance improvements on tasks affected by modality conflicts, with median increases of 8-10 points on standard evaluation metrics (e.g., F1-score, BLEU). We anticipate challenges for adaptation in settings where the morphological distance between image and text tokens is large, as may be the case for tasks involving abstract, high-level attribute (e.g., class vs color).

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Graph-based Analysis of Gradient Conflicts in Modality-shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based framework to visualize and analyze the layer-wise interplay between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR UMM. This will involve constructing a weighted graph where nodes represent transformer layers, edges represent gradient flows between layers, and edge weights capture the magnitude of gradient flows. We will leverage Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to analyze this graph structure and quantify gradient conflicts in a principled, layer-wise manner. The proposed framework will be trained and validated on visual question answering (VQA) and text-to-image generation tasks using the COCO Captions and ImageNet datasets, respectively.
CONTROLS: Analyze a baseline AR UMM model without modality-sharing, and compare the results with a simple ablation study that removes the vision branch.
COST: 670 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The graph-based analysis will reveal that gradient conflicts vary significantly across different layers, with more pronounced conflicts in intermediate layers. This analysis will help identify the root causes of inter-modal conflicts and guide the design of modality-aware AR UMMs. The proposed framework may fail if the graph structure is too complex to analyze accurately, or if the edge weights calculation is computationally expensive.

This will provide a theoretical justification for the need for more advanced and flexible modeling paradigms, such as those proposed in previous research questions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will use the recent video-description benchmark, VAPT (pronunciation, action, posture, object, text), as a modified benchmark to assess the ability of audiovisual MLLMs to describe emotions accurately, while grounding them in the relevant audiovisual cues. Concretely, we select 1500 real-world videos from existing MLLB datasets, featuring human faces with varied expressions (e.g., Amsterdam Dedicated Intonation Contour Set, AFIRe, MMI-Expression). We train a variety of MLLMs (Longformer, Swin, T5-3B), learning from a combination of real-world data and the text-prompted emotion instruction data. We then evaluate these MLLMs' emotion descriptions on VAPT without any hallucination-controlling fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Baseline is our implementation of existing LLaMA-based model reusing previously trained models, and ablation studies comparing several model configurations and hyperparameter adjustments for the MLLMs tested.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Given the tendency of MLLMs to hallucinate, we expect to observe such behavior in at least 150 out of the 1500 emotion-descriptions, indicating the models' lack of sufficient fine-grained understanding of emotional cues. We anticipate that grounding the responses in audio-specific features might reduce hallucination counts, but also risks being less effective in expressing emotional nuances compared to visual and flow features that better support multi-faceted representation.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Evaluating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs

TITLE: Audiovisual Emotion Grounding using Attention-weighted Max-pooling
PROPOSAL: To investigate the impact of audiovisual grounding on emotion perception, we develop and evaluate a novel attention-weighted max-pooling (AWMP) approach. AWMP weights the importance of different audio and visual features in emotion prediction by computing attention weights for each feature. We then use these weights to select the most relevant features through max-pooling. This approach encourages the model to focus on the most informative cues for emotion perception, potentially reducing hallucinations and improving accuracy. We incorporate AWMP into our previously modified MLLMs from (1) and (2), and evaluate their performance on the revised VAPT benchmark.
CONTROLS: Our baseline is the previous MLLM variants without AWMP, and we also conduct ablation studies removing the attendance weights and max-pooling components to assess their individual contributions.
COST: 7000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By focusing on the most relevant cues, AWMP may improve the accuracy and reduce hallucinations in emotion perception, especially when combined with the opponent-tuning technique from (2) and the explanation branch from the revised evaluation in (1). However, we also anticipate that the AWMP approach may introduce additional computational costs due to the extra attention and pooling layers, which could potentially offset some of the benefits.
