TITLE: Augmenting Emotion Benchmarks for Audiovisual MLLMs with Human Explanations
PROPOSAL: Develop an extension to the EMOTIVE-2024 dataset by includes human explanations for emotions and visual-audio features, enabling a more nuanced understanding of emotion reasoning processes. We crowdsource the explanations from crowd-workers, asking them to describe why certain visual-audio cues correlate with specific emotions. This dataset extension allows for novel analysis into human reasoning biases and emulates real-world scenarios more accurately, providing a more realistic benchmark for adequate MLLM performance on high-stakes emotion tasks. Towards establishing benchmark results, retrain ZS-VGT to condition the generated explanations on target emotions, and evaluate its performance on the original task (hallucination, reasoning error, perception error) on augmented benchmark.
CONTROLS: Conduct a control experiment using pre-existing annotator explanations from standard human evaluation protocols, such as BLEURT.
COST: 167,476
PREDICTION: The inclusion of human explanations significantly improves task performance on MLLMs but reveals instances of reasoning errors driven not just by model mistakes, but also by drifts in annotator explanations from the target labels, indicating the challenges of using human reasoning as a reference standard for guiding MLLM norm construction.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Augmenting Emotion Benchmarks for Audiovisual MLLMs with Human Explanations
PROPOSAL: Revisit proposal 2 and expand the human explanation protocol to collect both surface-level descriptions of key visual-audio features and deeper-level analyses of how these features contributed to the target emotion, including contextual and narrative elements. This expanded protocol will enable a more comprehensive understanding of how humans frame and reason about emotional experiences, and allow us to develop more nuanced and realistic evaluation metrics for assessing audiovisual MLLMs.
CONTROLS: Include a control experiment with existing human evaluation protocols, comparing the performance of MLLMs on the expanded human explanation task with the standard task.
COST: 180,000
PREDICTION: The expanded human explanation protocol reveals significant heterogeneity in how humans frame and reason about emotional experiences, with some annotators using more directly perceptual language and others incorporating deeper narrative and contextual elements. This result highlights the importance of developing evaluation metrics that can capture this diversity and accurately reflect the complexity of human emotion understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reducing Spurious Emotion-Audiovisual Cue Associations with Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel contrastive loss function that encourages the audiovisual MLLM to learn more robust and plausible emotion-audiovisual cue associations, reducing the impact of spurious associations driven by text priors in the language model backbone. We will implement this loss by contrasting the emotion predictions generated by the audiovisual MLLM with those generated by a text-only counterpart, using a data augmentation strategy to generate synthetic audiovisual data that aligns with the text.
CONTROLS: Compare this approach with standard loss functions and ablate different components of the strategy to understand the impact on emotion hallucination and reasoning error rates.
COST: 240,000
PREDICTION: The proposed contrastive loss function significantly reduces the severity of emotion hallucinations and reasoning errors, and yields more accurate and consistent emotion predictions that are grounded in the audiovisual cues. However, the extent to which this approach generalizes across different tasks and domains remains to be seen, and further investigation will be needed to fully understand its benefits and limitations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Instruction Tuning on Emotion Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: Investigate how instruction tuning data affects the severity of emotion hallucinations and reasoning errors in audiovisual MLLMs. We will fine-tune the model on a range of instruction-tuning datasets, including those that specifically target emotion understanding, and evaluate its performance on hallucination and reasoning error benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Include a control experiment with standard pre-training and fine-tuning protocols, and ablate different components of the instruction-tuning process to understand the impact on emotion predictions.
COST: 300,000
PREDICTION: Our results show that instruction-tuning data has a significant impact on emotion hallucination rates, with models fine-tuned on emotion-specific datasets exhibiting lower hallucination rates than those fine-tuned on general-domain tasks. However, we also observe that instruction-tuning can introduce domain-specific biases, which may compromise the model's ability to generalize to novel tasks and domains. Further investigation will be needed to balance the benefits and limitations of instruction tuning for emotion understanding.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Reducing Spurious Emotion-Audiovisual Cue Associations with Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: Refine the contrastive loss function proposed in proposal 3 by incorporating a novel temporally-aware similarity metric that captures the dynamic relationships between audiovisual cues and emotions over time. This metric will be computed using a chrono-encoder, a type of neural network that models temporal dependencies and relationships between input sequences. We expect this refinement to improve the model's ability to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant audiovisual cues, reducing hallucination and reasoning error rates.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the refined contrastive loss with the original proposal 3, and evaluate the impact of the chrono-encoder on emotion predictions.
COST: 375,000
PREDICTION: The incorporation of the temporally-aware similarity metric leads to a significant reduction in hallucination and reasoning error rates, and yields more accurate and consistent emotion predictions that capture the dynamic relationships between audiovisual cues and emotions. However, the extent to which this approach can be generalized to other tasks and domains remains to be seen.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Emotion-Aware Prompt Engineering for Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel prompt engineering framework that generates human-understandable and contextualized prompts for audiovisual MLLMs, leveraging insights from human explanations and emotion theories. This framework will use a combination of natural language processing and cognitive architectures to generate prompts that are tailored to the specific emotion, context, and visual-audio cues. We will evaluate the impact of these prompts on emotion predictions, hallucination rates, and reasoning error rates.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed prompt engineering framework with standard prompts and ablate different components to understand the impact of each factor.
COST: 432,130
PREDICTION: Our results show that the proposed prompt engineering framework leads to significant improvements in emotion predictions, hallucination rates, and reasoning error rates, and enables audiovisual MLLMs to generate more accurate and informative emotion-related responses. However, we also observe that the framework's effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the human explanations used to generate the prompts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Explanability Framework for Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive multimodal explainability framework that provides a detailed understanding of the video-language model's reasoning process and identifies the most critical audiovisual features responsible for emotion predictions. This framework will combine attention-based saliency maps, perceptual backpropagation, and layer-wise relevance analysis to generate a rich, image-speech-textual representation of the model's decision-making process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed framework with standard explainability methods and evaluate the impact on human trust and perceived reliability in audiovisual MLLMs.
COST: 534,751.85
PREDICTION: Our results show that the proposed multimodal explainability framework leads to significant improvements in human trust and perceived reliability in audiovisual MLLMs, while also providing valuable insights into the model's decision-making process. However, we also observe that the framework's effectiveness depends on the quality of the training data and the model's architecture.

TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment using the newly released EMOTIVE-2024 dataset, which includes rich, high-quality annotations for emotions and audiovisual features. Train a state-of-the-art video-language model (VLM) like Zero-Shot Visual Grounding Transformer (ZS-VGT) and a text-to-speech (TTS) model on the mixed-media emotive dataset, and evaluate their performance on hallucination, reasoning error, and perception error benchmarks. For this study, we use existing proposed evaluation metrics like BER (Behavior Evaluation on Reasoning), and PEAR (Perception Error Analysis and Risk) metrics. 
CONTROLS: Use standard models like BERT for comparison, and ablate different combinations of modules and dataset partitions to estimate how sensitive the results are to the model design.
COST: 240,000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that ZS-VGT will perform significantly better than BERT on emotion recognition tasks but will also tend to exhibit more severe hallucinations and reasoning errors. This discrepancy hints at the fine balancing act between the model's capacity to capture complex emotion cues and its susceptibility to spurious cue-emotion associations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Hallucination Failure Modes in Audiovisual Emotion MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the state-of-the-art (SOTA) Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) Challenge leaderboard models using the proposed Emotion Hallucination (EH) benchmark, which synthesizes new cases by masking and altering visual and audio components in a principled manner to create plausible new cases mimicking human hallucinations, then asking human evaluators to label their perceived emotion explanations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Run SOTA models on the original, unaltered EmotiW Challenge dataset; Ablation: Run SOTA models on the EH benchmark with varying masking patterns and alteration levels; Estimate standard deviation of human label annotations
COST: 1050
PREDICTION: The EH benchmark should reveal the extent to which current SOTA models are prone to hallucinations, with a prediction of 80% or higher propensity for EH, indicating significant room for improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual Emotion Reasoning Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Develop a counterfactual evaluation framework for audiovisual emotion reasoning, where the input video and audio are modified in a manner that isolates specific hallucinations or reasoning errors (e.g., removing facial expressions while retaining affective speech), then re-training the MLLM and human evaluators to re-task what emotion is inferred or explained.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Run SOTA models on the original, unaltered EmotiW Challenge; Baseline adaptation: re-run SOTA models on modified videos/audio; Ablation: retrain SOTA models on modified videos/audio minus the targeted hallucination/reasoning error; Run counterfactual evaluation with human evaluators on both modified and unaltered videos
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: By evaluating how the confidence in SOTA models decreases upon removal of specific hallucinations, we can pinpoint major hallucination paths and develop explanations for where MLLMs systematically err in conflict with human expectation of sound reason.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Hallucinations in Audiovisual Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale, real-world evaluation of existing MLLMs on various audiovisual emotion benchmarks, including the Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) challenge and the Audiovisual Emotion Dataset (AVED). Assess the prevalence of emotion hallucinations and reasoning errors using metrics such as accuracy, BERTS (a metric to quantify the model's ability to align emotion predictions with the actual input cues), and a modified version of the H Mei et al. self-knowledge distance (SKD) metric to quantify hallucinated cues. This study will serve as a baseline for future research.
CONTROLS: Compare three state-of-the-art MLLMs (e.g., CLIP, VisualBERT, and ViLBERT) on the above mentioned tasks and metrics, to demonstrate the issue's generality across model architectures.
COST: 333.8623
PREDICTION: We expect that all tested models will exhibit significant reasoning errors and emotion hallucinations, most notably on novel or out-of-distribution (OoD) data. We anticipate that while BERTS and SKD will be useful to quantify hallucinations, they often suffer from high variance in existing benchmarks, which might make it difficult to pin down outliers and could necessitate further improvements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Auditing Emotion Hallucinations via Adversarial Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial evaluation framework to assess and mitigate emotion hallucinations in MLLMs. This will involve utilizing data manipulation techniques such as perturbing audio and visual inputs to disrupt the model's ability to recognize emotional cues. In parallel, progressively challenging inputs that contain minimalistic, Creative Commons-based synthetic raw audio-visual samples of out-of-distribution data (that isolate the perturbations for evaluation) will be established to isolate vulnerability and train the models to eliminate hallucinations. We propose evaluating this on the WavEMo2o520 dataset and an extension of an empirically discovered general EmotionPie arbitrary gap defined by the minimum distance between diverse facial emotions.
CONTROLS: Compare the impact of three popular diffusion-based audio and two vision augmentations on the EmotionHallucination ErrorRate metric that we introduce, and a check for conceptual approval.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect to detect and quantify a range of emotion hallucinations on high-stakes novel or out-of-distribution data by pushing such data through our augmentations, which are calibrated for sensitivity in detecting decision mistakes on auditory and visual manifests.

TITLE: Evaluating Emotion Hallucinations in Audiovisual Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale, real-world evaluation of existing MLLMs on various audiovisual emotion benchmarks, including the Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EmotiW) challenge and the Audiovisual Emotion Dataset (AVED). Assess the prevalence of emotion hallucinations and reasoning errors using metrics such as accuracy, BERTS (a metric to quantify the model's ability to align emotion predictions with the actual input cues), and a modified version of the H Mei et al. self-knowledge distance (SKD) metric to quantify hallucinated cues. This study will serve as a baseline for future research.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization Strategies for Reducing Emotion Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate and implement several regularization techniques to reduce emotion hallucination in the audiovisual emotion recognition models:

- **Dual Adversarial Training**: Use an adversarial loss to encourage the model to focus on relevant cues and penalize hallucinations.
- **Confidence-weighted Regularization**: Assign different regularization weights based on the model's confidence in its predictions.
- **Knowledge Distillation**: Train a smaller network to predict the same outputs as the larger network, forcing the larger network to focus on relevant cues.

These techniques will be implemented on top of the iterative training framework proposed in proposal 1, and evaluated on the sub-benchmarks defined in proposal 1.

CONTROLS: Compare against the ERT-MLLM and ED-LLM models without these regularization techniques.
COST: 23.4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed regularization techniques will lead to a significant reduction in emotion hallucination, with improvements of up to 25% on the scarce-novelty sub-benchmark, and 15% on the surrounding-distractions sub-benchmark.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Explainability and Transparency in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a new evaluation framework for assessing the explainability and transparency of audiovisual emotion recognition models. The framework will consist of four components:

1. Abstract representation similarity (ARS): measures the similarity between the model-generated abstract representation and the human-generated abstract presentation
2. Causal attribution (CA): measures the causal relationship between the input features and the output predictions
3. Information content (IC): measures the amount of information contained in the model-generated explanations
4. Critic reason (CR): measures the model's ability to provide a coherent and logical explanation for its predictions

CONTROLS: Compare against a set of existing explainability metrics and techniques.
COST: 47.3779 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of the explainability and transparency of audiovisual emotion recognition models, enabling researchers to evaluate and improve the quality of these models' explanations.

TITLE: Regularization Strategies for Reducing Emotion Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate and implement several regularization techniques to reduce emotion hallucination in the audiovisual emotion recognition models:

- **Dual Adversarial Training**: Use an adversarial loss to encourage the model to focus on relevant cues and penalize hallucinations.
- **Confidence-weighted Regularization**: Assign different regularization weights based on the model's confidence in its predictions.
- **Knowledge Distillation**: Train a smaller network to predict the same outputs as the larger network, forcing the larger network to focus on relevant cues.

These techniques will be implemented on top of the iterative training framework proposed in proposal 1, and evaluated on the sub-benchmarks defined in proposal 1.

CONTROLS: Compare against the ERT-MLLM and ED-LLM models without these regularization techniques.
COST: 70.3 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed regularization techniques will lead to a significant reduction in emotion hallucination, with improvements of up to 25% on the scarce-novelty sub-benchmark, and 15% on the surrounding-distractions sub-benchmark.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interleaving Outcome and Trajectory-Based Rewards for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel reward scheme that combines outcome-based rewards with trajectory-based rewards, where each turn in the dialogue receives a reward based on the progress towards the final answer, while the overall outcome provides a corrective signal. We use a hinge loss function to calculate the trajectory rewards, and a learned reward template to combine the trajectory and outcome rewards.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome-only rewards; ablation: remove the learned reward template and use a fixed weighting between trajectory and outcome rewards
COST: 400
PREDICTION: This approach should improve sample efficiency and provide more fine-grained credit assignment, but may require careful tuning of the reward template and weighting. We anticipate a boost in performance on multi-hop question answering tasks, but may struggle on tasks where outcome-only rewards are sufficient.

TITLE: Detecting Advantage Collapse with Augmented Statistics
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method for detecting advantage collapse in multi-turn search agents, which involves augmenting the standard group statistics with additional features that track the diversity and novelty of search results. We use a modified version of the self-supervised loss function to guide the model to produce more informative and varied search results, even in cases where the outcome rewards are zero.

However, it may require careful tuning of the augmented statistics and self-supervised loss function to avoid over-complexity and poor convergence. We anticipate a moderate improvement on tasks that involve search results with varying diversity and novelty, such as multi-hop question answering.

TITLE: Interleaving Outcome and Trajectory-Based Rewards for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel reward scheme that combines outcome-based rewards with trajectory-based rewards, where each turn in the dialogue receives a reward based on the progress towards the final answer, while the overall outcome provides a corrective signal. We use a hinge loss function to calculate the trajectory rewards, and a learned reward template to combine the trajectory and outcome rewards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sequence-Wise Masking for Early Turn Prediction in Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We introduce a sequence-wise masking mechanism that enables the model to predict early turns as indicative of the overall outcome, allowing for more informed turn-level reward design. We mask the sequence after each turn, and use a self-supervised loss to guide the model to focus on relevant information.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: We propose a method to augment outcome rewards with contextualized embeddings of search results, allowing the model to learn from the relevance and coherence of search results in addition to the final outcome. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inverse Reinforcement Learning of Dense Process Rewards from Organized Multistep Trajectories
PROPOSAL: We propose to use Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) to recover a dense reward function from organized multistep trajectories obtained from matching partial search agent executions with correct full trajectories. We sample search agents to produce these organized trajectories, which serve as demonstrations of the correct reward signal for each turn. By learning from these demonstrations, the network can infer the desired reward function. We expect this method to learn rewards that are informative, dense, and anchored to the final objective.
CONTROLS: We compare to baselines where the reward is either outcome-only or process-based, using vanilla IRL with and without a structured reward prior, and one more where the demonstration set is generated without employing any partial-to-full matching, thus not being organized.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This IRL approach is expected to learn informative and dense process rewards that remain anchored to the final objective, outperforming baseline methods, but parts of the reward might still have high variance in difficult scenarios, where reinforced models tend to deviate from the demonstrated behavior more freely.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized SARSA-based Supervision for Robust Turn-level Rewards
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new, adaptive regularization scheme for turn-level rewards learned through actor-critic SARSA (Sarsa with eligibility traces). The regularizer serves to prioritize optimal behaviors, making the agent focus on the important decision-making steps in the search process. Specifically, we minimize the KL divergence between the predicted probabilities of the agent's action given its state and the probabilities under the learned turn-level reward for each turn.
CONTROLS: To validate our approach, we compare our regularized SARSA method to vanilla SARSA and an IRL-based baseline on various open-domain and multi-hop question answering tasks.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: This REGULARIZED SARSA approach should lead to more stable and informative turn-level rewards, narrowing the gap to IRL supervision and outperforming standard SARSA in terms of sample efficiency and search performance. The regularizer may occasionally lead the model to over-emphasize some steps, leading to suboptimal outcomes when faced with diverse or ambiguous environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inverse Reinforcement Learning of Dense Process Rewards from Organized Multistep Trajectories
PROPOSAL: We propose to use Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) to recover a dense reward function from organized multistep trajectories obtained from matching partial search agent executions with correct full trajectories. We sample search agents to produce these organized trajectories, which serve as demonstrations of the correct reward signal for each turn. By learning from these demonstrations, the network can infer the desired reward function. We expect this method to learn rewards that are informative, dense, and anchored to the final objective.
CONTROLS: We compare to baselines where the reward is either outcome-only or process-based, using vanilla IRL with and without a structured reward prior, and one more where the demonstration set is generated without employing any partial-to-full matching, thus not being organized.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This IRL approach is expected to learn informative and dense process rewards that remain anchored to the final objective, outperforming baseline methods, but parts of the reward might still have high variance in difficult scenarios, where reinforced models tend to deviate from the demonstrated behavior more freely.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized SARSA-based Supervision for Robust Turn-level Rewards
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new, adaptive regularization scheme for turn-level rewards learned through actor-critic SARSA (Sarsa with eligibility traces). The regularizer serves to prioritize optimal behaviors, making the agent focus on the important decision-making steps in the search process. Specifically, we minimize the KL divergence between the predicted probabilities of the agent's action given its state and the probabilities under the learned turn-level reward for each turn.
CONTROLS: To validate our approach, we compare our regularized SARSA method to vanilla SARSA and an IRL-based baseline on various open-domain and multi-hop question answering tasks.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: This REGULARIZED SARSA approach should lead to more stable and informative turn-level rewards, narrowing the gap to IRL supervision and outperforming standard SARSA in terms of sample efficiency and search performance. The regularizer may occasionally lead the model to over-emphasize some steps, leading to suboptimal outcomes when faced with diverse or ambiguous environments.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED TITLE FOR 1: Unsupervised Learning of Variational Turn-level Rewards from Initial-Condition Trajectory Probabilities
PROPOSAL: For the first proposal, we modify the Inverse Reinforcement Learning component to incorporate the probabilistic nature of the search agent's decision-making process by imposing a variational approximation. This variational approach allows us to learn a flexible and probabilistic turn-level reward model from the organized demonstrations, providing a lower bound on the true reward signal. The output is a turn-level reward policy, sampled from a probabilistic distribution over rewards, which guides our SARSA-based actor.
CONTROLS: For direct comparison, the first baseline remains the original IRL approach, resulting in a deterministic reward signal, while a more advanced baseline uses a model of the trajectory probabilities that is not informed by the demonstrations as variational objectives.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: By accounting for the decision-making uncertainty in the learning process, we expect the variational IRL to achieve better sample efficiency and more informed decision-making in the search process. Nevertheless, the total computational requirements and generalization to new, unseen scenarios might be higher due to the metropolis-hastings-flows involved.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-invariant Turn Rewards using Relative Divergence
PROPOSAL: We propose to train search agents to output turn rewards that are not directly dependent on the task-specific outcome. This is achieved through measuring the relative divergence (e.g., KL or JS divergence) between the log-probability of the current policy's intermediate turns and a reference distribution learned from the data. The agent aims to minimize the divergence across the trajectory, receiving dense rewards for coherent and informative turns.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No regularization term for the reference distribution, (3) Alternative distance measure: Use estimators for Hellinger distance or total variation distance
COST: 400
PREDICTION: This approach can improve generalization of search agents by providing a dense reward signal that abstracts away from task-specific details, making them more robust to changes in the search graph or imperfect information, but might struggle to capture multi-hop interactions and nuanced query types where balance between exploration and exploitation is crucial.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Path-Level Reward Contrast for Informative Turns
PROPOSAL: We propose a contrastive learning-based approach to reward informative turns in a multi-turn search trajectory. For each turn, we create positive and negative examples by constructing hypothetical "_completed" trajectories with the current turn inserted in place of an earlier turn. The agent is rewarded for turns that increase the similarity (using cosine similarity, for example) between the positive and negative examples in the motivational graph (e.g., a search graph constructed from knowledge graph and query embedding space). Controls include tuning the positive-negative ratio of samples and using alternative measure of similarity.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No contrastive learning term, (3) Competition: LEAR and GACE methods
COST: 600
PREDICTION: Path-Level Reward Contrast can efficiently guide the agent to focus on creating informative turns, improving search performance on complex queries; however, its performance might degrade for tasks requiring multiple reasoning hops between queries.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Path-Level Reward Contrast for Informative Turns with Improved Planning
PROPOSAL: We propose to revise Path-Level Reward Contrast by leveraging a graph-based attention mechanism to dynamically select the "seed" turn in the trajectory to manipulate in the creation of positive and negative examples. This turns the method into an end-to-end trainable process. Furthermore, we incorporate a behavioral cloning component to force the agent to assign higher rewards to turns with high information value, as determined by their semantic similarity to relevant, top-ranked search results.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No graph-based attention or behavioral cloning component, (3) Alternative method: Retrain the agent on augmented training data
COST: 734
PREDICTION: Revised Path-Level Reward Contrast should improve performance for tasks requiring multiple reasoning hops by directing the agent to selectively plan its search turns around the most important and informative pieces of the trajectory; the higher attachment complexity could however increase risk of overfitting.

TITLE: Intermediate State Augmentation for Reward Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose to augment the agent's intermediate states with the representation of retrieved documents or answers during the trajectory, and use this augmented state to compute rewards for each turn. PROPOSAL: We propose to train search agents using a context-conditional reward model that encourages informative turns in multi-hop search trajectories. This approach enables the agent to reason about the relevance and informativeness of its intermediate turns, leading to improved performance on complex search tasks.

CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No regularization term for the reference distribution, (3) Alternative distance measure: Use estimators for Hellinger distance or total variation distance
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This approach can improve generalization of search agents by providing a dense reward signal that abstracts away from task-specific details, making them more robust to changes in the search graph or imperfect information, but might struggle to capture multi-hop interactions and nuanced query types where balance between exploration and exploitation is crucial.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Path-Level Reward Contrast for Informative Turns
PROPOSAL: We propose a contrastive learning-based approach to reward informative turns in a multi-turn search trajectory. For each turn, we create positive and negative examples by constructing hypothetical "_completed" trajectories with the current turn inserted in place of an earlier turn. The agent is rewarded for turns that increase the similarity (using cosine similarity, for example) between the positive and negative examples in the motivational graph (e.g., a search graph constructed from knowledge graph and query embedding space). Controls include tuning the positive-negative ratio of samples and using alternative measure of similarity.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No contrastive learning term, (3) Competition: LEAR and GACE methods
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Path-Level Reward Contrast can efficiently guide the agent to focus on creating informative turns, improving search performance on complex queries; however, its performance might degrade for tasks requiring multiple reasoning hops between queries.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED  Path-Level Reward Contrast for Informative Turns
PROPOSAL: We propose to revise Path-Level Reward Contrast by leveraging a graph-based attention mechanism to dynamically select the "seed" turn in the trajectory to manipulate in the creation of positive and negative examples. This turns the method into an end-to-end trainable process. Furthermore, we incorporate a behavioral cloning component to force the agent to assign higher rewards to turns with high information value, as determined by their semantic similarity to relevant, top-ranked search results.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No graph-based attention or behavioral cloning component, (3) Alternative method: Retrain the agent on augmented training data
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: Revised Path-Level Reward Contrast should improve performance for tasks requiring multiple reasoning hops by directing the agent to selectively plan its search turns around the most important and informative pieces of the trajectory; the higher attachment complexity could however increase risk of overfitting.

TITLE: Dembia-Hop Reward Shaping for Contextual Search
PROPOSAL: We propose to train search agents using a context-conditional reward model that encourages informative turns in multi-hop search trajectories. Dembia-Hop Reward Shaping uses a multi-hop attention mechanism to learn contextual representations of intermediate turns, which are then used to predict informative rewards. This approach enables the agent to reason about the relevance and informativeness of its intermediate turns, leading to improved performance on complex search tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No Dembia-Hop attention mechanism, (3) Alternative method: Use a pre-trained contextual language model to generate contextual representations

PROPOSAL: We propose to further enhance Path-Level Reward Contrast by incorporating a novel temporal attention mechanism that selectively weighs the importance of each intermediate turn in the trajectory. We also extend the method to handle multi-hop search tasks by conditioning the temporal attention mechanism on the contextual representations of the intermediate turns.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline Outcome-based GRPO, (2) Ablation: No temporal attention mechanism, (3) Alternative method: Use a pre-trained contextual language model to condition the temporal attention mechanism

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Query-Augmented Sparse Supervision (QASS) Pre-Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel pre-training framework, QASS, which generates synthetic sparse queries by manipulating ground-truth labels, then uses these augmented queries to supervise SPMs. This framework takes advantage of real-world datasets where bounding box annotations are easily available but dense 3D occupancy labels are expensive.
CONTROLS: 
* Baseline: Random initialization
* Ablations: Same QASS with different types of query manipulation (translation, rotation, scaling) and different pre-training objectives (e.g., contrastive, masked autoencoding)
* Downstream-Leverage: Compare QASS-Sparse 3D Object Detectors and Query-based Occupancy Predictors on real-world datasets (e.g., KITTI, nuScenes)
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Improved performance on wildcard tasks compared to random initialization; the accuracy could release on a,True type problems of vanishing occupancies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering for Self-Supervised Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel self-supervised pre-training framework, 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering (3D-QANR), which leverages multi-view driving images to train sparse perception models. Inspired by 3D rendering techniques, 3D-QANR renders a 2.5D representation of the scene by sampling a sparse set of 3D queries and predicting their corresponding depths and colors. The rendered representation is then used to supervise the model's query decoder, enabling it to learn accurate 3D spatial relationships and query positions. To boost robustness and reduce memory requirements, we introduce a "query-aware" module to adaptively adjust the sampling density of 3D queries based on the model's current query positions and predicted depths.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed 3D-QANR method against a baseline of frozen ImageNet features and two pre-training methods designed for dense BEV-centric models: BEVFormer and UniPAD. To further evaluate the effectiveness of 3D-QANR, we will also conduct ablation studies using variants of our proposed framework with different query-aware settings and sampling densities.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: 3D-QANR is expected to outperform the baseline in terms of downstream performance on 3D object detection and semantic segmentation tasks. However, we anticipate that its high sampling density may lead to increased compute requirements and memory usage, potentially limiting its applicability to resource-constrained edge devices.

However, we also expect that the performance of 3D-QANR-pretrained models may degrade when transferred to models with significant architectural differences, such as SparseBEV.

TITLE: Depth aware Position Estimation for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel depth aware position estimation (DPE) approach to enhance the query positions in sparse perception models. By leveraging the predicted depth maps from 3D-QANR, our DPE method refines the query positions to better capture the spatial relationships between objects in the scene. This is achieved through a simple yet effective depth-aware transformation of the query positions, which is incorporated into the query decoder of the sparse perception models.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of sparse perception models with and without the DPE approach, using the same set of pre-trained models and evaluation metrics from our previous experiments.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: DPE is expected to improve the performance of sparse perception models on downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and semantic segmentation, particularly in scenarios with complex scene geometries. However, we anticipate that the gains may be marginal in scenes with simple geometry and sparse object layout.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Global and Query-Specific Adversarial Training for Robustness Enhancement of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel adversarial training approach to enhance the robustness of sparse perception models against various types of attacks, including white-box and black-box attacks. Our method, GQ-SAT, jointly trains the model against global and query-specific adversaries, where the global adversary aims to produce mis:classifications for the entire query set, while the query-specific adversary targets each query individually. This multi-advantageous training enables the model to generalize better and reduces its vulnerability to unexpected scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the robustness of sparse perception models pre-trained with 3D-QANR and fine-tuned with GQ-SAT against various types of attacks, and compare their performance against baseline models without GQ-SAT.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: GQ-SAT is expected to significantly enhance the robustness of sparse perception models, especially when paired with 3D-QANR pre-training. However, we anticipate that the additional training time may lead to increased computational requirements, limiting its applicability to resource-constrained edge devices.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Query-Aware Neural Rendering for Zero-Shot Generalization of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel meta-learning approach, Meta-3D-QANR, that enables zero-shot generalization of sparse perception models to unseen scenes and tasks. By learning to adapt to new query positions and scene representations through a meta-training process, our method evolves the 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering framework into a query-agnostic architecture that can generalize to various scenes and tasks without extensive re-training. This is achieved through a novel meta-query-aware sampling strategy and a learned meta-decoder that can invert the scene representation to recover the original query positions.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the zero-shot generalization performance of Meta-3D-QANR on various unseen scenes and tasks, and compare its performance against the original 3D-QANR method and other meta-learning approaches.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Meta-3D-QANR is expected to demonstrate significant zero-shot generalization capabilities, but may require additional computational resources and inference times due to the meta-learning process.

CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of E3D-QANR against the original 3D-QANR method and a baseline approach that uses a uniform sampling strategy on various real-world autonomous driving datasets, such as the Waymo Open Dataset and the nuScenes Dataset.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: E3D-QANR is expected to offer significant improvements in efficiency and robustness for real-world autonomous driving scenes, while maintaining or even surpassing the performance of the original 3D-QANR method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Query-Aware Neural Rendering for Zero-Shot Generalization of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel meta-learning approach, Meta-3D-QANR, that enables zero-shot generalization of sparse perception models to unseen scenes and tasks. By learning to adapt to new query positions and scene representations through a meta-training process, our method evolves the 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering framework into a query-agnostic architecture that can generalize to various scenes and tasks without extensive re-training. This is achieved through a novel meta-query-aware sampling strategy and a learned meta-decoder that can invert the scene representation to recover the original query positions.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the zero-shot generalization performance of Meta-3D-QANR on various unseen scenes and tasks, and compare its performance against the original 3D-QANR method and other meta-learning approaches.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: Meta-3D-QANR is expected to demonstrate significant zero-shot generalization capabilities, but may require additional computational resources and inference times due to the meta-learning process.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient and Adaptable 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering for Real-World Autonomous Driving Scenes
PROPOSAL (REVISED PROPOSAL 1): We revisit the 3D Query-Aware Neural Rendering framework to further optimize its efficiency and adaptability for real-world autonomous driving scenes. Our revised method, E2A-3D-QANR, builds upon the hierarchical sampling strategy and learned depth refinement module from E3D-QANR, and introduces a novel query-aware attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant regions and reduce computational complexities. Additionally, we propose a lightweight, scene-aware query decoder that adapts to the scene complexity and geometry.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of E2A-3D-QANR against the original E3D-QANR method and other state-of-the-art methods on various real-world autonomous driving datasets.
COST: 16800
PREDICTION: E2A-3D-QANR is expected to offer significant improvements in efficiency and adaptability, while maintaining or even surpassing the performance of the original 3D-QANR method and other state-of-the-art methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking and Comparative Analysis of Sparse Perception Models on Real-World Autonomous Driving Datasets
PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive benchmarking and comparative analysis framework to evaluate and compare the performance of various sparse perception models on real-world autonomous driving datasets. Our framework, SPM-Bench, provides a unified platform for evaluating and comparing the performance of different sparse perception models, including 3D-QANR, E3D-QANR, E2A-3D-QANR, and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: We will use the same set of real-world autonomous driving datasets and evaluation metrics to evaluate and compare the performance of different sparse perception models.
COST: 19200
PREDICTION: SPM-Bench is expected to provide a comprehensive and unbiased benchmarking and comparative analysis of state-of-the-art sparse perception models, and help identify the strengths and weaknesses of each method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Autonomous Driving: A Large-Scale Real-World Sparse Perception Model Replication Challenge
PROPOSAL: We propose a large-scale, real-world sparse perception model replication challenge, ASAP-Rep, to encourage the development of robust and generalizable sparse perception models for autonomous driving applications. Our challenge will provide a large-scale, real-world dataset, replication protocols, and leaderboard for competing methods. This will enable researchers and practitioners to showcase the performance and generalizability of their sparse perception models on real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the submitted methods using the same real-world autonomous driving datasets and evaluation protocols as SPM-Bench.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: ASAP-Rep is expected to stimulate significant advancements in the development of robust and generalizable sparse perception models, and accelerate the progress towards practical autonomous driving applications.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Query-Based Volumetric Rendering for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: 
- Develop a query-based 3D volumetric rendering method for SPMs, using a learned renderer that estimates 3D scene geometry and appearance conditioned on sparse queries.
- Train the renderer using multi-view driving images with a siamese loss function, contrasting rendered 3D volumes with sparse queries against random queries drawn from the same scene.
- Use the rendered 3D volumes as self-supervised targets for learning query embeddings and adapt these embeddings to downstream SPMs through task-specific decoders.

CONTROLS: BEVFormer and Lift-Splat-Shoot as BEV-centric baselines, DETR3D as an SPM baseline.

COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved performance for downstream SPMs, possibly at the cost of slower inference due to increased rendering complexity; failure risk: formation of inaccurate 3D volumes, especially for scenarios with large depth variations.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Enhancing Query-Based Volumetric Rendering for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: 
- Refine the query-based 3D volumetric rendering method (previous proposal) by incorporating a learned camera matrix and modeling geometric and photometric consistency in the scene through an iterative process.
- Introduce a novel rendering objective that maximizes mutual information between the rendered 3D volumes and sparse queries, ensuring query-adaptability and facilitating the transfer of knowledge to downstream SPMs.
- Utilize an additional scene-conditioned normalization step to reduce over-estimation and stabilize the rendering process.

CONTROLS: Same as before, with the addition of evaluation against video sequences captured from rotating cameras to validate improved geometric consistency.

COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved robustness and accuracy of the learned 3D scene representations; possible failure risk: increasing compute requirements for the iterative process.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Geometry-Aware Query Adaptation for Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: 
- Develop a query-adaptation strategy for transferring the learned knowledge from the query-based 3D volumetric rendering pre-training to diverse downstream SPMs.
- Introduce a geometry-aware query adaptation module that adjusts the query embeddings according to the geometry of the downstream task, using a joint embedding space informed by the shared geometry of both the pre-training and downstream scenarios.
- Train the adaptation module using a geometry-aware contrastive loss that maximizes the similarity of query-adapted embeddings across corresponding downstream tasks.

CONTROLS: Evaluate against a range of downstream tasks (e.g., object detection, semantic segmentation, and scene understanding) and compare against standard transfer learning strategies lacking geometry-aware adaptation.

COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved generalizability of the pre-trained models across diverse downstream tasks; possible failure risk: over-specialization of query-adaptation to specific tasks.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Annotator-Agnostic Pseudo-Labeling for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: 
- Develop an annotator-agnostic pseudo-labeling strategy to generate high-quality labels for large-scale unlabeled driving datasets, which can be utilized as self-supervisory signals for pre-training SPMs.
- Introduce a self-supervised learning-based approach that consists of a multi-scale feature fusion module and a pseudo-label refinement network, which iteratively refines the pseudo-labels to match the ground-truth through a clash reduction mechanism.
- Evaluate the proposed pseudo-labeling method on a wide range of driving datasets and contrast it with existing pseudo-labeling approaches, especially in scenarios with large domain shifts.

CONTROLS: Compare pseudo-label quality and pre-training efficiency with state-of-the-art methods, and also examine downstream task performance when trained on pseudo-labeled data.

COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved pseudo-label quality and downstream performance; possible failure risk: decreased stability and efficiency due to iterative refinement process.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Unified Multi-Task Pseudo-Labeling for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: 
- Refine the annotator-agnostic pseudo-labeling strategy (previous proposal) by incorporating a unified multi-task framework that leverages knowledge from diverse downstream tasks to jointly refine pseudo-labels for sparse perception tasks.
- Introduce a novel task-augmentation technique that augments the pseudo-labeling process with corrective signals from a range of related tasks (e.g., object detection, semantic segmentation), enabling the generation of high-quality labels for large-scale unlabeled driving datasets.

PROPOSAL: 
- Develop an uncertainty-based active learning strategy to selectively acquire high-quality annotations for downstream tasks, leveraging the confidence estimates from pre-trained SPMs.

CONTROLS: Compare against standard active learning strategies, as well as against a baseline of random sampling, and examine the effect on transfer performance, sample efficiency, and annotation costs.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Geometry-Aware Adversarial Training for Query Adaptation
PROPOSAL: 
- Refine the geometry-aware query adaptation strategy (previous proposal) by incorporating an adversarial training framework that learns to improve the robustness and generalizability of query embeddings.
- Introduce a novel geometry-aware adversarial loss that maximizes the distance between adapted query embeddings and misadapter fabricated embeddings based on semantic disparities, while reducing the distance between the correctly adapted query embeddings under similar semantics.
- Utilize a task-specific patch-replacement adversarial training mechanism to create richer and more challenging adaptations of query embeddings.

CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of geometry-aware adversarial training against existing adaptation methods, and examine its impact on transfer performance, robustness, and query stability.

COST: 5347.5185
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved robustness and generalizability of adapted query embeddings; possible failure risk: potential over-adaptation or embeddings potentially removable under existing conventional forms of domain shifts in driving datasets.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Efficient Knowledge Transfer across Heterogeneous Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: 
- Develop a method to transfer knowledge across heterogeneous SPMs with diverse query structures, decoder architectures, and scene representation capabilities.
- Introduce a novel knowledge distillation framework that transfers high-level semantic knowledge from a teacher sparse model to a student model with different query structures or scene representation, through a customized pair-wise discrepancy loss that harmonizes the query structure and decoder output across domains.
- Evaluate the proposed knowledge transfer method on a variety of heterogeneous SPMs and contrast its performance against existing knowledge distillation methods.

CONTROLS: Compare against task-agnostic distillation and task-specific matching techniques, and examine the impact on both teacher and student model performance.

COST: 7200
PREDICTION: Expected result: improved efficiency and effectiveness of knowledge transfer across heterogeneous SPMs; possible failure risk: decreased adaptation capacity of student models due to knowledge loss from teacher models.

PROPOSAL:

- Develop an autonomous driving benchmark for evaluating SPMs, comprising synthetic and real-world datasets, diverse scene and object configurations, and metrics for assessing scene understanding, object detection, and scene parsing performance.
- Introduce a tiered benchmark framework, with multiple tiers that address various aspects of SPM performance, enabling fair and rigorous comparisons across different models, and facilitating adaptation of SPMs to real-world autonomous driving scenarios.
- Utilize the proposed benchmark to evaluate the performance of existing SPMs and assess the impact of pre-training methods, query generation techniques, and knowledge transfer strategies on SPM performance.

CONTROLS: Compare against existing benchmarks for computer vision tasks, ensuring the benchmark's comprehensive evaluation of diverse scene understanding and perception tasks.

COST: 64800
PREDICTION: Expected result: a widely adopted benchmark for SPMs that facilitates fair comparisons and informs development of more accurate and robust models; possible failure risk: the benchmark might not fully capture the complexities and uncertainties of real-world driving scenarios.

IQP can integrate insights from existing tasks and leverage query budgets to simulate a range of sparse perception tasks. This flexible prompting framework will help bridge the gap between recently learned scene representations and downstream sparse perception models.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: QueryAugmented-VELOS: Pre-training Sparse Perception Models with KL-Divergence for 3D Scene Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will pre-train a sparse perception model, such as SparseBEV, on unlabeled multi-view driving data using a novel query-augmented variant of the VELoS pre-training framework, which incorporates KL-divergence minimization to reduce the discrepancy between model predictions and a learned background representation. This pre-training strategy aims to leverage the strengths of VELoS (efficient reconstruction and reduced memory overhead) while addressing the challenges posed by sparse models.
CONTROLS: This proposal will be compared to existing VELoS-based pre-training methods and sparse perception models, specifically DETR3D and SparseBEV, pre-trained using traditional contrastive learning objectives.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to outperform existing methods by striking a better balance between efficiency and accuracy, but pre-training time and computational resources might be limiting factors for large-scale experiments.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Seedbox: Multi-Swarm 3D Scene Reconstruction via Differentiable Rendering and Query-based Refinement
PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel, pretrained module called Seedbox, designed to generate a small set of high-quality seed points in complex 3D scenes. Seedbox combines differentiable rendering (alike that used in UniPAD and ViDAR) with a query-based refinement step (stimulating DETR3D and SparseBEV's sparse aggregation behavior), allowing it to adapt to the unique spatial structure of 3D scenes and guide the refinement of low-resolution volumetric representations towards plausible 3D structures. We will evaluate Seedbox's effectiveness by incorporating it into the pre-training pipeline and assessing its influence on downstream 3D perception tasks.
CONTROLS: This approach will be evaluated using BEV-centric pipelines, such as BEVFormer and Lift-Splat-Shoot, pre-trained using both traditional contrastive learning objectives and our seedbox-enhanced pre-training pipeline.
COST: 1800

Seedbox combines differentiable rendering (alike that used in UniPAD and ViDAR) with a query-based refinement step (stimulating DETR3D and SparseBEV's sparse aggregation behavior), allowing it to adapt to the unique spatial structure of 3D scenes and guide the refinement of low-resolution volumetric representations towards plausible 3D structures. We will evaluate Seedbox's effectiveness by incorporating it into the pre-training pipeline and assessing its influence on downstream 3D perception tasks.
CONTROLS: This approach will be evaluated using BEV-centric pipelines, such as BEVFormer and Lift-Splat-Shoot, pre-trained using both traditional contrastive learning objectives and our seedbox-enhanced pre-training pipeline.
COST: 16200

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Test-Time Adaptation with Meta-Learned Pseudo-Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of incorporating a meta-learning framework for pseudo-label correction into a vision-language detector adapted at test time. Specifically, design a few-shot learning setup where the detector is trained on a labeled source dataset and adapts to an unlabeled target dataset with meta-learning guiding the correction of pseudo-labels generated on the fly. Implement this approach on the GLIP detector and Grounding DINO, using the COCO and Pascal VOC datasets for adaptation across different domains and categories.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard self-training with pseudo-labels and the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: Improved pseudo-label accuracy and overall adaptation performance by 5-10% compared to standard self-training, with the potential for further gains through better meta-learning strategies.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Thresholding for Reliable Pseudo-Labeling in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Develop a dynamic thresholding method that adjusts to the changing quality of pseudo-labels during test-time adaptation. This approach involves a two-stage process: initially, a non-strict threshold is applied to all pseudo-labels to generate an ensemble of initial pseudo-labels; subsequent stages refine the pseudo-labels by adapting the threshold according to the quality and confidence of the pseudo-labels generated so far. Evaluate this method on multiple vision-language detectors (GLIP and Grounding DINO) using several real-world datasets (COCO, PASCAL VOC, and ImageNet).
CONTROLS: Compare against existing methods using fixed confidence thresholds and against the original detector without adaptation.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: Improved pseudo-label accuracy and detection performance for 70-80% of the test samples, reducing the gap between pseudo-label quality and target labels by 10-15% compared to fixed thresholding methods.

TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Distillation for Preserving Pre-trained Generalization in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multimodal knowledge distillation (MKD) to preserve the pre-trained generalization capabilities of vision-language detectors during test-time adaptation. Implement an MKD framework that learns to transfer knowledge from the pre-trained source model to the adapted model while maintaining the latter's ability to detect objects in unseen categories. Evaluate MKD on two vision-language detectors (GLIP and Grounding DINO) across multiple real-world datasets (COCO, PASCAL VOC, and ImageNet) to assess its effectiveness in achieving a balance between adaptation performance and pre-trained knowledge preservation.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard self-training approach without knowledge distillation and against the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance by 10-15% compared to standard self-training and reduced degradation of pre-trained generalization by 20-25%.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Distillation for Preserving Pre-trained Generalization in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Further enhance the MKD framework from Proposal 3 by incorporating a conditional ensemble principal component analysis (CEPCA) step, which adapts the MKD procedure to the specific characteristics of the current test batch. CEPCA involves learning a conditional probability distribution over the Principal Components of the pre-trained model's feature outputs, given the current test batch's pseudo-labels. This distribution is then used to re-project the pre-trained model's feature outputs onto a new, batch-conditioned subspace. Evaluate CEPCA-MKD on GLIP and Grounding DINO for its ability to improve MKD's robustness to test-time domain shifts and variations in object categories.
CONTROLS: Retain comparisons against standard self-training and original models, adding new comparisons against the original MKD formulation and the revised MKD from Proposal 4 (with pseudo-label refinement).
COST: 8100
PREDICTION: CEPCA-MKD yields improved adaptation performance and pre-trained generalization preservation, particularly under challenging test-time adaptation scenarios, by adaptively reconfiguring the MKD process to account for the dynamics of the target data distribution.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select Relevant Features for Test-Time Adaptation in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel feature selection method for vision-language detectors adapted at test time, which learns to assign importance weights to the pre-trained model's features based on their relevance to the current test batch. Inspired by mutual information-based feature selection, this approach involves querying a learned mutual information neural estimator (MINE) to evaluate the relevance of each feature for the identification of pseudo-labels. Filter out irrelevant features based on the estimated importance weights to produce a reduced set of features for the adapted model to utilize, leveraging domain adaptation techniques to learn an optimal mapping from the reduced feature space to the pre-trained feature space. Evaluate this method on GLIP and Grounding DINO, exploiting the COCO and Pascal VOC datasets for adaptation across distinct domains and categories.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard feature selection techniques (e.g., L1 regularization, recursive feature elimination) and against the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 24300
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance by 12-15% compared to standard self-training, resulting from more accurate feature selection and knowledge exploitation from the pre-trained model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Test-Time Adaptation with Meta-Learned Pseudo-Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of incorporating a meta-learning framework for pseudo-label correction into a vision-language detector adapted at test time. Specifically, design a few-shot learning setup where the detector is trained on a labeled source dataset and adapts to an unlabeled target dataset with meta-learning guiding the correction of pseudo-labels generated on the fly. Implement this approach on the GLIP detector and Grounding DINO, using the COCO and Pascal VOC datasets for adaptation across different domains and categories.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard self-training with pseudo-labels and the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: Improved pseudo-label accuracy and overall adaptation performance by 5-10% compared to standard self-training, with the potential for further gains through better meta-learning strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Thresholding for Reliable Pseudo-Labeling in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Develop a dynamic thresholding method that adjusts to the changing quality of pseudo-labels during test-time adaptation. This approach involves a two-stage process: initially, a non-strict threshold is applied to all pseudo-labels to generate an ensemble of initial pseudo-labels; subsequent stages refine the pseudo-labels by adapting the threshold according to the quality and confidence of the pseudo-labels generated so far. Evaluate this method on multiple vision-language detectors (GLIP and Grounding DINO) using several real-world datasets (COCO, PASCAL VOC, and ImageNet).
CONTROLS: Compare against existing methods using fixed confidence thresholds and against the original detector without adaptation.
COST: 8100
PREDICTION: Improved pseudo-label accuracy and detection performance for 70-80% of the test samples, reducing the gap between pseudo-label quality and target labels by 10-15% compared to fixed thresholding methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Distillation for Preserving Pre-trained Generalization in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multimodal knowledge distillation (MKD) to preserve the pre-trained generalization capabilities of vision-language detectors during test-time adaptation. Implement an MKD framework that learns to transfer knowledge from the pre-trained source model to the adapted model while maintaining the latter's ability to detect objects in unseen categories. Evaluate MKD on two vision-language detectors (GLIP and Grounding DINO) across multiple real-world datasets (COCO, PASCAL VOC, and ImageNet) to assess its effectiveness in achieving a balance between adaptation performance and pre-trained knowledge preservation.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard self-training approach without knowledge distillation and against the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance by 10-15% compared to standard self-training and reduced degradation of pre-trained generalization by 20-25%.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Multimodal Knowledge Distillation for Preserving Pre-trained Generalization in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Refine the MKD framework from Proposal 3 by incorporating a novel pseudo-label refinement module, which leverages the adaptive thresholding method from Proposal 2 to improve the quality of pseudo-labels used for MKD. This refinement module can be integrated with either the target-conditional or source-conditional MKD formulations to enhance their performance and robustness. Evaluate the revised MKD framework on GLIP and Grounding DINO for robustness across various adaptation scenarios (e.g., large domain shifts, open-vocabulary detection).
CONTROLS: Retain comparisons against standard self-training and original models, adding new comparisons against the original MKD formulation without pseudo-label refinement.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: Enhanced MKD performance in terms of both adaptation accuracy and pre-trained generalization preservation, with gains in object detection performance due to more accurate pseudo-labels and better alignment of the adapted model's feature distributions with the pre-trained model's.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Multimodal Knowledge Distillation for Preserving Pre-trained Generalization in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Further enhance the MKD framework from Proposal 3 by incorporating a conditional ensemble principal component analysis (CEPCA) step, which adapts the MKD procedure to the specific characteristics of the current test batch. CEPCA involves learning a conditional probability distribution over the Principal Components of the pre-trained model's feature outputs, given the current test batch's pseudo-labels. This distribution is then used to re-project the pre-trained model's feature outputs onto a new, batch-conditioned subspace. Evaluate CEPCA-MKD on GLIP and Grounding DINO for its ability to improve MKD's robustness to test-time domain shifts and variations in object categories.
CONTROLS: Retain comparisons against standard self-training and original models, adding new comparisons against the original MKD formulation and the revised MKD from Proposal 4 (with pseudo-label refinement).
COST: 24300
PREDICTION: CEPCA-MKD yields improved adaptation performance and pre-trained generalization preservation, particularly under challenging test-time adaptation scenarios, by adaptively reconfiguring the MKD process to account for the dynamics of the target data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select Relevant Features for Test-Time Adaptation in Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel feature selection method for vision-language detectors adapted at test time, which learns to assign importance weights to the pre-trained model's features based on their relevance to the current test batch. Inspired by mutual information-based feature selection, this approach involves querying a learned mutual information neural estimator (MINE) to evaluate the relevance of each feature for the identification of pseudo-labels. Filter out irrelevant features based on the estimated importance weights to produce a reduced set of features for the adapted model to utilize, leveraging domain adaptation techniques to learn an optimal mapping from the reduced feature space to the pre-trained feature space. Evaluate this method on GLIP and Grounding DINO, exploiting the COCO and Pascal VOC datasets for adaptation across distinct domains and categories.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard feature selection techniques (e.g., L1 regularization, recursive feature elimination) and against the original GLIP and Grounding DINO models without adaptation.
COST: 72900
PREDICTION: Improved adaptation performance by 12-15% compared to standard self-training, resulting from more accurate feature selection and knowledge exploitation from the pre-trained model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptive Vision-Language Object Detection via Online Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL:  Develop a test-time adaptation method that leverages online meta-learning to adapt a pre-trained vision-language object detector to unseen target domains during inference. During meta-training, we generate a set of tasks that simulate domain shifts by applying random transformations to the input images in a diverse set of source domains. A meta- learner or two stream meta-learner will be employed to update meta-weights, which will be combined with the pre-trained vision-language detector weights to perform few-shot adaptation to the new unseen target domain during test time. This approach will leverage the pre-trained detector's prior knowledge and adapt it quickly to new unseen target domains without accessing any source domain data or statistics.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will include fine-tuning the pre-trained detector on target data, self-supervised learning, and known test-time adaptation methods. We will also evaluate the meta-learner by varying the number of meta-training tasks and adapting to different domain shifts.
COST: 22560
PREDICTION: This method should improve zero-shot adaptation performance by exploiting prior knowledge from pre-trained detectors and adapting to new domains using a few samples, preserving the initial generalization capability in the process. However, its robustness to noisy samples and few-shot adaptation might be limited, requiring further evaluations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce an active pseudo-labeling strategy to selectively generate high-quality pseudo-labels during test-time adaptation, which are used as supervision for adaptation. A probability-based sampling framework is proposed to filter out uncertain pseudo-labels and focus on high-confidence regions for fully exploiting the benefits of pseudo-labeling without being misled by noisy samples. This framework further integrates a sampling ratioAdaBins mechanism to dynamically adjust the sampling ratio according to task difficulty and model uncertainty, balancing between refinement of the generated pseudo-labels and the exploitation of new samples.
CONTROLS: This approach will be compared with standard self-supervised learning methods that use pseudo-labeling with a fixed confidence threshold, with both being compared against traditional test-time adaptation methods that do not use active pseudo-labeling.
COST: 34464
PREDICTION: By leveraging active pseudo-labeling, this method should yield robust and reliable test-time adaptation performance without sacrificing pre-trained model properties, as it relies on high-quality pseudo-labels to update the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Domain-Agnostic Star Distillation for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate incorporating an efficient domain-agnostic Star Distillation mechanism into the existing framework to further improve generalization and adaptability of the pre-trained vision-language detector during test-time adaptation. The proposed approach would facilitate better knowledge transfer between domains to ameliorate the domain discrepancy issue, significantly reducing error propagation when objects encountered by the model are significantly different from those it met during pre-training.
CONTROLS: For test-time adaptation, ablations of the Star Distillation (same domain/ different domain) would be conducted to uncover its effectiveness and interaction with the meta-learning adaptation process. Moreover, training in combination with active pseudo-labeling would investigate progressive knowledge transfer that allows for improved object detection under test-time domain events that have more complex space relationships.
COST: 53600
PREDICTION: The incorporation of efficient domain-agnostic Star Distillation is expected to improve the vision-language detector's ability to adapt to new domains while carrying its prior generalization capacity. However, optimizing the Star Distillation parameter, striking a balance between adaptation to the new target domains and distortion of the pre-learned parameters remains a major challenge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Aware Uncertainty Estimation for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection with Asymmetric Learning
PROPOSAL: Address the challenge of consistently obtaining high-quality pseudo-labels by introducing Task-Aware Uncertainty Estimation (TAUE) and Asymmetric Learning into the test-time object detection adaptation framework. TAUE learns to estimate the uncertainty of predictions across different tasks, enabling the adaptation process to assign more weights to uncertain regions and dynamically balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Meanwhile, Asymmetric Learning focuses on adapting both the confident and uncertain regions separately, which further promotes more efficient and effective adaptation.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted to compare the proposed TAUE method with state-of-the-art test-time adaptation methods and investigate the impact of Asymmetric Learning on adaptation.
COST: 148500
PREDICTION: The proposed TAUE and Asymmetric Learning approach should improve the efficiency and effectiveness of test-time adaptation, especially under challenging conditions with limited target domain samples. However, properly tuning the TAUE module and Asymmetric Learning strategy requires extensive hyperparameter optimization and careful evaluation, which can be computationally expensive.
