ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptive Vision-Language Object Detection via Online Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL:  Develop a test-time adaptation method that leverages online meta-learning to adapt a pre-trained vision-language object detector to unseen target domains during inference. During meta-training, we generate a set of tasks that simulate domain shifts by applying random transformations to the input images in a diverse set of source domains. A meta- learner or two stream meta-learner will be employed to update meta-weights, which will be combined with the pre-trained vision-language detector weights to perform few-shot adaptation to the new unseen target domain during test time. This approach will leverage the pre-trained detector's prior knowledge and adapt it quickly to new unseen target domains without accessing any source domain data or statistics.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will include fine-tuning the pre-trained detector on target data, self-supervised learning, and known test-time adaptation methods. We will also evaluate the meta-learner by varying the number of meta-training tasks and adapting to different domain shifts.
COST: 67680
PREDICTION: This method should improve zero-shot adaptation performance by exploiting prior knowledge from pre-trained detectors and adapting to new domains using a few samples, preserving the initial generalization capability in the process. However, its robustness to noisy samples and few-shot adaptation might be limited, requiring further evaluations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce an active pseudo-labeling strategy to selectively generate high-quality pseudo-labels during test-time adaptation, which are used as supervision for adaptation. A probability-based sampling framework is proposed to filter out uncertain pseudo-labels and focus on high-confidence regions for fully exploiting the benefits of pseudo-labeling without being misled by noisy samples. This framework further integrates a sampling ratioAdaBins mechanism to dynamically adjust the sampling ratio according to task difficulty and model uncertainty, balancing between refinement of the generated pseudo-labels and the exploitation of new samples.
CONTROLS: This approach will be compared with standard self-supervised learning methods that use pseudo-labeling with a fixed confidence threshold, with both being compared against traditional test-time adaptation methods that do not use active pseudo-labeling.
COST: 103440
PREDICTION: By leveraging active pseudo-labeling, this method should yield robust and reliable test-time adaptation performance without sacrificing pre-trained model properties, as it relies on high-quality pseudo-labels to update the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Domain-Agnostic Star Distillation for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate incorporating an efficient domain-agnostic Star Distillation mechanism into the existing framework to further improve generalization and adaptability of the pre-trained vision-language detector during test-time adaptation. The proposed approach would facilitate better knowledge transfer between domains to ameliorate the domain discrepancy issue, significantly reducing error propagation when objects encountered by the model are significantly different from those it met during pre-training.
CONTROLS: For test-time adaptation, ablations of the Star Distillation (same domain/ different domain) would be conducted to uncover its effectiveness and interaction with the meta-learning adaptation process. Moreover, training in combination with active pseudo-labeling would investigate progressive knowledge transfer that allows for improved object detection under test-time domain events that have more complex space relationships.
COST: 161280
PREDICTION: The incorporation of efficient domain-agnostic Star Distillation is expected to improve the vision-language detector's ability to adapt to new domains while carrying its prior generalization capacity. However, optimizing the Star Distillation parameter, striking a balance between adaptation to the new target domains and distortion of the pre-learned parameters remains a major challenge.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Improved Test-Time Adaptive Vision-Language Object Detection via Online Meta-Learning with Curriculum Learning
PROPOSAL: Extend the original Test-Time Adaptive Vision-Language Object Detection via Online Meta-Learning approach and integrate Curriculum Learning to educate the meta-learner to effectively adapt to easy-to-hard domain shifts by introducing a gradual curriculum during training. This will select tasks with gradually increasing difficulty, from simple to challenging tasks, which guides the meta-learner for better adaptation to new unseen target domains during test time. As a result, the proposed approach can adapt to new domains more effectively, especially when there are limited target domain samples.
CONTROLS: For comparison and validation of the proposed Curriculum Learning mechanism, a standard self-supervised learning approach and several test-time adaptation methods without Curriculum Learning will be conducted for contrast.
COST: 204800
PREDICTION: Incorporating Curriculum Learning into the online meta-learning framework should improve the detector's adaptation performance, enabling it to deploy seamlessly in real-time. However, overfitting remains a concern and phenomenological behavior where extension, again, in these conditions, inherently lead in advance in delay of potential developing conditions and aforementioned growth out seems unnoticed, susceptible areas.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain-Agnostic Collaborative Learning for Test-Time Adaptive Vision-Language Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Introduce Domain-Agnostic Collaborative Learning (DACL) into the test-time object detection adaptation framework, enabling knowledge exchange and collaborative updating between different vision-language detectors during adaptation. Specifically, the proposed approach allows detectors to mutually facilitate each other's adaptation to unseen target domains, especially in low-shot scenarios where adaptation is most challenging. This collaborative learning strategy is hypothesized to strengthen the overall adaptability and robustness of the test-time adaptation framework.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Address the challenge of consistently obtaining high-quality pseudo-labels by introducing Task-Aware Uncertainty Estimation (TAUE) and Asymmetric Learning into the test-time object detection adaptation framework. TAUE learns to estimate the uncertainty of predictions across different tasks, enabling the adaptation process to assign more weights to uncertain regions and dynamically balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Meanwhile, Asymmetric Learning focuses on adapting both the confident and uncertain regions separately, which further promotes more efficient and effective adaptation.

TITLE: Investigating Domain-Agnostic Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection Using Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will adapt pre-trained vision-language models such as GLIP and Grounding DINO for offline domain adaptation to different target domains using maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) regularization, with the goal of obtaining a domain-agnostic detector that can be fine-tuned during testing. Specifically, we will pre-train GLIP and Grounding DINO on a large-scale image-text dataset and then use MMD-based offline domain adaptation to adapt them to various target domains. We will evaluate their performance on a set of real-world benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Baseline adapted models without MMD regularization, baseline pre-trained models.

PREDICTION: We expect the MMD-regularized pre-trained models to show improved domain-agnostic detection performance, but they may overfit to the pre-training data and fail to adapt to completely novel domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Adaptation with Implicit Object Priors
PROPOSAL: Design a novel adaptation framework that incorporates implicit object priors learned from a pre-trained vision-language model, allowing it to adapt to target domains without requiring explicit source-target feature alignment or pseudo-labeling. This framework leverages a lightweight secondary branch that selectively refines the pre-trained detector's outputs based on visual and semantic cues extracted from the target images. We hypothesize that this two-branch architecture will enable the model to retain its pre-trained generalization capabilities while adapting to the target domain's nuances.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with baseline self-training methods and a non-adaptive version of the proposed framework, using a fixed adaptation step size and a range of thresholds for selective refinement.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The proposed framework demonstrates improvement in detection performance on the target domain, although the adaptation may still struggle with extreme distribution shifts, and the selective refinement mechanism may require careful tuning to avoid under-refining or over-refining the detector's outputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Pseudo-Label Filter for Reliable Vision-Language Detector Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive pseudo-label filter to address the challenge of obtaining high-quality pseudo-labels in every test batch. The filter employs a dynamic confidence threshold that adjusts itself based on the current batch's pseudo-label distribution, network uncertainty estimates, and the relevance of the pseudo-labels to the target domain. This adaptive approach aims to strike a balance between exploiting informative pseudo-labels and avoiding noisy ones.
CONTROLS: Analysis of filter configurations (e.g., incorporating different uncertainty metrics, using domain-specific perturbations) and ablations to isolate the impact of the adaptive filter.
COST: 82.95
PREDICTION: The adaptive pseudo-label filter significantly improves the reliability of pseudo-labels, especially in scenarios where resources are scarce and high-quality pseudo-labels are difficult to obtain, but may occasionally produce suboptimal results if the filter struggles to adapt to complex pseudo-label distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Adaptation with Implicit Object Priors
PROPOSAL: Design a novel adaptation framework that incorporates implicit object priors learned from a pre-trained vision-language model, allowing it to adapt to target domains without requiring explicit source-target feature alignment or pseudo-labeling. This framework leverages a lightweight secondary branch that selectively refines the pre-trained detector's outputs based on visual and semantic cues extracted from the target images. We hypothesize that this two-branch architecture will enable the model to retain its pre-trained generalization capabilities while adapting to the target domain's nuances.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with baseline self-training methods and a non-adaptive version of the proposed framework, using a fixed adaptation step size and a range of thresholds for selective refinement.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: The proposed framework demonstrates improvement in detection performance on the target domain, although the adaptation may still struggle with extreme distribution shifts, and the selective refinement mechanism may require careful tuning to avoid under-refining or over-refining the detector's outputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Pseudo-Label Filter for Reliable Vision-Language Detector Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive pseudo-label filter to address the challenge of obtaining high-quality pseudo-labels in every test batch. The filter employs a dynamic confidence threshold that adjusts itself based on the current batch's pseudo-label distribution, network uncertainty estimates, and the relevance of the pseudo-labels to the target domain. This adaptive approach aims to strike a balance between exploiting informative pseudo-labels and avoiding noisy ones.
CONTROLS: Analysis of filter configurations (e.g., incorporating different uncertainty metrics, using domain-specific perturbations) and ablations to isolate the impact of the adaptive filter.
COST: 250
PREDICTION: The adaptive pseudo-label filter significantly improves the reliability of pseudo-labels, especially in scenarios where resources are scarce and high-quality pseudo-labels are difficult to obtain, but may occasionally produce suboptimal results if the filter struggles to adapt to complex pseudo-label distributions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Neighborhood-based Concatenation of Contextualized Visual Features
 PROPOSAL: Modify the vision-language detector's feature extraction process using a neighborhood-based concatenation approach. This involves aggregating contextualized image features with a specific radius using a learnable attention mechanism and concatenating them with the corresponding text features. The goal is to capture a more comprehensive visual context that can help the detector adapt to the target domain's peculiarities without requiring explicit pseudo-labeling or alignment.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with a architecture that uses only single-scale features and a baseline model without neighborhood-based concatenation, using real-world datasets like PASCAL VOC and MS COCO.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: The neighborhood-based feature aggregation significantly enhances the detector's ability to adapt to the target domain, but its performance might degrade if the neighborhood radius is too large or too small, and the model may require additional tuning for optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Context-dependent Confidence Threshold Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Enhance the adaptive pseudo-label filter by incorporating a context-dependent confidence threshold adaptation mechanism. This mechanism adjusts the confidence threshold based on the contextualized visual features extracted from the target images, allowing the filter to adapt to diverse visual and semantic cues in the target domain.
CONTROLS: Experiments with different contextualization techniques (e.g., using learned embeddings, global features, or local features) and a baseline without context-dependent adaptation, using a range of real-world adaptation scenarios.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: The context-dependent confidence threshold adaptation significantly improves the reliability and accuracy of the pseudo-labels, but may introduce complexity and require careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradual Adaptation with Exponential Moving Averages
PROPOSAL: Explore a gradual adaptation mechanism that progressively updates the model's parameters using exponential moving averages. This approach aims to mitigate the risk of overfitting to the target domain's noise and adapts to the target distribution in a stable and incremental manner.
CONTROLS: Comparative experiments with a traditional one-shot adaptation approach and a model with fast but unstable adaptation, using real-world datasets with complex distribution shifts and noisy target data.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: The gradual adaptation with exponential moving averages shows promise in providing a stable and effective adaptation process, but its performance may suffer if the model's inertial property causes it to be overly cautious and reluctant to adapt to significant changes in the target domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a curriculum learning approach for test-time adaptation, where the model is presented with a sequence of tasks or samples of increasing difficulty or complexity. This approach aims to enable the model to learn and adapt to the target domain's nuances in a more efficient and effective manner.
CONTROLS: Experiments with different curriculum learning strategies (e.g., difficulty-based, complexity-based) and a baseline without curriculum learning, using a range of real-world adaptation scenarios with varying difficulty levels.
COST: 750
PREDICTION: The curriculum learning approach shows promise in accelerating the adaptation process and improving model performance, but its success may depend on the choice of curriculum learning strategy and the quality of the curriculum.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning-based Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Employ a meta-learning approach to adapt vision-language detectors to new target domains. This involves training a meta-learner that can quickly learn to adjust the detector's parameters for a given target domain, based on a few examples or even no examples.
CONTROLS: Experiments with different meta-learning algorithms (e.g., Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML),-Reinforced Meta-Learning) and a baseline without meta-learning, using a range of synthetic and real-world adaptation scenarios.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The meta-learning-based adaptation approach shows promise in achieving rapid adaptation to new target domains, but its success may depend on the choice of meta-learning algorithm and the availability of adaptation data.

PREDICTION: The ensemble methods show promise in achieving more robust and accurate adaptation results, but their performance may suffer if the individual detectors are poorly adapted or if the ensemble method is over-fitting to the training data.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Confidence-Based Pseudo-Label Filtering for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a series of experiments to study the impact of pseudo-label filtering on the performance of test-time adaptive object detection using a pre-trained vision-language detector. Specifically, we will vary the confidence thresholds applied to pseudo-labels generated on the fly and measure their effects on detection accuracy, adaptation speed, and robustness to noisy samples.
CONTROLS: Faster R-CNN with self-training as a baseline, pseudo-label filtering ablations with fixed and dynamic threshold settings.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect that varying the confidence threshold will lead to trade-offs between detection accuracy and adaptation speed, and that a dynamic threshold setting will yield better results than a fixed one. However, extensive experimentation may reveal the complexity of real-world scenarios and a specific thresholding approach may fail to generalize.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Selective Domain Alignment for Vision-Language Detectors in Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel selective domain alignment approach that identifies and focuses on the most informative features across different domains, thereby reducing the need for extensive domain statistics. Specifically, we will utilize a robust statistical test to measure the similarity between feature distributions in the source and target domains, and selectively align those that are significantly different.
CONTROLS: Alignment of all features as a baseline, no domain alignment as an ablation.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect that selective domain alignment will yield better detection accuracy and adaptation performance compared to baseline methods while also addressing the issue of requiring extensive source domain statistics. However, the test's robustness in determining similar feature distributions might be questioned when real-world datasets are used, requiring further analysis.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Selective Domain Alignment for Vision-Language Detectors in Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to incorporate an additional Inference-guided domain discovery component that dynamically selects the most relevant domains for alignment based on the pre-trained vision-language detector's confidence scores on the test data. This component selects the domains where the detector's confidence is lowest, implying a higher likelihood of domain shift and need for alignment.
CONTROLS: Same as before, with added ablation of domain discovery disabled.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating the inference-guided domain discovery will improve adaptation performance and detection accuracy by focusing on the most problematic domains. However, the added complexity might lead to overfitting on the test data or increased computational overhead.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection with Incomplete Pseudo-Labels
PROPOSAL: We propose a curriculum learning approach that gradually increases the difficulty of test-time adaptation based on the quality and availability of pseudo-labels. Easy samples with high-quality pseudo-labels are prioritized in early iterations, while harder samples with incomplete or noisy pseudo-labels are progressively included as the adaptation process advances.
CONTROLS: No curriculum learning as a baseline, curriculum learning with a fixed schedule as an ablation.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: We expect that our curriculum learning approach will improve detection accuracy and adaptation performance by effectively handling incomplete and noisy pseudo-labels, especially in scenarios where pseudo-label quality is uncertain. However, the design of the curriculum schedule and the choice of difficulty metrics might be domain-dependent, requiring additional experiments to determine the best approach for different datasets.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Explanation-Based Dropout for Robust Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose an explanation-based dropout method that regularly removes and reconstructs pseudo-labels based on the vision-language detector's explanations (e.g., attention maps, feature importance scores) to improve robustness to noisy pseudo-labels and adapt to changing test domains.
CONTROLS: Baseline data augmentation with dropout, explanation-based dropout ablation with minimum and maximum explained variance thresholds.
COST: 3600

However, the choice of explanation thresholds and the frequency of dropout might influence the algorithm's performance on specific datasets, requiring extensive evaluation.

TITLE: Hard Sample Mining and Re-weighting for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hard sample mining and re-weighting approach that identifies and re-weights challenging samples based on their pseudo-label quality and detector uncertainty to improve adaptation efficiency and robustness. This approach reduces overfitting to noise and mis-labeling by prioritizing high-confidence samples.
CONTROLS: Baseline data sampling with equal weights, hard sample mining and re-weighting ablation with uniform weights.

TITLE: Uncertainty-Guided Active Learning for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-guided active learning approach that identifies the most uncertain samples and selects the most informative unlabeled data to directly query human annotators, reducing the need for pseudo-labels and improving adaptation performance in the presence of label noise and domain shift.
CONTROLS: Baseline pseudo-label-based adaptation, uncertainty-guided active learning ablation with fixed number of samples.
COST: 8100

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Euclidean TSP: Critical Scaling Exponent
PROPOSAL: We investigate the scaling of the average performance of a fixed-capacity, trained single-neuron GRU over Euclidean TSP instances with varying edge counts. Our hypothesis is that there exists a critical scaling exponent such that the average performance approaches a smooth function of the number of edges, roughly independent of the exponent's value for sufficiently large edge counts. We train the GRU using backpropagation until convergence on various synthetic TSP instances with a fixed model closeness measure (0.003), measuring its performance across the range of edge counts (5, 20, 100).
CONTROLS: We compare this to the average performance of the GRU when trained with random initialization and various easability parameters (0.5, 1.5).
COST: 31623
PREDICTION: As expected, we anticipate that the average performance of a fixed-capacity single-neuron GRU should smooth out the scaling exponent and approach a consistent trend at around 20-50 edge counts. We hypothesize, however, that we may start to observe noise at even higher edge counts due to a reduced "neighborhood" of neighbor enumerable TSP edge changes, affecting model training over broader ranges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Learning Curve for Nearest Neighbor
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the learning curve for a nearest neighbor model on the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for varying solution space sizes, represented by the number of cities to visit. We'll fix the representation space size at a constant dimensionality. We'll train the nearest neighbor model to solve the TSP on synthetic instances of the problem, observed on a variety of network topologies and edge weights. The goal is to identify any predictable trends in the learning curve as the solution space size increases.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with three baselines: a fixed-size nearest neighbor model with a small capacity, a fixed-size nearest neighbor model with a large capacity, and a model trained to find approximate shortest paths using a greedy construction heuristic (e.g., the nearest neighbor algorithm with a limited neighborhood radius).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a steep initial learning curve (fast decreases in error curve) as the number of cities increases from a small value to moderate value and then it quickly plateau or asymptotically saturate. The error of the model may reach a point of diminishing returns when a particular solution space size is reached. It may ultimately fail when the representation space size becomes too large or when the growing combinatorial complexity overwhelms the fixed capacity of our nearest neighbor model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Independent Scaling Experiments for General Problem Complexity
PROPOSAL: We will develop a theorem to model the learning process when independently scaling the size of the solution space and the representation space, to the square and beyond. For the Euclidean TSP, we'll scale the number of cities (solution space) and the dimensionality of the city locations (representation space) to analyze the effects of both complex scaling individually and together. By leveraging symmetric function approximation capabilities, using given models (e.g. random features and GCNs), this design isolates the additive contribution of increasing complexity to the representation space from that in the solution space. Considering known theoretical bounds of the TSP's solution and efficiency, we'll consider how well it holds up when the given problem complexity reaches the square of the function size.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with the first baseline in (Analyzing the Learning Curve for Nearest Neighbor), exploring the impact of different graph structure and vertex properties (such as cluster number) on our learning objectives.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We anticipate much steeper growth in the number of possible solutions as the dimensionality of the representation space increases, and much softer growth as more cities are added to the solution space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Approximation Algorithms for Comparing Complexities
PROPOSAL: We will develop a new scalable approximation algorithm to compare the complexities of multiple Euclidean TSP instances with varying solution spaces and representation spaces. This algorithm will leverage the strengths of each previous proposal to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between problem complexity and model performance. By using reduced-dimensionality approximations, we'll design a computationally feasible way to compute pairwise Frechet and Wasserstein distances between multiple Euclidean TSP distributions.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approximation algorithm against a naive approach that simply computes distances for each individual distribution and average them. We will also study the convergence rate of our algorithm to the true distances.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect our scalable approximation algorithm to provide a faster and more efficient way to compute distances between complex TSP distributions, which will enable us to analyze and compare the complexities of multiple instances more effectively.

We scale the size of the solution space decoupled from the size of the representation space using a multi-scale TSP setup, where the input graph is partitioned into multiple subgraphs and the model is trained to find all feasible sub-solutions, which are then combined to a full solution. We use a 2D-TSP instance with 14,400 vertices, generated using a Voronoi tessellation, as a synthetic benchmark.
CONTROLS: Control experiments include models with fixed representation size trained on random permutations of the input graph, and models with fixed solution size trained on small input graphs.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: If the scaling laws hold, we expect to observe a smooth trend with the size of the solution space, while the size of the representation space should remain relatively constant. We predict that the performance of the model will degrade smoothly as the solution space grows combinatorially, as it will be forced to explore an exponentially large search space. However, the degradation may start to be more pronounced for extremely large sub-graph sizes, potentially due to the model's inability to maintain coherent representations across disparate regions of the input graph.

TITLE: Influence of Training Dynamics on Solution Space Scaling
PROPOSAL: We investigate whether the learning dynamics of the model influence its performance when scaling the solution space. We propose a gradual solution-space scaling scheme where the model starts with a small sub-problem and iteratively increases the solution space size. We interleave training with an increasing number of iterations, regularizing the model's solutions to be consistent across each sub-problem, and analyze how the selected solutions influence the performance on the growing solution space. We use the same multi-scale TSP setup as in proposal 1.
CONTROLS: We compare our experimental setup with a scheme where the full solution space is trained at once, and another where the model starts with the full solution space but reduces it through an iterative validation loop. 
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: If the project findings confirm that the learning dynamics indeed impact the performance of the scaling law, then we would anticipate significant deviations from the baseline model across varying sub-problem increments, as it either becomes less effective at capturing mean-field relationships or, conversely finds misleading optimals impacting subsequent sub-problems parsed.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revision of Proposal 1: Multiscale TSP with Hierarchical Clustering
PROPOSAL: We modify our initial setup for scaling the solution space and representation space by incorporating hierarchical clustering into the multi-scale TSP scheme. In this modified setup, we group the vertices of the input graph into clusters based on their similarity and perform TSP on each cluster separately. We then combine the solutions found on each cluster to obtain a solution for the entire graph. By doing so, we attempt to reduce the dimensionality of the search space and make it more amenable to neural network optimization. This change allows us to scale the solution space exponentially without drastically increasing the number of nodes in the graph, and maintain coherent representations across disparate cluster regions. We investigate how the behavior of the scaling law changes with the hierarchical clustering step in place.
CONTROLS: We include a control experiment where the hierarchical clustering step is applied but the model is not trained to find solutions on each cluster separately, and another where we use a random clustering partition instead of an optimal one.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: If hierarchical clustering successfully captures the structure of the input graph, then we expect the performance of the model to improve significantly due to reduced dimensionality and an evident structural plan inherent within. Conversely, failure to improve with clustering might suggest that neural networks struggle to find coherent features to place and iterate on as they scale.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dimensionality Increase and Curse of Dimensionality in Representation Space
PROPOSAL: We investigate how the curse of dimensionality affects the growth of the representation space as we scale the size of the problem. We design an experiment where we incrementally add new features to the input data for the TSP task, while keeping the representation size fixed. This will help us understand how the growth of the solution space and the dimensionality of the representation space interact. We use a synthetic dataset where the input features are incremented from 2 to 20 dimensions gradually. We compare the performance of our model in this setting to the performance obtained when the dimensionality is fixed at 20 using a feature learning approach.
CONTROLS: Control experiments include training the model with a fixed representation size on an increased input space dimensionality and contrasting with an output space dimensionality increase, where a fixed input space is attempted.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant decrease in performance due to the curse of dimensionality when model's learned features, fixed size, conflict with input space size growth. Upon expanding dimensions, rather than improving, generalization should degrade and error will accumulate in a discontinuous manner consistent with worsened optimality.

TITLE: Model Capacity and Performance Boundaries
PROPOSAL: We investigate how the performance of the model is affected by its capacity, particularly when trained close to its performance limit. We design an experiment where we incrementally add new parameters to the model while scaling the solution space, and compare its performance to a fixed-size model trained on the same data. PREDICTION: If we observe a performance ceiling as we increase the model capacity, we would anticipate finding a critical value of capacity beyond which the additional parameters do not improve performance. This boundary could be indicative of fundamental limits on the model's ability to express complex relationships between solution variables, setting a lower bound on the achievable performance and highlighting the necessity of efficient closure systems for overcomingSEE limitations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Consistency Evaluation for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a cross-lingual consistency evaluation framework, leveraging pre-trained multilingual language models such as mBART or mT5, can be effective in evaluating the quality of multilingual documents independently of their language. This involves training a shared latent representation space across languages and assessing the consistency of quality judgments across languages using the MMIDsI test set and the web pages in the ClueWeb09 dataset.
CONTROLS: Ablate the use of mBART/mT5 and compare the performance of the cross-lingual framework with existing fine-grained multilingual benchmarks (FineWeb2-HQ, for example).
COST: 120
PREDICTION: This approach shows promise for consistency across languages, but performance may suffer due to the difficulty in capturing language-specific features using a shared latent space; evaluation on a diverse set of languages will be particularly challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Learning for Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Design a distributed federated learning framework to train a multilingual data quality rater across diverse datasets and languages, leveraging parallel processing and decentralized data hosting. This will enable effective data selection strategies without relying on benchmark-derived supervision and promote diversity in the pretraining corpus. A potential baseline is a centralized training setup with the same datasets, and ablation studies will be conducted on the effect of coalition size and participation rate on the selection performance.
CONTROLS: Investigate the impact of differential privacy on the learning process by introducing noise to the gradients shared across clients and measure its effect on the rater's accuracy.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: The federated learning framework significantly outperforms the centralized baseline, but the effect of noise on the gradients may vary depending on the level of participation and datasets involved; convergence may be slower due to communication losses and limited data availability at each client.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment across Languages anddomains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of using transfer learning to adapt a multilingual data quality rater to new languages and domains without requiring retraining from scratch. This involves pre-training the rater on a diverse corpus of English, Spanish, or other domains, and then fine-tuning it on a small target dataset for a new language or domain. Evaluate the quality and consistency of the fine-tuned rater and compare its performance to the task of retraining from scratch using only the target dataset.
CONTROLS: Investigate the impact of the number and diversity of pre-training languages and domains on the adaptation performance and analyze the effect of pre-training on the rater's ability to capture language-specific features.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: Transfer learning demonstrates remarkable potential for adapting quality raters across languages and domains, but may struggle with small or low-quality target datasets and may be less effective for very dissimilar domains, where a retraining approach is needed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Downstream Effects of Improved Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of the proposed multilingual data quality assessment methods on the performance of downstream machine translation and language modeling tasks, using a range of evaluation metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and human evaluation. Evaluate the robustness of the results to different dataset compositions, rater architectures, and fine-tuning strategies. Compare the downstream performance of models trained on data selected using the proposed methods with models trained on the full datasets or using existing heuristic filtering techniques.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of using the proposed data quality assessment methods on the computational resources required for model training and fine-tuning, and analyze the trade-off between model performance and computational efficiency.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The proposed data quality assessment methods significantly improve the downstream performance of machine translation and language modeling tasks, particularly when used in combination with transfer learning, and demonstrate superior performance compared to existing heuristic filtering techniques. However, may require more computational resources and may not generalize well to all languages and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Consistency Evaluation for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a cross-lingual consistency evaluation framework, leveraging pre-trained multilingual language models such as mBART or mT5, can be effective in evaluating the quality of multilingual documents independently of their language. This involves training a shared latent representation space across languages and assessing the consistency of quality judgments across languages using the MMIDsI test set and the web pages in the ClueWeb09 dataset.
CONTROLS: Ablate the use of mBART/mT5 and compare the performance of the cross-lingual framework with existing fine-grained multilingual benchmarks (FineWeb2-HQ, for example).
COST: 360
PREDICTION: This approach shows promise for consistency across languages, but performance may suffer due to the difficulty in capturing language-specific features using a shared latent space; evaluation on a diverse set of languages will be particularly challenging.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Learning for Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Design a distributed federated learning framework to train a multilingual data quality rater across diverse datasets and languages, leveraging parallel processing and decentralized data hosting. This will enable effective data selection strategies without relying on benchmark-derived supervision and promote diversity in the pretraining corpus. A potential baseline is a centralized training setup with the same datasets, and ablation studies will be conducted on the effect of coalition size and participation rate on the selection performance.
CONTROLS: Investigate the impact of differential privacy on the learning process by introducing noise to the gradients shared across clients and measure its effect on the rater's accuracy.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: The federated learning framework significantly outperforms the centralized baseline, but the effect of noise on the gradients may vary depending on the level of participation and datasets involved; convergence may be slower due to communication losses and limited data availability at each client.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Diverse Rater Architectures for Effective Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: REVISE Proposal 1: Cross-Lingual Consistency Evaluation for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment to emphasize the role of diverse architectures for improving quality assessment across languages. Compare the performance of existing models (e.g., mBART, mT5) with cross-lingual transformers, such as XLM-R and LPC-T5, and incorporate techniques like multi-task learning and knowledge distillation to optimize the quality of the rater. Utilize a composite metric (e.g., F1-score on a sample data set) that captures the strengths of each model to determine the most effective approach.
CONTROLS: Investigate the relative importance of different training objectives (perplexity reduction, masked language modeling, and translation tasks) by individually optimizing each objective and analyzing their impact on the quality assessment performance.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: This revised approach garners substantial benefits from diverse architectures, yielding improved quality assessment across languages, but its success might be mainly attributed to specific languages where cross-lingual models thrive; performance might dip when transferring to lesser-studied languages.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Supervised Learning of Multilingual Quality Raters for Web-Scale Pretraining Data
PROPOSAL: To address question 1, we will adapt the DCLM approach to leverage multilingual pretraining data and learn quality indicators alongside the LLM, using supervision from expert-rated data in multiple languages. Specifically, we will pretrain a Transformer-based classifier on a meta-learning task, where the input consists of document pairs drawn from a diverse set of languages and quality judgments from human raters, with the goal of learning a single universal quality estimator that can be applied to pretraining data in any language.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against DCLM's FastText classifier, using the same dataset but without the meta-learning component. Additionally, we will evaluate the performance of the joint LMM quality estimator across a range of synthetic and real-world test sets in multiple languages.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our model-based rater generalizes well to unseen languages, achieving comparable or better performance than DCLM's language-specific raters, particularly when trained on large-scale multilingual pretraining data. However, potential pitfalls include noise in human raters' quality judgments and the risk of overfitting to individual languages within the training set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Model-Based Data Selection on LLM Pretraining for Low-Resource Languages
PROPOSAL: To address question 3 and provide insight into whether selecting pretraining data with a multilingual quality signal leads to better downstream performance, we will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of our multilingual quality rater in a wide range of low-resource languages. We will create a mixed-pretraining setup, where half of the pretraining data is selected based on our rater's quality judgments and the other half is selected randomly. We will then compare the downstream performance (e.g., median Supersense and PropBank tagging accuracy on challenging languages) of two models pre-trained with each setup.
CONTROLS: We will compare our selected-pretraining results against baseline models pre-trained with randomly selected data for each language and both pre-trained with conventional English-centric data (presumably lacking quality judgment).
COST: 1064.94129 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our multilingual quality rater will lead to better downstream performance, especially for challenging languages, but there's a high risk that model pretrained with unselected corpus will unexpectedly utils pre-training biases suggesting high resource languages benefits might stagnate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Hyperparameter Tuning for Multilingual Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: To improve the performance of our multilingual quality estimators, we will develop an adaptive hyperparameter tuning framework that leverages the insights from our previous proposals. Specifically, we will implement a meta-learning approach to adjust the hyperparameters of our quality estimators based on the feedback from the LLM's performance on downstream tasks, enabling more effective and efficient quality estimation for diverse languages.
CONTROLS: We will compare our adaptive hyperparameter tuning approach against a range of baseline hyperparameter settings and meta-learning methods.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our adaptive hyperparameter tuning framework significantly improves the quality estimation performance across languages, leading to better LLM performance on downstream tasks. However, potential challenges include the risk of overfitting to the metadata and the difficulty in balancing model complexity with adaptability.

TITLE: Supervised Learning of Multilingual Quality Raters for Web-Scale Pretraining Data
PROPOSAL: To address question 1, we will adapt the DCLM approach to leverage multilingual pretraining data and learn quality indicators alongside the LLM, using supervision from expert-rated data in multiple languages. Specifically, we will pretrain a Transformer-based classifier on a meta-learning task, where the input consists of document pairs drawn from a diverse set of languages and quality judgments from human raters, with the goal of learning a single universal quality estimator that can be applied to pretraining data in any language.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against DCLM's FastText classifier, using the same dataset but without the meta-learning component. Additionally, we will evaluate the performance of the joint LMM quality estimator across a range of synthetic and real-world test sets in multiple languages.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our model-based rater generalizes well to unseen languages, achieving comparable or better performance than DCLM's language-specific raters, particularly when trained on large-scale multilingual pretraining data. However, potential pitfalls include noise in human raters' quality judgments and the risk of overfitting to individual languages within the training set.

PROPOSAL: To overcome the challenges and costs associated with expert-rater supervision, we will explore unsupervised meta-learning approaches for learning multilingual quality estimators. Specifically, we will examine whether pretraining a meta-learner on multilingual document pairs with diverse quality (e.g., mismatching in writing languages and in style) enables effective quality assessment for samples from the target language without relying on explicit supervision.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Rater Training: Weak Supervision via Web-Scale Curation
PROPOSAL: We compare a novel weak supervision approach to FineWeb2-HQ on multilingual web crawl data.
FineWeb2-MWS trains a multilingual rater using an automatic curation criterion, which highlights information-dense and low-noise samples from web search results, weakly supervising a multilingual language model. This compares to FineWeb2-HQ, which relies on established benchmark datasets as positive supervision.
We define an automatic curation criterion, keyed to relevance and uniqueness, and then adapt a keyphrase extraction approach to indicate high-quality samples within web search results. This produces approximately 2-7% true positives in weak supervision, based on a language-agnostic quality evaluation metric used in FineWeb2-HQ.

COST: 2400
PREDICTION: FineWeb2-MWS results in significant gains in learning effective signal on minority languages and reproduces effectiveness, making it suitable as a web-scale, data-quality filtering component, potentially opening up for appraise cross-lingual pre-training.

TITLE: REVISED TITLE: Avoiding Domain-Adaptation Bias in FineWeb2-MWS: A Hierarchical Data Augmentation Approach

TITLE: Modeling 3D Reflectance Fields with Neural Occupancy Fields
PROPOSAL: We will extend the Neural Occupancy Field (NOF) model of neural spoke shown to model dense 3D scenes to incorporate explicit view-dependent reflectance information. NOFs learn a probability field of an object's occupancy of a pixel in 3D space from multiple views. We will augment this field by predicting a separate probability over 3D normals and diffuse albedo at each point on the surface, allowing for the capture of view-dependent effects like shading and highlights.
CONTROLS: We will compare our NOF-Reflectance to a NOF-only model, a neural spoke model trained on synthetic views with known normals and albedo, and a SOTA model on geometry-only occupancy field.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: This should greatly improve view-dependent appearance capture and potential outperform existing models in our benchmarks, but may struggle for diffuse or uniform objects.

PROPOSAL: We will extend the Neural Occupancy Field (NOF) model of neural spoke shown to model dense 3D scenes to incorporate explicit view-dependent reflectance information. NOFs learn a probability field of an object's occupancy of a pixel in 3D space from multiple views. We will augment this field by predicting a separate probability over 3D normals and diffuse albedo at each point on the surface, allowing for the capture of view-dependent effects like shading and highlights.
CONTROLS: We will compare our NOF-Reflectance to a NOF-only model, a neural spoke model trained on synthetic views with known normals and albedo, and a SOTA model on geometry-only occupancy field.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: This should greatly improve view-dependent appearance capture and potential outperform existing models in our benchmarks, but may struggle for diffuse or uniform objects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Joint 3D Geometry and View-Dependent Appearance Reconstruction with Pixel-Wise Correspondences
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel approach to improve joint 3D geometry and view-dependent appearance reconstruction by incorporating pixel-wise correspondences between images of the same scene taken from different viewpoints. This approach uses the correspondences to transfer surface normal and albedo information between images, allowing the model to leverage information from multiple views to improve its reconstruction quality. We will use a combination of image features and view-dependent distance metrics to establish the correspondences.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to state-of-the-art joint 3D geometry and view-dependent appearance reconstruction models that do not incorporate pixel-wise correspondences, and to a model that incorporates correspondences but does not use view-dependent distance metrics.
COST: 120000
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve the reconstruction quality of joint 3D geometry and view-dependent appearance models, especially for scenes with complex geometry and appearance, but may be challenging to scale to larger scenes with many viewpoints.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Modeling 3D Reflectance Fields with Neural Occupancy Fields
PROPOSAL: We will further extend the Neural Occupancy Field (NOF) model to incorporate a hierarchical prediction mechanism, allowing it to jointly capture geometry and appearance at multiple scales and resolutions. This hierarchical mechanism will use progressively finer scales to capture more detailed features of the scene geometry and appearance, enabling the model to effectively model complex scenes and scenes with large variations in geometry and appearance.
CONTROLS: We will compare the hierarchical NOF to the original NOF model, to a non-hierarchical version of the NOF model that learns geometry and appearance separately, and to a state-of-the-art mesh-based model that captures geometry and appearance in a hierarchical manner but requires significant amounts of pre-processing.
COST: 160000
PREDICTION: This updated NOF model should provide improved reconstruction quality for scenes with complex geometry and appearance, and also reduce the need for data augmentation techniques or very large datasets.

TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Convergence Properties of Joint Geometry and View-Dependent Appearance Models
PROPOSAL: We will provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of our joint geometry and view-dependent appearance models. We will study the conditions under which these models converge to the true geometry and appearance of a scene, and derive bounds on the convergence rate. This analysis will help us understand the fundamental limits of these models and provide a framework for resolving some of the open questions in the field.
CONTROLS: We will compare our convergence bounds to those derived for state-of-the-art models that do not model joint geometry and view-dependent appearance.

PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis should provide valuable insights into the convergence properties of joint geometry and view-dependent appearance models, but may require the derivation of complex mathematical proofs to establish the convergence bounds.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Joint Geometric-Appearance Learning from Multiview RGB Images
PROPOSAL: We experiment with learning a novel 3D representation using a combination of a compact neural occupancy field (NotOcNet) and a view-agnostic appearance encoder (ViT+FoG). The NotOcNet will be trained on synthetically synthesized Manhattan-world datasets like ShapeNet with ground truth occupancy and randomly positioned cameras capturing six different views of each object. In parallel, ViT+FoG will take in multiview images of the same objects, learn per-pixel features with a ViT model, and fuse them through a spatial graph Fourier transform-like module to produce a view-agnostic appearance encoding. We'll then combine the two encodings by showing the NotOcNet latent space alongside the appearance features extracted from the original RGB images using SL Simmons loss. The combined representation should effectively model view-dependent appearance while still capturing geometric variations across objects. 
CONTROLS: NotOcNet trained on a grid-based latent with identical geometry and appearance representations for a baseline comparison; ViT+FoG with a random noise vector added to its latent space, simulating a view-agnostic appearance model; models that use NotOcNet but no appearance encoder. 
COST:  9600
PREDICTION: The joint NotOcNet-ViT+FoG model outperforms baseline models in mesh reconstruction accuracy, preserves high-frequency textural details in the output mesh and has lower intensity artifacts, benefiting from the direct accounting of appearance from the multiview images. Its success may not fully generalize, though, if difficulty arises in exactly capturing  geometrical shape present in the symmetry axis-aligned grid, e.g., if images come from outward viewing angles such those not precisely hitting a grid axis.

TITLE: Hybrid 3D Reconstruction from RGB Images using Point Cloud Completion
PROPOSAL: We propose a hybrid 3D reconstruction method that combines the strengths of point cloud completion (PCC) and image-based 3D reconstruction. Our method, called PC-Net, consists of two stages. In the first stage, we use a point cloud completion network to obtain a sparse point cloud from a set of RGB images. In the second stage, we use a dense 3D reconstruction network to refine the point cloud and obtain a high-fidelity 3D model. We experiment with different combination strategies to fuse the features from both stages, such as concatenation, element-wise addition, and spatial pyramid pooling. We evaluate our method on real-world datasets like ScanNet and compare it with state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline method with only PCC; baseline method with only dense 3D reconstruction; multi-view stereo (MVS) for comparison
COST: 28769.478
PREDICTION: Our hybrid method, PC-Net, shows significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of 3D reconstruction quality and efficiency. The point cloud completion network provides a good initial estimation of the 3D scene, which is then refined by the dense 3D reconstruction network. However, our method may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not perform well on scenes with complex geometry or occlusions.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of 3D Reconstruction Models to Out-of-Distribution Data
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction models to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We propose a new benchmark dataset that includes images from various domains, such as art, architecture, and toys, which are different from the original training datasets. We evaluate the performance of the 3D reconstruction models on this OOD dataset and study how they generalize to unseen environments. We also analyze the feature importance of the models and investigate how the models' robustness correlates with their generalizability.
CONTROLS: Ablation study with different architectures and training protocols; evaluation on in-distribution datasets
COST: 35400
PREDICTION: Our study highlights the limitations of current 3D reconstruction models in generalizing to OOD data. We observe that the models tend to focus on the most informative features, such as textures and shapes, and neglect the background and ذات environment. This lack of robustness is particularly evident in models that use a single-frame approach, whereas models that use multi-frame approaches tend to be more robust. However, this trend may not hold for all OOD datasets, and further investigations are needed to develop robust 3D reconstruction models that generalize well to unseen environments.

TITLE: Qualitative Analysis of 3D Reconstructions using Human Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We propose a qualitative analysis of 3D reconstructions using human evaluation. We design a user study to assess the quality of 3D reconstructions from a human perspective. Participants are asked to evaluate the similarity between the 3D reconstruction and the real-world object, and to identify any errors or inaccuracies in the reconstruction. We investigate how different architectures and training protocols affect the quality of the reconstructions, and how human ratings correlate with quantitative metrics.
CONTROLS: Ablation study with different architectures and training protocols; evaluation on in-distribution datasets
COST: 41312
PREDICTION: Our study highlights the importance of human evaluation in assessing the quality of 3D reconstructions. We observe that human ratings are highly correlated with quantitative metrics, and that architectures and training protocols have a significant impact on the quality of the reconstructions. Furthermore, we identify some limitations of the current 3D reconstruction models, such as the tendency to over-smooth or over-fit, which can lead to errors in the reconstruction. Our study suggests that incorporating human evaluation and feedback into the 3D reconstruction task can lead to more accurate and realistic reconstructions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse Voxel Volumetric Fusion for Joint 3D Geometry-Appearance Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose a model that jointly infers 3D geometry and appearance from a single input image using a sparse voxel representation. The model consists of three main components: a traditional 2D convolutional foundation vision model that predicts multiview images from the input image, a spatial transformer network that re-samples the predicted images to adhere to a sparse voxel grid conforming to the geometry of the object, and a 3D U-Net that fuse information from the re-sampled images with the sparse voxel grid features to predict the texture and material properties of the object. We will optimize the parameters of the model using a chosen real-world benchmark for 3D object reconstruction, specifically the ModelNet dataset.
CONTROLS: We will train a standard 3D U-Net as a baseline for geometry only, using the same ModelNet training split, to evaluate the effectiveness of our joint 3D geometry-appearance model. Additionally, we will perform an ablation study by removing the spatial transformer network to evaluate its contribution to the trained model's performance.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed model to outperform the 3D U-Net baseline in terms of generating realistic 3D objects that capture both geometry and appearance, with a noticeable reduction in view-dependent errors. However, we may struggle with cases that exhibit high-frequency detail in the object's appearance due to the limitations of the sparse voxel representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Grid-based Representations: Optimizing Spatial Resolution and Memory Trade-Off in 3D Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: To better understand the limitations of existing grid-based 3D representations, we will conduct a systematic study to evaluate the effects of varying spatial resolution and memory usage on reconstruction performance. Specifically, we will explore different variants of the occupancy-based signed distance field representation, adjusting the spatial resolution and data type (float16, float32, or float64) to observe their impact on reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. We will benchmark our experiments on a range of real-world datasets, including the online 3D scanning database, showcasing objects ranging from simple household items to intricate sculptures.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our grid-based representation to that of existing geometry-only methods, using the released codebases to implement common variants such asleston *distance-field representation, to ensure a fair comparison. Additionally, we will analyze the performance of the signed distance field representation with respect to grid size and precision.
COST: 10500
PREDICTION: Our analysis will help reveal the optimal trade-offs between spatial resolution and memory usage for grid-based representations, showing the highest performance for certain object categories, and highlighting potential avenues for improvement in current methods. However, the small size of the objects in the online 3D scanning database may not well represent a large and varied set of possible objects, which might lead to inconsistencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Textured 3D Mesh Reconstruction via Prismatic Decomposition and Masked Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for textured 3D mesh reconstruction from a single input image. Inspired by recent advances in prismatic decomposition and masked convolutional networks, our method first uses a prismatic decomposition to identify the structural elements of the object, followed by a masked convolutional network to predict the material properties (color, texture, and normal map) for each element, and finally aggregates these predictions to obtain the complete textured 3D mesh. We will implement a three-stage optimization strategy using the Pix3D and ShapeNet datasets as benchmarks, evaluating the quality of our generated 3D meshes using the IU-HD, ML-HD and CM metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with the prior work, *SmartMeshagger, which also predicts 3D meshes with texture and normals. We will also compare with prior work using examined view point based, which has better prior properties. Additionally, we will examine the effect of choosing the different prismatic decomposition granularities on the performance of our method.
COST: 56000
PREDICTION: Our method is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results on Pix3D and ShapeNet, demonstrating the effectiveness of prismatic decomposition and masked convolutional networks for textured 3D mesh reconstruction. However, it may struggle with scenes bearing high-frequency details in the texture, where prismatic decomposition may fail to capture the variability among the surface features.

PROPOSAL: We propose an unsupervised learning approach to discover 3D part-segments from images, in conjunction with image-to-3D object reconstruction. We evaluate our method on the Pix3D and ShapeNet datasets, considering both quantitative and qualitative metrics.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Joint 3D Geometry-Appearance Inference Models to Real-World Variability
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art joint 3D geometry-appearance inference models to real-world variability in lighting, texture, and viewpoint using a range of real-world datasets (e.g., ModelNet, Pix3D, and real-world scans). We also analyze the robustness of these models to domain shift by comparing their performance on real-world scans versus synthetic data. PREDICTION: Our evaluation will demonstrate the robustness of joint 3D geometry-appearance inference models to real-world variability and domain shift, providing insights into their limitations and potential areas for improvement. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse Voxel Volumetric Fusion for Joint 3D Geometry-Appearance Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose a model that jointly infers 3D geometry and appearance from a single input image using a sparse voxel representation. The model consists of three main components: a traditional 2D convolutional foundation vision model that predicts multiview images from the input image, a spatial transformer network that re-samples the predicted images to adhere to a sparse voxel grid conforming to the geometry of the object, and a 3D U-Net that fuse information from the re-sampled images with the sparse voxel grid features to predict the texture and material properties of the object. We will optimize the parameters of the model using a chosen real-world benchmark for 3D object reconstruction, specifically the ModelNet dataset.
CONTROLS: We will train a standard 3D U-Net as a baseline for geometry only, using the same ModelNet training split, to evaluate the effectiveness of our joint 3D geometry-appearance model. Additionally, we will perform an ablation study by removing the spatial transformer network to evaluate its contribution to the trained model's performance.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed model to outperform the 3D U-Net baseline in terms of generating realistic 3D objects that capture both geometry and appearance, with a noticeable reduction in view-dependent errors. However, we may struggle with cases that exhibit high-frequency detail in the object's appearance due to the limitations of the sparse voxel representation.

TITLE: Evaluation of Grid-based Representations: Optimizing Spatial Resolution and Memory Trade-Off in 3D Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: To better understand the limitations of existing grid-based 3D representations, we will conduct a systematic study to evaluate the effects of varying spatial resolution and memory usage on reconstruction performance. Specifically, we will explore different variants of the occupancy-based signed distance field representation, adjusting the spatial resolution and data type (float16, float32, or float64) to observe their impact on reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. We will benchmark our experiments on a range of real-world datasets, including the online 3D scanning database, showcasing objects ranging from simple household items to intricate sculptures.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our grid-based representation to that of existing geometry-only methods, using the released codebases to implement common variants such asleston *distance-field representation, to ensure a fair comparison. Additionally, we will analyze the performance of the signed distance field representation with respect to grid size and precision.
COST: 31500
PREDICTION: Our analysis will help reveal the optimal trade-offs between spatial resolution and memory usage for grid-based representations, showing the highest performance for certain object categories, and highlighting potential avenues for improvement in current methods. However, the small size of the objects in the online 3D scanning database may not well represent a large and varied set of possible objects, which might lead to inconsistencies.

TITLE: Textured 3D Mesh Reconstruction via Prismatic Decomposition and Masked Convolutional Network
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for textured 3D mesh reconstruction from a single input image. Inspired by recent advances in prismatic decomposition and masked convolutional networks, our method first uses a prismatic decomposition to identify the structural elements of the object, followed by a masked convolutional network to predict the material properties (color, texture, and normal map) for each element, and finally aggregates these predictions to obtain the complete textured 3D mesh. We will implement a three-stage optimization strategy using the Pix3D and ShapeNet datasets as benchmarks, evaluating the quality of our generated 3D meshes using the IU-HD, ML-HD and CM metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method with the prior work, *SmartMeshagger, which also predicts 3D meshes with texture and normals. We will also compare with prior work using examined view point based, which has better prior properties. Additionally, we will examine the effect of choosing the different prismatic decomposition granularities on the performance of our method.

However, it may struggle with scenes bearing high-frequency details in the texture, where prismatic decomposition may fail to capture the variability among the surface features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the use of Point Cloud CNNs on Real-World 3D Data
PROPOSAL: Trained on MPI-INF-3DHP and SHREC'19 datasets, this experiment will employ Point Cloud CNNs to evaluate their effectiveness in learning compact 3D representations that jointly capture geometry and appearance from real-world data. Compared to shape-only representations, we will assess whether Point Cloud CNNs can better preserve view-dependent effects such as reflections and highlights, given a fixed computational budget.
CONTROLS: 1. Classical Point Cloud-based geometry-only representation ( e.g., PointNetClassic); 2. Geometry-only occupancy representation trained with SDF-VAE; and 3. Baseline image-based appearance-only representation
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Point Cloud CNNs have a better capability to capture view-dependent effects than geometry-only representations within the same computation budget; they may, however, underperform compared to geometry+appearance SDF-VAE in reconstruction tasks where appearance is not the primary focus. It could fail, if practices from computer vision give us (already successful) techniques sufficient enough to extract these object-specific materials from given points in this shared-present domain context.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Counterfactual Learning for One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: We will train a one-step generator by learning to minimize the reverse KL-divergence between the generator's output and that of the teacher AR model over many pairs of inputs, where the inputs are pairs of real image and noised image. The noised image is generated by applying a Rademacher distribution on the discrete random variable defined by all the context parameters then filtered by rejection-sampling to maximize the teacher model's decoder likelihood. By maximizing the decoder likelihood of the teacher model of each generation of noised images, we can help the generator avoid converging to spurious local minima.
CONTROLS: Perform the same experiments with unconditional one-step GAN model trained on the same real data; multiscale one-step GAN; query-efficient method (e.g. fuzzing), which produce the same input to the teacher model by repeatedly refining noise under adaptive legal probabilistic client embeddings.
COST: 1512
PREDICTION: This unsupervised approach should offer faster training, if yet less direct, and should have as good or better performance compared to existing state-of-the-art DD1, though ignoring label efficiency may ultimately limit the performance further more than relying on noise-to-data mapping.

TITLE: Randomized Topology for Efficient One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the inherent difficulty of the generator learning an invertible mapping from a fixed latent space to the AR model's token sequence space, we will randomize the topology of the generator network by randomly selecting either traditional feedforward or recurrent connectivity for each layer during training. This randomized topology can facilitate more efficient search for generator weights that match the teacher AR model, and could also confer robustness to individual layers failing during training.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with analogous experiments on the conditional model without random topology; fixed topology; ablation studies for partial randomization (e.g., randomize half the layers).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Counterfactual Learning for One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: We will train a one-step generator by learning to minimize the reverse KL-divergence between the generator's output and that of the teacher AR model over many pairs of inputs, where the inputs are pairs of real image and noised image. The noised image is generated by applying a Rademacher distribution on the discrete random variable defined by all the context parameters then filtered by rejection-sampling to maximize the teacher model's decoder likelihood. By maximizing the decoder likelihood of the teacher model of each generation of noised images, we can help the generator avoid converging to spurious local minima.
CONTROLS: Perform the same experiments with unconditional one-step GAN model trained on the same real data; multiscale one-step GAN; query-efficient method (e.g. fuzzing), which produce the same input to the teacher model by repeatedly refining noise under adaptive legal probabilistic client embeddings.
COST: 4536
PREDICTION: This unsupervised approach should offer faster training, if yet less direct, and should have as good or better performance compared to existing state-of-the-art DD1, though ignoring label efficiency may ultimately limit the performance further more than relying on noise-to-data mapping.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Randomized Topology for Efficient One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the inherent difficulty of the generator learning an invertible mapping from a fixed latent space to the AR model's token sequence space, we will randomize the topology of the generator network by randomly selecting either traditional feedforward or recurrent connectivity for each layer during training. This randomized topology can facilitate more efficient search for generator weights that match the teacher AR model, and could also confer robustness to individual layers failing during training.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with analogous experiments on the conditional model without random topology; fixed topology; ablation studies for partial randomization (e.g., randomize half the layers).
COST: 9013
PREDICTION: This randomized topology should yield a more flexible generator architecture that achieves state-of-the-art one-step sampling without relying on predefined noise-to-data mapping, at least for large enough datasets.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Unsupervised Counterfactual Learning for One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: To improve the diversity and informativeness of the generator's training set, we will replace rejection-sampling with perturb-and-detect; the pair of real image and noised image are split into two separate sets of image-patch pairs first. Then the generator is trained to minimize the reverse KL-divergence between its output and that of the teacher AR model over all image-patch pairs from the real set as the input context, while the noised image set serves as a consistency check for robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with original rejection-sampling method; analysis of perturb-and-detect parameter impact on performance.
COST: 6039
PREDICTION: Improved sampling quality from perturb-and-detect over rejection-sampling could give a boost in generator performance.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: REVISED Unsupervised Counterfactual Learning for One-Step AR Generators
PROPOSAL: To further improve robustness and mitigate mode collapse by leveraging the teacher AR model, we will introduce a secondary loss term that encourages the generator to produce diverse outputs that are equally likely under the teacher AR model's output distribution. Specifically, we will minimize a regularized KL-divergence between the teacher AR model's output distribution over the generator's output and a uniform distribution over the output space.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with original unsupervised counterfactual learning setting; analysis of regularization parameter impact on performance.
COST: 7412
PREDICTION: This additional regularization term should lead to more diverse and representative generator outputs, thereby improving generator robustness and mitigating mode collapse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Variational Autoencoder for One-Step AR Sampling
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency of the generator, we will design a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) that maps an input noise variable drawn from a normal distribution to a probabilistic discrete token sequence that matches the teacher AR model's output distribution. The CVAE will consist of an encoder network that maps the input noise to a probabilistic latent space, and a decoder network that maps the latent space to the probabilistic token sequence.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance with original unsupervised counterfactual learning and randomized topology methods; analysis of CVAE architecture impact on performance.
COST: 13680
PREDICTION: The CVAE-based method could potentially learn a more efficient mapping from noise to token sequence, achieving a better balance between sampling efficiency and quality.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
